(Benefit)

Ibn ʿAqil said in his debate with some of the Muʿtazilites: "You relied, in negating plurality (al-tathniyah), on the argument of mutual prevention (dalil al-tamanuʿ), and this same argument turns back against you regarding the creation of acts, because if we suppose that He, Exalted is He, wills to move a body and the servant wills to keep it still, then it cannot be that... to the end."

The act of God does not fall under the power of the servant, and the act of the servant does not fall under the power of God according to you. So you have no escape at all from this question, so where is your tawhid?!

His saying, ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾. Faith and obedience are among the most excellent of blessings; indeed, they are the most excellent blessings absolutely. They come from Him, Glorified is He, through teaching, guidance, inspiration, enabling success, will, and creation. It is not correct to say that they are merely a command and an explanation, for that is found in relation to disbelievers and disobedient people. Then His blessing upon the most disbelieving of creatures would be like His blessing upon the people of faith, obedience and righteousness among them, since the blessing of explanation and guidance is shared. This is the view of the Qadariyyah (the sect who deny that Allah predestines human acts), and many of them have stated it explicitly. They did not make it a blessing of Allah upon the servant that He wills, creates, and does the act, and enables him when he does it. This is among their statements by which they separated themselves from all the Messengers and Books. They applied this consistently when they did not make it a favor of Allah upon the servant in giving him the reward; rather they said that it is purely his due, over which Allah has no favor. They argued with His saying: ﴿For them is a reward that is never cut off﴾.

They said: that is, not bestowed upon them as a favor, since it is the recompense of their deeds and their wages. They said: favor spoils the blessing and the gift. These people did not leave any room for ignorance of Allah, but they compared His favor to the favor of creatures. They are anthropomorphists (mushabbihah) in acts and negators (mu'attilah) of attributes. In reality, favor belongs to Allah alone. He is the Bestower of favor by His grace, and the people of His heavens and the people of His earth are in His pure favor. Allah says: ﴿They consider it a favor to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has bestowed favor upon you that He guided you to faith, if you are truthful﴾. He also said to His interlocutor Musa: ﴿And We bestowed favor upon you another time﴾. And He said: ﴿And We bestowed favor upon Musa and Harun﴾. And He said: ﴿And We wished to bestow favor upon those who were oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders and make them the inheritors﴾.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Ansar: "Did I not find you astray, and Allah guided you through me? And in need, and Allah enriched you through me?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger are most bountiful (amann)."

The Messengers said to their peoples: ﴿We are only humans like you, but Allah bestows favor upon whom He wills of His servants﴾. So from Him, Glorified and Exalted is He, comes pure beneficence, grace and mercy, and the life of the people of Paradise is not pleasant there except by His favor upon them. For this reason its people said, when some of them turned to others asking one another: ﴿Indeed, we were before among our people fearful. So Allah bestowed favor upon us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾.

So they gave thanks, out of their knowledge of their Lord and of His right over them, that He saved them from the punishment of the scorching wind by His pure favor upon them.

The most knowledgeable of creation about Allah, the most beloved to Him, the nearest to Him, and the most obedient to Him, said: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even me, unless Allah covers me with His mercy and grace."

He also said: "If Allah were to punish the people of His heavens and His earth, He would punish them while not being unjust to them. And if He were to have mercy on them, His mercy to them would be better than their deeds." The first is in the Sahih, and the second is in the Musnad and the Sunan, and al-Hakim and others authenticated it.

So the master of the worlds and of those who work informed us that no one enters Paradise by his deeds. The Qadariyyah say that they enter it by their deeds, so that their bliss is not spoiled by Allah's will; rather that bliss becomes a recompense. The Salaf from among the Companions, the Successors, and those after them did not shoot at the Qadariyyah from one bow except because of the enormity of their innovation and its contradiction to what Allah sent His prophets and messengers with. If the servants brought every act of obedience, and all their breaths were acts of obedience to Allah, they would still be in His pure favor and grace, and the favor would be His upon them. Whenever the obedience of the servant grows, the favor of Allah upon him grows greater. He is the Bestower of favor by His grace. Whoever denies His favor has denied His beneficence.

As for His saying: ﴿For them is a reward that is never cut off﴾, the people of knowledge of Allah, His Messenger and His Book have not disagreed that its meaning is "uncut." From this comes the phrase "rayb al-manun," which means death, because it cuts off life.

(A Weighty Principle)

I have reflected on this matter, and I found its root to be that you know all blessings are from Allah alone: the blessings of acts of obedience and the blessings of pleasures. So you turn to Him, asking Him to inspire you and to enable you to give thanks for them. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah; then when harm touches you, to Him you cry out﴾.

He also says: ﴿So remember the bounties of Allah that you may succeed﴾.

And He says: ﴿And be grateful for the favor of Allah, if it is Him you worship﴾.

Just as those blessings are from Him and are purely of His bounty, remembering them and giving thanks for them is not attained except by His enabling success. Sins come from His abandonment and His leaving His servant, and leaving him between himself and his soul. If He does not uncover that for His servant, there is no way for the servant to uncover it for himself. So he is compelled to humble supplication and pleading to Him that He repel from him its causes, so that they do not proceed from him. And if they occur by the decree of destiny and the requirement of human nature, he is compelled to humble supplication and prayer that He repel from him their necessary consequences and punishments. The servant is never free from his need for these three foundations, and there is no success for him except by them: gratitude, seeking well-being, and sincere repentance.

Then I reflected, and I found that this revolves around desire (raghbah) and fear (rahbah). Neither of them is in the hand of the servant, but in the hand of the Turner of hearts, who directs them however He wills. If He grants His servant success, He turns his heart toward Him and fills it with desire and fear. If He forsakes him, He leaves him to himself, does not turn his heart toward Him, and does not make him ask for that. What Allah wills happens, and what He does not will does not happen.

Then I reflected on whether success and abandonment have a cause, or whether they are by mere will with no cause. Their cause is the suitability or unsuitability of the recipient. He, Glorified, is the Creator of recipients which differ greatly in readiness and acceptance. Inanimate things do not accept what living beings accept, and each of the two kinds differs in acceptance. The rational speaking animal accepts what the brute beast does not accept, and it varies in acceptance to the greatest degree. Likewise the brute beast varies in acceptance, but there is not among one kind the difference that there is among the human species. When the recipient is capable of receiving a blessing, in such a way that it knows the blessing, knows its worth and significance, thanks the Benefactor for it, praises Him for it, magnifies Him for it, and knows that it comes from pure generosity and the very essence of favor, without it deserving it, nor it being its own, nor by itself, but it is Allah's alone and by Him alone, then it makes Him alone the source of its blessing, in sincerity, and directs it in love of Him as thanks. It witnesses in it His pure generosity as favor, recognizes its own deficiency and shortcoming in giving thanks for it as weakness, inability, or negligence, and knows that if He continues it upon him, that is His pure charity and beneficence; and if He strips it from him, he is deserving of that and entitled to it. The more blessings He increases for him, the more he increases in humility, submission, and prostration before Him, standing in His thanks, and fearing that He will strip them from him for failing to fulfill their thanks, just as He stripped His blessing from those who did not know it nor observed its due. If he does not give thanks for His blessing and meets it with the opposite of what is fitting, He will strip it from him without doubt. Allah says: ﴿And thus We tested some of them by means of others, that they might say, "Is it these whom Allah has favored from among us?" Is not Allah most knowing of the grateful?﴾

They are those who knew the worth of the blessing, accepted it, loved it, praised the Benefactor for it, loved Him, and stood in His thanks. Allah says: ﴿And when a sign comes to them, they say, "We will never believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of Allah." Allah knows best where to place His message.﴾

(A Principle)

The foundation of all good is that you know that what Allah wills happens, and what He does not will does not happen. Be certain then that good deeds are from His blessing, so you thank Him for them and humbly ask Him not to cut them off from you. And know that evil deeds are from His abandonment and punishment, so you plead with Him to come between you and them, and not to leave you to yourself in doing good and abandoning evil.

The knowers have agreed that every good has its root in Allah's enabling success for the servant, and every evil has its root in His abandoning His servant.

They also agreed that success is that Allah does not leave you to yourself, and abandonment is that He leaves you between yourself and yourself. If every good has its root in success, which is in the hand of Allah and not in the hand of the servant, then its key is supplication, need, sincere seeking of refuge, and desire and fear directed toward Him. Whenever He gives the servant this key, He has intended to open for him; and whenever He misguides him away from the key, the door of good remains locked before him.

The Commander of the Faithful Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "I do not carry the concern of being answered, but the concern of supplication. When I am inspired to supplicate, the answer comes with it." Upon the servant's measure of resolve, aspiration, will, desire, and fear in that, the success and aid of Allah, Glorified, are established. So the help of Allah descends upon the servants according to the measure of their resolve, steadfastness, desire, and fear.

Abandonment descends upon them according to the same measure. Allah, Glorified, is the Most Wise of judges and the Most Knowing of the knowers. He places success in its fitting places, and abandonment in its fitting places. He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.

[Section: The Evil Effects of Sins]

Among them: the sin of one person brings its harm upon other people and animals as well, so he and others are burned by the evil consequences of sins and wrongdoing.

Abu Hurayrah said: "Indeed, the houbara bustard dies in its nest because of the oppression of the oppressor."

Mujahid said: "Indeed, the beasts curse the disobedient among the children of Adam when the drought becomes severe and the rain is withheld, and they say: 'This is because of the sin of the son of Adam.'"

Ikrimah said: "The creatures of the earth and its insects, even the beetles and the scorpions, say: 'We have been denied rain because of the sins of the children of Adam.'"

So the sinner is not satisfied with the punishment for his sin, until he is cursed by those who have no sin.

[Milk]

God Almighty says: ﴿And indeed there is a lesson for you in livestock: We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, from between digestive contents and blood, pure milk, palatable to those who drink it.﴾ [al-Nahl: 66]

And He says about Paradise: ﴿In it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste never changes.﴾ [Muhammad: 15].

In the "Sunan," it is related with a raised (marfu') report: "Whoever God feeds food, let him say: 'O God, bless us in it and provide us with something better than it. And whoever God gives milk to drink, let him say: O God, bless us in it and increase us from it, for I know of nothing that suffices in place of food and drink except milk.'"

Milk, although it appears simple to the senses, is naturally composed in its original creation of three natural substances: the cheesy (al-jubnnah), the buttery (al-samniyyah), and the watery (al-maiyyah). The cheesy is cold and moist, nourishing to the body; the buttery is moderate in heat and moisture, suitable for a healthy human body, and abundant in benefits; the watery is hot and moist, loosening the natural constitution and moistening the body. Milk in general is colder and moister than what is moderate.

It is said: its strength at the time of milking is heat and moisture. It is also said that it is moderate in heat and cold.

Milk is at its best the moment it is milked, and then its quality continues to decline over the passage of hours, so that at the time of milking it is less cold and more moist, while sour milk is the reverse. Milk is preferred forty days after birth. Its best quality is when its whiteness is intense, its smell is pleasant, its taste is delicious, it has a slight sweetness and moderate richness, its consistency is balanced between thinness and thickness, and it is milked from a young, healthy animal of moderate flesh, grazing and drinking in good places.

It is praiseworthy: it produces good blood, moistens the dry body, nourishes well, and benefits from whisperings (waswas), sorrow, and melancholic diseases. When drunk with honey, it cleanses internal ulcers of corrupt humors, and drinking it with sugar greatly improves the complexion. Fresh milk counteracts the harm of intercourse, suits the chest and lungs, and is good for those with consumption (al-sull); it is harmful to the head, stomach, liver and spleen, and excessive consumption harms the teeth and gums, so one should rinse the mouth with water after it. In the "Two Sahihs" it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) drank milk, then asked for water and rinsed his mouth, and said: "It has fattiness (dasam)."

It is harmful for those with fever and headache, harmful to the brain and to a weak head, and constant use of it causes dimness of sight and cataracts, joint pain, blockage of the liver, and bloating of the stomach and intestines; its remedy is honey and preserved ginger or the like. All of this applies to one who is not accustomed to it.

(Section)

Reflect on the lesson that God Almighty mentioned regarding livestock, and what He gives us to drink from their bellies: pure milk, pleasant, wholesome and easy to digest, emerging from between digestive contents and blood. Consider how the food descends from their mouths into the stomach, and some of it turns into blood by God's leave, which flows in their veins, organs, fats and flesh. When the veins send it along their channels to all parts of the body, each organ, sinew, cartilage, hair, nail and hoof transforms it into its own nature. Then the blood remains in those reservoirs that belong to it, since by it the animal's existence is sustained. Then its heavier residue settles into the paunch and becomes dung, and what remains transforms into pure white milk, palatable to those who drink it, emerging from between the digestive contents and the blood. Thus, when a sheep or other animal is milked to exhaustion, blood tinged with redness would come out if it were not for God, glorified be He, who separates the finest part from the residue by the first cooking, so it passes to the liver and becomes blood, mixed with the four humors. God, the Mighty and Majestic, then sends each humor to its proper place and reservoir prepared for it: the gall bladder, the spleen and the kidney. The remaining pure blood enters the hepatic veins, and from those vessels it is directed to the udder, where God, blessed and exalted, changes it from the form, nature and taste of blood into the form, nature and taste of milk. So it is extracted from between digestive contents and blood. Ask then the denier who disbelieves: who arranged this arrangement, decreed this measure, perfected this craft, and made this subtlety so refined, other than the Subtle, the All-Aware?

**Subtle point: on the difference between saying *kull min kull al-thamarat* and *kull min al-thamarat kulliha***

If it is said: when the two constructions are equivalent, as in your saying *kull min kull al-thamarat* and *kull min al-thamarat kulliha*, why is one arrangement specific to the Qur'an in one place and not in another?

The answer: this does not follow, because each of them is eloquent. Yet there must be a benefit in the specific choice. As for His saying, ﴿Then We brought forth by it fruits of every kind﴾, the *min* (from) here expresses the kind (*li-bayan al-jins*), not partition (*li-l-tab'id*), and the prepositional phrase stands in the position of the object, not the position of an adverb of place. What is intended is the fruits themselves, except that something was extracted from them, and *min* was introduced to express the whole kind. Had He said *akhrajna bihi min al-thamarat kulliha* ("We brought forth by it from the fruits, all of them"), the mind would have thought that the prepositional phrase was in the position of an adverb, and that the object of *akhrajna* comes after it. That would not have been suspected with *kull* placed first, because the addressees know that when *kull* precedes, it implies encompassing the whole kind, and when it follows as an emphasizing element (*tawkid*), it implies encompassing only the emphasized noun, whether it is a general kind or a known, specific thing.

As for His saying, ﴿Then eat of every kind of fruit﴾, and He did not say *min al-thamarat kulliha*, there is in it the same wisdom as in the preceding verse, and an additional benefit. Before it, in the arrangement, He had said, ﴿And of the fruits of the date-palms and the grapes﴾. Had He said after it *kuli min al-thamarat kulliha*, the mind would have gone to the fruits mentioned before this, namely "the fruits of the date-palms and the grapes," because the definite article (*al*) refers to what is already known. Thus beginning with *kull* is more protective of the meaning, more comprehensive of the kind, further from ambiguity, and more elegant in arrangement. So reflect on it.

**[Section: Explanation that there is healing in honey for people]**

People have differed concerning His saying, ﴿There issues from their bellies a drink, varying in its colours, wherein is healing for mankind﴾ [al-Nahl: 69]: does the pronoun in *fihi* ("in it") refer to the drink, or does it refer to the Qur'an? There are two opinions.

The correct opinion is that it refers to the drink. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, and most scholars. It is because the drink is what is mentioned, and the discourse was brought for its sake, while there is no mention of the Qur'an in the verse. The authentic hadith, his saying, "Allah has spoken the truth" (*sadaqa Allah*), is virtually explicit in this. And Allah knows best.

**[Section: Reflecting on the states of the bee and the signs and lessons in them]**

Look at the bee, at its diligence in making honey, and at its building of hexagonal cells, which are among the most perfect of shapes, most beautiful in roundness, and most firm in construction. When some of them are joined to others, there is no gap or flaw between them. All of this is done without a measure, without a tool, and without a compass. This is from the effect of Allah's creation, His inspiration to them, and His revelation to them, as He said, ﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee: "Take for yourselves dwellings in the mountains..."﴾ up to His words, ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought﴾.

Then reflect on the bee's perfect obedience and its good compliance with the command of its Lord. It takes its dwellings in three places: in the mountain crevices, in trees, and in the houses of people, where they build trellises (*ya'rishun*), meaning they build the roofs (*'urush*), which are the houses. So no dwelling of the bee is seen other than these three, absolutely.

Reflect also on how most of its dwellings are in the mountains and crevices, which is the first dwelling mentioned in the verse. Then in trees, which are among its most common dwellings. And what people build, the bee has the fewest of its dwellings among them. As for the mountains and trees, they have great dwellings from which a very large amount of honey is taken.

Reflect on how good obedience led it to first take dwellings. When a dwelling is settled for it, it goes out from it, grazes, and eats from the fruits, then returns to its dwellings. This is because its Lord, glory be to Him, commanded it to take dwellings first and then to eat after that. Then when it has eaten, it follows the paths of its Lord, made smooth, with nothing difficult upon it. It grazes, then returns.

Among the marvels of its condition is that it has a leader called *al-yaʿsub* (the drone-king). Its going out, its return, its work, and its pasture are not complete without him. It obeys his command, listens to him, and obeys him. He has over it obligation, command, and prohibition. It is his subjects, submitting to his command and following his opinion. He manages them as a king manages the affairs of his subjects. So much so that when they return to their dwellings, he stands at the entrance of the house and does not let one of them crowd another, nor precede it in passing. Rather, they pass into their dwellings one after another, without crowding, collision, or pile-up, as a commander does when he reaches with his army a narrow crossing, through which only one may pass at a time.

Whoever reflects on their conditions, their governance, their guidance, the unity of their gathering, the orderliness of their affairs, the management of their kingdom, and the assignment of each task to one of them, will be astonished at them with the utmost wonder. He will know that this is not within their capacity, nor from their own essence. These are firm works, perfected to the utmost of firmness and precision. When you look at the one who performs them, you see that he is among the weakest of Allah's creatures, the most ignorant of himself and his own condition, and the least able to attend to his own welfare, let alone to the marvellous matters that come from him.

Among the wonders of their condition is that they have two leaders who do not come together in one dwelling, nor do they command a single group. When two groups of them and two leaders gather, they kill one of the two leaders, cut him off, and agree upon the one remaining leader, without any enmity among them or harm of some toward others. Rather, they become one hand and one army.

**[Section]**

Among the most wondrous of their affairs is what most people do not perceive or recognize: their offspring (*nitaj*), whether it occurs through birth and reproduction or through transformation (*istihalah*). Few know this or notice it. Their offspring is not in either of these two ways. Rather, their offspring occurs by a matter among the most wondrous wonders. When they go to pasture, they take those pure particles upon the leaves, from roses, flowers, grass, and other things, which is the dew (*tall*), and they suck it, and that is the material of honey. Then they press the gathered particles on the surface of the leaf and bind them on their legs like a lentil, and they fill the empty hexagons with honey. Then their leader stands at his dwelling, beginning from it, and he blows into it. Then he circles those dwellings, house by house, and blows into all of them. Life stirs in them by the permission of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. They move, and they come out as birds by the permission of Allah. This is one of the signs and wonders, of which few are aware. All of this is from the fruit of that divine inspiration, which conferred upon them and provided them with this management, travel, livelihood, building, and offspring. So ask the one who denies (the Creator): who revealed to them their affair, and placed in their nature what He placed?

And who made their paths easy for them, smooth and submissive, not resistant to them, not difficult for them, and not lost to them despite their distance?

And who guided them to their business? And who sent down for them from the dew that which, when they gather it, they return as pure honey, varying in its colours, in the utmost sweetness, delight, and benefit? Among it is white, in which a face is seen more clearly than in a mirror. Tell me, who brought it and said, "This is the finest of what people know of honey, the purest, and the best"? When one tastes it, it is the most delicious of sweets. And among it are red, green, rose-coloured, black, and yellowish-white and other colours and flavours, varying according to its pastures and materials.

When you reflect on the benefits and healing in it, and its entry into most medicines, to the point that the earlier scholars did not know sugar, and it is not mentioned in their books at all, and what they used in medicines was honey. And it is mentioned in the books of those people. By the life of Allah, it is more beneficial than sugar, more effective, more clearing of the humours, more suppressive of them, more removing of their harm, stronger for the stomach, more exhilarating to the soul, strengthening to the spirits, facilitating the medicine, and helping it to draw out the disease from the depths of the body. For this reason, nothing in the hadith ever mentions sugar, nor did they know it at all. If it were absent from the world, they would not need it. If honey were absent, the need for it would be intense. Sugar came to dominate some cities, to the point that they abandoned honey, considered sugar more pleasant than it, and saw it as less sharp and less hot. They did not know that among the benefits of honey is that very sharpness and heat. When it does not suit the one who uses it, its counteraction breaks it, and it becomes more beneficial to him than sugar.

We will, if Allah wills, devote a treatise in which we will show the superiority of honey over sugar through many ways that cannot be refuted and numerous proofs that cannot be repelled. Whenever you see sugar clearing phlegm, dissolving a humour, or curing a disease, that is only its effect in helping the medicine reach the veins, because of its fineness and sweetness.

As for the healing that comes from honey, Allah has deprived many people of it, to the point that they disparage it and fear its harm because of its heat and sharpness. There is no doubt that its being a healing, and the Qur'an being a healing, and prayer being a healing, and the remembrance of Allah and turning to Him being a healing, is a matter that does not apply to all temperaments and souls. This Book of Allah is the beneficial healing, and it is the greatest healing. Yet how few are those who seek healing by it! Rather, it does not increase corrupt temperaments in corruption, nor does it increase the wrongdoers except in loss.

Likewise, the remembrance of Allah, turning to Him, repentance to Him, and resorting to prayer: how many a sick person has been cured by it, how many an ill person has been restored to health by it, and how much it has taken the place of many medicines, which do not come close to its effect in healing. And you see many people, indeed most of them, who have no share of healing through it at all.

I have seen in some books of Muslim physicians, in the mention of single-ingredient medicines, the mention of prayer under the letter *sad* (ṣ), and they mention, among its benefits for the body that bring about healing, numerous aspects, and among its benefits for the spirit and the heart.

I heard our shaykh Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, say when some pain befell him, and a physician said to him, "The most harmful thing for you is speech about knowledge, thinking about it, focusing on it, and remembrance." He said, "Do you not claim that when the soul is strengthened and gladdened, its joy gives it a power by which nature is aided in repelling the affliction, for it is its enemy, and when it prevails over it, it overcomes it?" The physician said, "Yes." He said, "When my soul occupies itself with focus, remembrance, and speech about knowledge, and attains what is difficult for it of that, it rejoices in it and is strengthened, and that causes the removal of the affliction, or something like this from speech."

The point is that the neglect of many people in seeking healing by honey does not remove it from being a healing, just as the neglect of most of them in seeking healing by the Qur'an for diseases of the hearts does not remove it from being a healing for them. It is a healing for what is in the breasts, even if most of the sick do not seek healing by it, as He said, ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord, and a healing for what is in the breasts, and a guidance and mercy for the believers﴾.

So He encompassed it with admonition and healing, and specified it with guidance and knowledge. It is itself a healing, whether one seeks healing by it or not. Allah has described in His Book only the Qur'an and honey as healing. These two are the two healings. This is the healing of hearts from the diseases of their error and misguidance, and the ailments of their doubts and desires. And that is the healing of bodies from many of their illnesses, humours, and afflictions.

During my stay in Makkah, various ailments befell me, with no physician there and no medicines as there were in other cities. So I sought healing with honey and Zamzam water, and I saw in them a marvellous healing. Reflect on His report, glory and exalted be He, about the Qur'an, that it is itself a healing. And about honey He said, ﴿wherein is healing for mankind﴾. Yet what is itself a healing is more eloquent than what has been made to contain a healing. This is not the place to exhaust the benefits and advantages of honey.

**[Another section]**

The matter of the bee in its guidance is among the greatest wonders. For it has a leader and manager, the *yaʿsub*, who is larger in body than all the bees and better in colour and shape. The female bees give birth in the spring, and most of their offspring are female. If a male enters among them, they do not leave him among them, but either drive him away or kill him, except for a small group who remain around the king. The male does no work and earns nothing. Then the mothers and their young gather around the king, and he goes out with them to pasture in the meadows, gardens, orchards, and pastures by the most direct and nearest paths, and they gather their sufficiency. Then the king returns with them. When they reach the hives, he stands at its door and lets no male or foreign bee enter it. When they have completely entered, he enters after them. The bees settle in their seats and places. The king begins the work as if teaching it to them. The bees take up the work and hasten to it, and the king leaves the work and sits aside where he can see the bees. The bees begin to produce wax from the gummy substance of leaves and flowers. Then the bees divide into groups. One group remains with the king and never leaves him, does no work, and earns nothing; they are the king's retinue of males. Another group prepares and shapes the wax, which is the residue of honey and has a sweetness like that of figs. The bees take great care of it, more than of honey. They clean it, purify it, and free it from what mixes with it of their excrement and other things. Another group builds the cells. Another group carries water and bears it on their backs. Another group sweeps the hives and cleans them of filth, carcasses, and dung. If they see among them a lazy, contemptible bee, they cut it off and kill it, so that it does not corrupt the rest of the workers and infect them with its idleness and baseness. The first thing built in the hive is the king's seat and dwelling. A square chamber resembling a bed or throne is built for him, on which he sits. Around him gather a group of bees resembling the commanders, servants, and courtiers, who never leave him. They place before him something like a basin, into which they pour the purest honey they can produce, and they fill it. This becomes food for the king and his courtiers. Then they begin building the cells in equal rows, as if they were streets and quarters. Their cells are hexagonal, with equal sides, as if they had read Euclid's book, so that they knew the shapes best suited for their cells, because what is required in building dwellings is strength and spaciousness, and the hexagonal shape, above all other shapes, when some of its shapes are joined together, becomes a rounded shape like the roundness of a millstone. No gap or flaw remains in it, and it binds itself together until it becomes one firm layer, into which not even the heads of needles can enter between its cells. Blessed is He who inspired them to build their cells in this firm construction, which human beings cannot match. So they knew that they needed to build their cells from shapes described by two qualities. The first: their corners should not be narrow, so that no narrow space is left idle. The second: these cells should be shaped in such a way that when some are joined to others and the open ground is filled with them, nothing is left wasted. Then they knew that the shape described by these two qualities is the hexagon alone. For triangles and squares, although the ground may be filled with them, their corners are narrow. As for other shapes, although their corners are wide, the ground is not filled with them, but spaces that are empty and wasted remain between them. The hexagon alone is described by these two qualities. So He, glory be to Him, guided them to build their cells in this shape, without a ruler, without a tool, and without a model to follow. And the most skilled of the children of Adam cannot build a hexagonal house except with great machines. Blessed is He who guided them to follow the paths of their pastures, with their strength and their weakness, made smooth for them, not resistant to them, and not lost to them, and to gather the best and finest of what is in the pasture, and to return to their empty dwellings and pour into them a drink of varying colours. (*wherein is healing for mankind; surely in that is a sign for a people who give thought*)

When I have finished building the hives, I go out, lean and hungry, wandering over plains and mountains. I feed on the sweetness raised up on the heads of flowers and the leaves of trees, and then I return full. God, glory be to Him, placed in their mouths a heat that ripens what they have gathered, turning it into sweetness and maturity. Then they regurgitate it into the hives. When the hives are full, they seal their openings with refined wax. When those hives are full, they make for another place, if they find one, build hives there, and do as they did with the first hives.

When the air turns cold, the pasture fails, and they are prevented from gathering, they remain in their hives and feed on the honey they have stored. In the days of gathering and striving, they go out in the morning and wander through the pastures, and each group carries out the work assigned to it. When evening comes, they return to their hives. When it is time for them to return, one of them stands guard at the entrance of the hive, with assistants. Every bee that wants to enter is sniffed and examined by the guard. If he finds an offensive smell on her, or sees on her a smear of filth, he prevents her from entering and sets her aside to one side until all the others have entered. Then he returns to those set aside and barred from entering, examines them, and checks their condition a second time. Whoever he finds has touched something foul or unclean, he cuts in two; and whoever's offence is light, he leaves outside the hive. This is the guard's practice every evening.

As for the king, he rarely leaves the hive, only occasionally, when he desires to take a walk. He goes out with the amirs of the bees and their attendants, and he roams the meadows, gardens and orchards for an hour of the day, then returns to his place. Among the wonders of his condition: he may be harmed by the bees, or by the owner of the hive, or by his attendants, and then he becomes angry, leaves the hive, and withdraws far from it, and all the bees follow him, leaving the hive empty. When the owner sees this and fears that the bees will take the hive and go off with it to another place, he devises a way to recover it and seeks the king's contentment. He locates the place to which the king has gone by means of the bees, recognising it by the gathering of the bees around him, for they do not leave him and cluster about him until they become a single bunch. When he goes out in anger, he sits on a raised place on the tree, and the bees circle around him and gather to him until he becomes like a ball. The owner of the bees takes a spear or a long reed, ties on its head a bundle of pleasant-smelling, fragrant, clean plants, and brings it near the king's place. With him are either a lute, a flute, or some instrument of music, which he plays while that grass is brought close to the king. He keeps doing this until the king is pleased. When he is pleased and his anger subsides, he leaps and lands on the bundle, and his attendants and all the bees follow him. The owner carries him to the hive, and he descends and enters it with his soldiers. The bees do not settle on carrion, an animal, or food.

Among the wonders of their nature: they kill tyrannical, corrupt kings, and they do not submit to their obedience. The small bees with compact bodies are the workers, and they strive to fight the tall ones of little benefit, expelling them and banishing them from the hives. When they do this, the honey becomes good. They strive to kill whatever they wish to kill outside the hive, in order to protect the hive from its carcass. There is among them a kind that is of little benefit and large in body, and there is war between it and the workers: it targets them and ambushes them, opens its hives to them, and seeks their destruction. The workers are highly alert and cautious against it. When it attacks them in their hives, they confront it and force it toward the hive doorways, where it becomes smeared with honey and is unable to fly; and the long-lived glutton does not escape them. When the war ends and the fighting subsides, they return to the dead, carry them, and cast them outside the hive.

We have mentioned that the king does not come out except on occasion, and when he does, he comes out with a host of young and mature bees. When he intends to go out, he remains for a day or two beforehand, instructing the young, placing them in their proper stations and arranging them. Then he goes out and they go out with him, in an order and system that he has arranged for them, and they do not depart from it. When male bees are born in his presence, he recognises that they seek the kingship, so he appoints each of them over a group of young bees. No king among them kills another king, because that would bring corruption and destruction upon the subjects and scatter them. When the owner of the hive sees that the kings have multiplied in the hive and fears that the bees will be scattered because of them, he devises a plan against them and takes all the kings except one. He keeps the remaining ones in a vessel and leaves enough honey with the bees to suffice them. Then, if the appointed king suffers an illness or death, or becomes corrupt and the bees kill him, he takes one of those confined and places him in his stead, lest the bees be left without a king and their affairs scatter.

Among the wonders of their nature: when the king goes out for recreation with the amirs and soldiers, he may be overcome by weariness, and then the young bees carry him. Among the bees are noble, industrious workers, possessed of striving, resolve and diligence; and among them are base, lazy ones of little benefit, who prefer idleness. The noble ones constantly drive them out and banish them from the hive, and do not share the hive with them, out of fear that they will infect the noble ones and corrupt them. The bee is among the most refined and purest of animals, and therefore it does not drop its dung except when it flies, and it dislikes stench and foul odours. Its young and its offspring are more vigilant and more diligent than the adults, sting less, and produce better honey; and their sting, when they sting, does less harm than the sting of the adults.

Since the bee is among the most beneficial and blessed of animals, it has been singled out by the inspiration and guidance of the Lord, exalted is He, in a way that no other creature shares. Since what issues from its bellies is a substance of healing from illnesses, and a light that shines in darkness, like the guides among mankind, most animals are its enemies, and its enemies are among the least beneficial and blessed of animals. This is the way of God with His creation, and He is the All-Mighty, the All-Wise.

**Subtle point: on the difference between saying *kull min kull al-thamarat* and *kull min al-thamarat kulliha***

If it is said: when the two constructions are equivalent, as in your saying *kull min kull al-thamarat* and *kull min al-thamarat kulliha*, why is one arrangement specific to the Qur'an in one place and not in another?

The answer: this does not follow, because each of them is eloquent. Yet there must be a benefit in the specific choice. As for His saying, ﴿Then We brought forth by it fruits of every kind﴾, the *min* (from) here expresses the kind (*li-bayan al-jins*), not partition (*li-l-tab'id*), and the prepositional phrase stands in the position of the object, not the position of an adverb of place. What is intended is the fruits themselves, except that something was extracted from them, and *min* was introduced to express the whole kind. Had He said *akhrajna bihi min al-thamarat kulliha* ("We brought forth by it from the fruits, all of them"), the mind would have thought that the prepositional phrase was in the position of an adverb, and that the object of *akhrajna* comes after it. That would not have been suspected with *kull* placed first, because the addressees know that when *kull* precedes, it implies encompassing the whole kind, and when it follows as an emphasizing element (*tawkid*), it implies encompassing only the emphasized noun, whether it is a general kind or a known, specific thing.

As for His saying, ﴿Then eat of every kind of fruit﴾, and He did not say *min al-thamarat kulliha*, there is in it the same wisdom as in the preceding verse, and an additional benefit. Before it, in the arrangement, He had said, ﴿And of the fruits of the date-palms and the grapes﴾. Had He said after it *kuli min al-thamarat kulliha*, the mind would have gone to the fruits mentioned before this, namely "the fruits of the date-palms and the grapes," because the definite article (*al*) refers to what is already known. Thus beginning with *kull* is more protective of the meaning, more comprehensive of the kind, further from ambiguity, and more elegant in arrangement. So reflect on it.

**[Section: Explanation that there is healing in honey for people]**

People have differed concerning His saying, ﴿There issues from their bellies a drink, varying in its colours, wherein is healing for mankind﴾ [al-Nahl: 69]: does the pronoun in *fihi* ("in it") refer to the drink, or does it refer to the Qur'an? There are two opinions.

The correct opinion is that it refers to the drink. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, and most scholars. It is because the drink is what is mentioned, and the discourse was brought for its sake, while there is no mention of the Qur'an in the verse. The authentic hadith, his saying, "Allah has spoken the truth" (*sadaqa Allah*), is virtually explicit in this. And Allah knows best.

**[Section: Reflecting on the states of the bee and the signs and lessons in them]**

Look at the bee, at its diligence in making honey, and at its building of hexagonal cells, which are among the most perfect of shapes, most beautiful in roundness, and most firm in construction. When some of them are joined to others, there is no gap or flaw between them. All of this is done without a measure, without a tool, and without a compass. This is from the effect of Allah's creation, His inspiration to them, and His revelation to them, as He said, ﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee: "Take for yourselves dwellings in the mountains..."﴾ up to His words, ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought﴾.

Then reflect on the bee's perfect obedience and its good compliance with the command of its Lord. It takes its dwellings in three places: in the mountain crevices, in trees, and in the houses of people, where they build trellises (*ya'rishun*), meaning they build the roofs (*'urush*), which are the houses. So no dwelling of the bee is seen other than these three, absolutely.

Reflect also on how most of its dwellings are in the mountains and crevices, which is the first dwelling mentioned in the verse. Then in trees, which are among its most common dwellings. And what people build, the bee has the fewest of its dwellings among them. As for the mountains and trees, they have great dwellings from which a very large amount of honey is taken.

Reflect on how good obedience led it to first take dwellings. When a dwelling is settled for it, it goes out from it, grazes, and eats from the fruits, then returns to its dwellings. This is because its Lord, glory be to Him, commanded it to take dwellings first and then to eat after that. Then when it has eaten, it follows the paths of its Lord, made smooth, with nothing difficult upon it. It grazes, then returns.

Among the marvels of its condition is that it has a leader called *al-yaʿsub* (the drone-king). Its going out, its return, its work, and its pasture are not complete without him. It obeys his command, listens to him, and obeys him. He has over it obligation, command, and prohibition. It is his subjects, submitting to his command and following his opinion. He manages them as a king manages the affairs of his subjects. So much so that when they return to their dwellings, he stands at the entrance of the house and does not let one of them crowd another, nor precede it in passing. Rather, they pass into their dwellings one after another, without crowding, collision, or pile-up, as a commander does when he reaches with his army a narrow crossing, through which only one may pass at a time.

Whoever reflects on their conditions, their governance, their guidance, the unity of their gathering, the orderliness of their affairs, the management of their kingdom, and the assignment of each task to one of them, will be astonished at them with the utmost wonder. He will know that this is not within their capacity, nor from their own essence. These are firm works, perfected to the utmost of firmness and precision. When you look at the one who performs them, you see that he is among the weakest of Allah's creatures, the most ignorant of himself and his own condition, and the least able to attend to his own welfare, let alone to the marvellous matters that come from him.

Among the wonders of their condition is that they have two leaders who do not come together in one dwelling, nor do they command a single group. When two groups of them and two leaders gather, they kill one of the two leaders, cut him off, and agree upon the one remaining leader, without any enmity among them or harm of some toward others. Rather, they become one hand and one army.

**[Section]**

Among the most wondrous of their affairs is what most people do not perceive or recognize: their offspring (*nitaj*), whether it occurs through birth and reproduction or through transformation (*istihalah*). Few know this or notice it. Their offspring is not in either of these two ways. Rather, their offspring occurs by a matter among the most wondrous wonders. When they go to pasture, they take those pure particles upon the leaves, from roses, flowers, grass, and other things, which is the dew (*tall*), and they suck it, and that is the material of honey. Then they press the gathered particles on the surface of the leaf and bind them on their legs like a lentil, and they fill the empty hexagons with honey. Then their leader stands at his dwelling, beginning from it, and he blows into it. Then he circles those dwellings, house by house, and blows into all of them. Life stirs in them by the permission of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. They move, and they come out as birds by the permission of Allah. This is one of the signs and wonders, of which few are aware. All of this is from the fruit of that divine inspiration, which conferred upon them and provided them with this management, travel, livelihood, building, and offspring. So ask the one who denies (the Creator): who revealed to them their affair, and placed in their nature what He placed?

And who made their paths easy for them, smooth and submissive, not resistant to them, not difficult for them, and not lost to them despite their distance?

And who guided them to their business? And who sent down for them from the dew that which, when they gather it, they return as pure honey, varying in its colours, in the utmost sweetness, delight, and benefit? Among it is white, in which a face is seen more clearly than in a mirror. Tell me, who brought it and said, "This is the finest of what people know of honey, the purest, and the best"? When one tastes it, it is the most delicious of sweets. And among it are red, green, rose-coloured, black, and yellowish-white and other colours and flavours, varying according to its pastures and materials.

When you reflect on the benefits and healing in it, and its entry into most medicines, to the point that the earlier scholars did not know sugar, and it is not mentioned in their books at all, and what they used in medicines was honey. And it is mentioned in the books of those people. By the life of Allah, it is more beneficial than sugar, more effective, more clearing of the humours, more suppressive of them, more removing of their harm, stronger for the stomach, more exhilarating to the soul, strengthening to the spirits, facilitating the medicine, and helping it to draw out the disease from the depths of the body. For this reason, nothing in the hadith ever mentions sugar, nor did they know it at all. If it were absent from the world, they would not need it. If honey were absent, the need for it would be intense. Sugar came to dominate some cities, to the point that they abandoned honey, considered sugar more pleasant than it, and saw it as less sharp and less hot. They did not know that among the benefits of honey is that very sharpness and heat. When it does not suit the one who uses it, its counteraction breaks it, and it becomes more beneficial to him than sugar.

We will, if Allah wills, devote a treatise in which we will show the superiority of honey over sugar through many ways that cannot be refuted and numerous proofs that cannot be repelled. Whenever you see sugar clearing phlegm, dissolving a humour, or curing a disease, that is only its effect in helping the medicine reach the veins, because of its fineness and sweetness.

As for the healing that comes from honey, Allah has deprived many people of it, to the point that they disparage it and fear its harm because of its heat and sharpness. There is no doubt that its being a healing, and the Qur'an being a healing, and prayer being a healing, and the remembrance of Allah and turning to Him being a healing, is a matter that does not apply to all temperaments and souls. This Book of Allah is the beneficial healing, and it is the greatest healing. Yet how few are those who seek healing by it! Rather, it does not increase corrupt temperaments in corruption, nor does it increase the wrongdoers except in loss.

Likewise, the remembrance of Allah, turning to Him, repentance to Him, and resorting to prayer: how many a sick person has been cured by it, how many an ill person has been restored to health by it, and how much it has taken the place of many medicines, which do not come close to its effect in healing. And you see many people, indeed most of them, who have no share of healing through it at all.

I have seen in some books of Muslim physicians, in the mention of single-ingredient medicines, the mention of prayer under the letter *sad* (ṣ), and they mention, among its benefits for the body that bring about healing, numerous aspects, and among its benefits for the spirit and the heart.

I heard our shaykh Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, say when some pain befell him, and a physician said to him, "The most harmful thing for you is speech about knowledge, thinking about it, focusing on it, and remembrance." He said, "Do you not claim that when the soul is strengthened and gladdened, its joy gives it a power by which nature is aided in repelling the affliction, for it is its enemy, and when it prevails over it, it overcomes it?" The physician said, "Yes." He said, "When my soul occupies itself with focus, remembrance, and speech about knowledge, and attains what is difficult for it of that, it rejoices in it and is strengthened, and that causes the removal of the affliction, or something like this from speech."

The point is that the neglect of many people in seeking healing by honey does not remove it from being a healing, just as the neglect of most of them in seeking healing by the Qur'an for diseases of the hearts does not remove it from being a healing for them. It is a healing for what is in the breasts, even if most of the sick do not seek healing by it, as He said, ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord, and a healing for what is in the breasts, and a guidance and mercy for the believers﴾.

So He encompassed it with admonition and healing, and specified it with guidance and knowledge. It is itself a healing, whether one seeks healing by it or not. Allah has described in His Book only the Qur'an and honey as healing. These two are the two healings. This is the healing of hearts from the diseases of their error and misguidance, and the ailments of their doubts and desires. And that is the healing of bodies from many of their illnesses, humours, and afflictions.

During my stay in Makkah, various ailments befell me, with no physician there and no medicines as there were in other cities. So I sought healing with honey and Zamzam water, and I saw in them a marvellous healing. Reflect on His report, glory and exalted be He, about the Qur'an, that it is itself a healing. And about honey He said, ﴿wherein is healing for mankind﴾. Yet what is itself a healing is more eloquent than what has been made to contain a healing. This is not the place to exhaust the benefits and advantages of honey.

**[Another section]**

The matter of the bee in its guidance is among the greatest wonders. For it has a leader and manager, the *yaʿsub*, who is larger in body than all the bees and better in colour and shape. The female bees give birth in the spring, and most of their offspring are female. If a male enters among them, they do not leave him among them, but either drive him away or kill him, except for a small group who remain around the king. The male does no work and earns nothing. Then the mothers and their young gather around the king, and he goes out with them to pasture in the meadows, gardens, orchards, and pastures by the most direct and nearest paths, and they gather their sufficiency. Then the king returns with them. When they reach the hives, he stands at its door and lets no male or foreign bee enter it. When they have completely entered, he enters after them. The bees settle in their seats and places. The king begins the work as if teaching it to them. The bees take up the work and hasten to it, and the king leaves the work and sits aside where he can see the bees. The bees begin to produce wax from the gummy substance of leaves and flowers. Then the bees divide into groups. One group remains with the king and never leaves him, does no work, and earns nothing; they are the king's retinue of males. Another group prepares and shapes the wax, which is the residue of honey and has a sweetness like that of figs. The bees take great care of it, more than of honey. They clean it, purify it, and free it from what mixes with it of their excrement and other things. Another group builds the cells. Another group carries water and bears it on their backs. Another group sweeps the hives and cleans them of filth, carcasses, and dung. If they see among them a lazy, contemptible bee, they cut it off and kill it, so that it does not corrupt the rest of the workers and infect them with its idleness and baseness. The first thing built in the hive is the king's seat and dwelling. A square chamber resembling a bed or throne is built for him, on which he sits. Around him gather a group of bees resembling the commanders, servants, and courtiers, who never leave him. They place before him something like a basin, into which they pour the purest honey they can produce, and they fill it. This becomes food for the king and his courtiers. Then they begin building the cells in equal rows, as if they were streets and quarters. Their cells are hexagonal, with equal sides, as if they had read Euclid's book, so that they knew the shapes best suited for their cells, because what is required in building dwellings is strength and spaciousness, and the hexagonal shape, above all other shapes, when some of its shapes are joined together, becomes a rounded shape like the roundness of a millstone. No gap or flaw remains in it, and it binds itself together until it becomes one firm layer, into which not even the heads of needles can enter between its cells. Blessed is He who inspired them to build their cells in this firm construction, which human beings cannot match. So they knew that they needed to build their cells from shapes described by two qualities. The first: their corners should not be narrow, so that no narrow space is left idle. The second: these cells should be shaped in such a way that when some are joined to others and the open ground is filled with them, nothing is left wasted. Then they knew that the shape described by these two qualities is the hexagon alone. For triangles and squares, although the ground may be filled with them, their corners are narrow. As for other shapes, although their corners are wide, the ground is not filled with them, but spaces that are empty and wasted remain between them. The hexagon alone is described by these two qualities. So He, glory be to Him, guided them to build their cells in this shape, without a ruler, without a tool, and without a model to follow. And the most skilled of the children of Adam cannot build a hexagonal house except with great machines. Blessed is He who guided them to follow the paths of their pastures, with their strength and their weakness, made smooth for them, not resistant to them, and not lost to them, and to gather the best and finest of what is in the pasture, and to return to their empty dwellings and pour into them a drink of varying colours. (*wherein is healing for mankind; surely in that is a sign for a people who give thought*)

When I have finished building the hives, I go out, lean and hungry, wandering over plains and mountains. I feed on the sweetness raised up on the heads of flowers and the leaves of trees, and then I return full. God, glory be to Him, placed in their mouths a heat that ripens what they have gathered, turning it into sweetness and maturity. Then they regurgitate it into the hives. When the hives are full, they seal their openings with refined wax. When those hives are full, they make for another place, if they find one, build hives there, and do as they did with the first hives.

When the air turns cold, the pasture fails, and they are prevented from gathering, they remain in their hives and feed on the honey they have stored. In the days of gathering and striving, they go out in the morning and wander through the pastures, and each group carries out the work assigned to it. When evening comes, they return to their hives. When it is time for them to return, one of them stands guard at the entrance of the hive, with assistants. Every bee that wants to enter is sniffed and examined by the guard. If he finds an offensive smell on her, or sees on her a smear of filth, he prevents her from entering and sets her aside to one side until all the others have entered. Then he returns to those set aside and barred from entering, examines them, and checks their condition a second time. Whoever he finds has touched something foul or unclean, he cuts in two; and whoever's offence is light, he leaves outside the hive. This is the guard's practice every evening.

As for the king, he rarely leaves the hive, only occasionally, when he desires to take a walk. He goes out with the amirs of the bees and their attendants, and he roams the meadows, gardens and orchards for an hour of the day, then returns to his place. Among the wonders of his condition: he may be harmed by the bees, or by the owner of the hive, or by his attendants, and then he becomes angry, leaves the hive, and withdraws far from it, and all the bees follow him, leaving the hive empty. When the owner sees this and fears that the bees will take the hive and go off with it to another place, he devises a way to recover it and seeks the king's contentment. He locates the place to which the king has gone by means of the bees, recognising it by the gathering of the bees around him, for they do not leave him and cluster about him until they become a single bunch. When he goes out in anger, he sits on a raised place on the tree, and the bees circle around him and gather to him until he becomes like a ball. The owner of the bees takes a spear or a long reed, ties on its head a bundle of pleasant-smelling, fragrant, clean plants, and brings it near the king's place. With him are either a lute, a flute, or some instrument of music, which he plays while that grass is brought close to the king. He keeps doing this until the king is pleased. When he is pleased and his anger subsides, he leaps and lands on the bundle, and his attendants and all the bees follow him. The owner carries him to the hive, and he descends and enters it with his soldiers. The bees do not settle on carrion, an animal, or food.

Among the wonders of their nature: they kill tyrannical, corrupt kings, and they do not submit to their obedience. The small bees with compact bodies are the workers, and they strive to fight the tall ones of little benefit, expelling them and banishing them from the hives. When they do this, the honey becomes good. They strive to kill whatever they wish to kill outside the hive, in order to protect the hive from its carcass. There is among them a kind that is of little benefit and large in body, and there is war between it and the workers: it targets them and ambushes them, opens its hives to them, and seeks their destruction. The workers are highly alert and cautious against it. When it attacks them in their hives, they confront it and force it toward the hive doorways, where it becomes smeared with honey and is unable to fly; and the long-lived glutton does not escape them. When the war ends and the fighting subsides, they return to the dead, carry them, and cast them outside the hive.

We have mentioned that the king does not come out except on occasion, and when he does, he comes out with a host of young and mature bees. When he intends to go out, he remains for a day or two beforehand, instructing the young, placing them in their proper stations and arranging them. Then he goes out and they go out with him, in an order and system that he has arranged for them, and they do not depart from it. When male bees are born in his presence, he recognises that they seek the kingship, so he appoints each of them over a group of young bees. No king among them kills another king, because that would bring corruption and destruction upon the subjects and scatter them. When the owner of the hive sees that the kings have multiplied in the hive and fears that the bees will be scattered because of them, he devises a plan against them and takes all the kings except one. He keeps the remaining ones in a vessel and leaves enough honey with the bees to suffice them. Then, if the appointed king suffers an illness or death, or becomes corrupt and the bees kill him, he takes one of those confined and places him in his stead, lest the bees be left without a king and their affairs scatter.

Among the wonders of their nature: when the king goes out for recreation with the amirs and soldiers, he may be overcome by weariness, and then the young bees carry him. Among the bees are noble, industrious workers, possessed of striving, resolve and diligence; and among them are base, lazy ones of little benefit, who prefer idleness. The noble ones constantly drive them out and banish them from the hive, and do not share the hive with them, out of fear that they will infect the noble ones and corrupt them. The bee is among the most refined and purest of animals, and therefore it does not drop its dung except when it flies, and it dislikes stench and foul odours. Its young and its offspring are more vigilant and more diligent than the adults, sting less, and produce better honey; and their sting, when they sting, does less harm than the sting of the adults.

Since the bee is among the most beneficial and blessed of animals, it has been singled out by the inspiration and guidance of the Lord, exalted is He, in a way that no other creature shares. Since what issues from its bellies is a substance of healing from illnesses, and a light that shines in darkness, like the guides among mankind, most animals are its enemies, and its enemies are among the least beneficial and blessed of animals. This is the way of God with His creation, and He is the All-Mighty, the All-Wise.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 16, verse 73–74:

Regarding His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which possesses for them no provision from the heavens and the earth at all﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: that "shay'an" (anything) is a substitute (badal) for "rizqan" (provision), and "rizqan" is more explicit than "shay'an" because it is more specific, and the more specific is clearer than the more general. This is permissible because of the preceding negation, since an indefinite noun (nakirah) conveys its meaning when it is predicated after a negation. So when the negation implied a general meaning, the general term mentioned, which is the most indefinite of indefinite nouns, and the benefit was achieved through the negation, it became suitable to be a substitute for "rizq." Do you not see that if you dropped the first noun and confined yourself to the second, the sentence would not be deficient?

The second opinion: that "shay'an" here is the object (maf'ul) of the verbal noun "al-rizq," and its implied sense is: they do not possess the ability to provide anything. This is the view of most scholars, except that it is objected to them that "al-rizq" here is a noun (ism), not a verbal noun (masdar), because it follows the pattern of "al-dhabh" (the slaughter) and "al-tahn" (the grinding), meaning the thing slaughtered and the thing ground. Had the verbal noun been intended, it would have come with a fatha, as in the statement of the poet addressing Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him and pardon him:

"Aim for good and do not hold back, and provide for the dependents of the Muslims their provision."

This may be answered by saying that "al-rizq" is among the verbal nouns that come in the pattern "fi'l" with an initial kasra, like "al-fisq," and it is applied to both the verbal noun and the noun with one form. This is like "al-naskh" for both the act of abrogating and the thing abrogated, and its category. This answer is the better one. As for the verse of poetry, we do not concede that its "ra'" is fatha; rather it is kasra, and this is what suits the condition of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and the poet, for he asked him to provide for the dependents of the Muslims with the provision of Allah, which is the wealth that is provided, not that he would provide them in the manner of Allah's provision, which is the verbal noun. This is not something that anyone sensible would address to someone or intend. And Allah knows best.
