The Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 16, verses 75–76:

It means: if a male slave who owns nothing and has no power over anything is not equal to a free man of wealth whom Allah has given provision and who spends from what Allah has given him, then how can you make the idol, which is in a worse state than this slave, a partner of Allah?

Likewise, if two men are not equal in your view: one of them is mute, who neither understands nor speaks, and is moreover powerless, unable to do anything, while the other is upon a straight path in his words and deeds, commanding justice and acting upon it, because he is on a ﴿straight path﴾, then how can you equate Allah with the idol in worship?!

Similar examples are abundant in the Qur'an and in the hadith, such as his (ﷺ) saying in the hadith of al-Harith al-Ash'ari:

"Allah has commanded you to worship Him and not to associate anything with Him. The likeness of one who associates others with Allah is like a man who bought a slave with his own pure wealth and said to him, 'Work and pay me,' but the slave worked and paid to someone else. Which of you would like his slave to be like that?" So Allah, glorified is He, is not to be given the likenesses in which He and His creation share, neither by equating nor by comparison. Rather, what is applied to His right is ﴿qiyas al-awla﴾ (analogy from what is more fitting), as has been explained earlier.

(Benefit)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not set up similitudes for Allah. Indeed, Allah knows, and you do not know﴾

They said: whoever contemplates this verse with true contemplation will realize that it is a clear text nullifying and prohibiting ﴿qiyas﴾ (analogical reasoning). This is because all qiyas is the setting forth of likenesses for the religion, and the comparison of what has no text with what has a text. Whoever makes a likeness of what Allah has not stated as prohibited or obligatory, by what He has prohibited or made obligatory, has set up similitudes for Allah. Had He, glorified is He, known that what He was silent about is like what He stated, He would have informed us of it, and He would not have neglected it, glorified is He: ﴿And your Lord is not forgetful﴾ [Maryam: 64]. And He would have clarified for us what we should guard against, as He informed about Himself when He said, glorified is He: ﴿And Allah would never send astray a people after He had guided them until He has made clear to them what they should avoid﴾ [al-Tawbah: 115].

When He left it to our opinions and our analogies, which contradict one another, one person analogizes what he holds to what he claims is its counterpart, then his opponent comes and analogizes the opposite of his analogy in every respect, and presents a common attribute (al-wasf al-jami') like what his opponents presented or more apparent than it. It is impossible that both analogies come from Allah, while neither is preferable to the other. So they are not from Him. This alone is sufficient to nullify qiyas.

(Section)

These two examples contain two analogies of the ﴿qiyas al-'aks﴾ (reverse analogy), which is the negation of a ruling because its cause and its effect are negated. Qiyas is of two kinds: ﴿qiyas al-tard﴾ (direct analogy), which requires establishing the ruling in the branch (furu') because the cause of the origin (asl) is established in it; and ﴿qiyas al-'aks﴾, which requires negating the ruling from the branch because the cause of the ruling is negated in it.

So the first example is what Allah, glorified is He, set forth for Himself and for the idols. Allah, glorified is He, is the Owner of everything; He spends as He wills upon His servants, secretly and openly, by night and by day. His hand is full, and it is not diminished by constant expenditure, night and day. The idols are owned, powerless, and unable to do anything. So how do they make them partners to Me and worship them besides Me, with this great disparity and manifest difference?

This is the statement of Mujahid and others. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a likeness Allah set forth for the believer and the disbeliever. The believer's likeness is in the good that is with him; then Allah gave him good provision from it, and he spends from it on himself and others, secretly and openly. The disbeliever is like a powerless slave who has no power over anything, because there is no good with him. Would the two men be equal in the sight of any intelligent person? The first statement is closer to the intended meaning, for it is more manifest in nullifying shirk, clearer to the one addressed, greater in establishing proof, and closer in connection with His saying: ﴿And they worship besides Allah what does not possess for them any provision from the heavens and the earth at all, nor are they able﴾ [al-Nahl: 73], ﴿So do not set up similitudes for Allah. Indeed, Allah knows, and you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 74]. Then He said: ﴿Allah presents an example of a slave owned, who has no power over anything﴾ [al-Nahl: 75]. Among the necessary implications and rulings of this likeness is that the monotheist believer is like one to whom He has given good provision, and the disbelieving associator is like the owned slave who has no power over anything. So this is what the likeness indicates and points to. Ibn 'Abbas mentioned it as an alert to its intended meaning, not that the verse is restricted to it. So reflect on it, for you will find it frequent in the words of Ibn 'Abbas and others among the early generations (salaf) in understanding the Qur'an. One may think that this is the meaning of the verse, while it has no other meaning, so one reports his statement.

(Section)

As for the second example, it is a likeness Allah, glorified and exalted is He, set forth for Himself and also for what is worshipped besides Him. The idol worshipped besides Him is like a man who is mute, who neither understands nor speaks; rather, he is mute of heart and tongue, having lost both inner and outward speech. Moreover, he is powerless and cannot do anything at all. Furthermore, wherever you send him, he does not bring you any good, and he does not fulfill any need for you. Allah, glorified is He, is Living, Powerful, Speaking, commanding justice, and He is the Straight Path. This is a description of Him with the utmost perfection and praise. His commanding justice, which is the truth, includes that He, glorified is He, is knowing of it, teaching it, pleased with it, commanding His servants to it, loving its people, and not commanding anything other than it. Rather, He is exalted above its opposite, which is oppression, injustice, foolishness, and falsehood. Indeed, His command and His legislation are entirely justice, and the people of justice are His allies and beloved ones, and they are those who will be near Him on His right side upon pulpits of light. His commanding justice encompasses both the legislative, religious command and the decreed, existential command, and both are justice in which there is no injustice in any way, as in the authentic hadith: "O Allah, I am Your servant, son of Your servant, son of Your maidservant. My forelock is in Your hand, Your judgment over me is executed, Your decree concerning me is just." So His decree is His existential command.

When He wills a thing, His command is only to say to it "Be," and it is. So He commands only with truth and justice, and His decree and destiny that stands by it are truth and justice. Even if the thing decreed and destined contains what is oppression and injustice, the decree is other than the thing decreed, and the destiny is other than the thing destined. Then He, glorified is He, informed that He is upon a straight path. This is similar to the saying of His Messenger [Hud]: ﴿Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ [Hud: 56]. So His saying ﴿there is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ is similar to His saying "My forelock is in Your hand," and His saying ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ is similar to His saying "Your judgment is just."

The first is His dominion, and the second is His praise. He, glorified is He, has dominion and has praise. His being upon a straight path requires that He says only the truth, commands only justice, and does only what is benefit, mercy, wisdom, and justice. So He is upon the truth in His words and deeds. He does not judge a servant in a way that would be unjust to him, nor does He seize him for other than his sin, nor does He diminish any of his good deeds, nor does He burden him with the sins of others which he did not commit nor was the cause of, nor does He hold anyone accountable for the sin of another, nor does He ever do what is not praiseworthy, nor for which He is not praised, and in which there are not praiseworthy outcomes and desired ends for Him. For His being upon a straight path rejects all of that.

Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: His saying ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ [Hud: 56] means: indeed my Lord is on the path of truth, rewarding the one who does good among His creatures for his goodness and the one who does evil for his evil, not wronging any of them in anything, and accepting from them only Islam for Him and faith in Him. Then he related from Mujahid, through the chain of Shibl ibn Abi Najih from him: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ [Hud: 56], he said: "the truth." Similarly, Ibn Jurayj related it from him.

A group said: it is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. This is a difference of expression, for His being ever watchful is the recompense of the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil.

A group said: there is an omission in the speech; its implied meaning is: indeed my Lord guides you to a straight path and urges you to it. As for these, if they meant that this is the meaning of the verse intended, then it is not as they claimed, and there is no evidence for this implied assumption. Allah, glorified is He, has distinguished between His being a commander of justice and His being upon a straight path. And if they meant that His urging to the straight path is among the implications of His being upon a straight path, then they are correct.

Another group said: the meaning of His being upon a straight path is that the return of all servants and affairs is to Allah, and nothing of them escapes Him. As for these, if they meant that this is the meaning of the verse, then it is not so; and if they meant that this is among the necessary implications of His being upon a straight path and its requirement and consequence, then it is true.

Another group said: its meaning is that everything is under His power, subjugation, dominion, and grip. This, although it is true, is not the meaning of the verse. Shu'ayb distinguished between His saying ﴿there is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ [Hud: 56] and His saying ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ [Hud: 56], and these are two independent meanings.

So the saying of Mujahid is the correct one, and it is the saying of the imams of tafsir, and Arabic does not allow any other meaning except with difficulty. Jarir said, praising 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz:

"The Commander of the Believers is upon a path,
straight when the watering places become crooked."

Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Whomever Allah wills, He sends astray; and whomever He wills, He puts him upon a straight path﴾ [al-An'am: 39]. And if He, glorified is He, is the One who placed His messengers and their followers upon the straight path in their words and deeds, then He is more worthy of being upon a straight path in His speech and His action. And although the path of the messengers and their followers is conformity with His command, His path, upon which He is, is what His praise, perfection, and glory require of the speech and action of truth. And success is from Allah.

In the verse there is a second statement, similar in meaning to the first, that it is a likeness Allah set forth for the believer and the disbeliever. What this statement contains has already been mentioned. And success is from Allah.

He said in Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah:

So the first likeness is for the idol and its worshippers. The second likeness: Allah the Exalted set it forth for Himself, and that He commands justice, and He is upon a straight path.

How then is He equated with the idol, which has the worst likeness? What the Lord, blessed and exalted, does with His servants is the utmost of wisdom, goodness, and justice, in empowering them, giving to them, withholding from them, and commanding and forbidding them.

So the claim of the one who claims that this is analogous to a master leaving his male and female slaves to fornicate with one another, and to take captives from one another, is the most false and baseless claim. The difference between them is clearer and greater than needing to be mentioned or pointed out. And praise belongs to Allah, the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. His complete self-sufficiency is distinct, and His praise, His dominion, His might, His wisdom, His knowledge, His goodness, His justice, His religion, His legislation, His judgments, His generosity, His love for forgiveness and pardon of offenders, His forgiveness of those who do wrong, His acceptance of the repentance of the penitent, the patience of the patient, and the gratitude of the grateful, who prefer Him over others, seek His pleasure, worship Him alone, and conduct themselves among His servants with justice, goodness, and sincere counsel, and who strive against His enemies, sacrificing their blood and wealth in love of Him and seeking His pleasure. So that the wicked is distinguished from the good, and His ally from His enemy, and the good things of these and the wicked things of those come out, and their effects that are beloved to the Lord, the Exalted, follow from them: reward and punishment, praise for His allies, and blame for His enemies.

Man, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾. In his original creation, man is created empty and blank, without any knowledge whatsoever, of intelligibles or sensibles. The first faculty that is created in him is the sense of touch, by which he perceives kinds of existing things such as heat, moisture, dryness, softness, roughness and others. Touch is incapable of [perceiving] colours and sounds; indeed, these are as though non-existent in relation to him. Then the faculty of sight is created for him, by which he perceives colours, shapes, nearness and distance, smallness and largeness, length and shortness, motion and rest, and other things.

Then the faculty of hearing opens for him, and he hears plain sounds and melodies. Then he advances in the perceptions of this faculty gradually, until he hears from a distance what he did not hear before. People differ greatly in the strength and weakness of these two perceptions, to the extent that one person perceives something which another is certain is false, while the perceiver is a witness to it and cannot deny it to himself; his fault, in the eyes of the one who denies it to him, is that he alone has perceived it and not the other. Then the faculty of taste is created for him, by which he perceives the differences of flavours: sweetness, sourness, bitterness and what lies between these, of which he had no awareness before. Likewise smell, which is its most complete form. He has no trace, no sign, no perception and no report of intelligibles at this stage.

Then discernment (al-tamyiz) is created in him, which is another stage of his existence. In this stage he perceives other matters, beyond the sensibles, which he did not perceive before. Then he advances to another stage by which he perceives the necessary, the possible and the impossible, that the judgement of a thing is the judgement of its like, that opposites do not combine, that of two contradictories, when one is true the other is false, and similar primary knowledge. Then he advances to another stage in which he derives theoretical knowledge from those primary truths whose knowledge preceded it. Then he advances in this stage from one matter to a matter above it and more abstruse, the relation of the earlier to the later being like the relation of the senses to the intellect. Beyond all of that is another stage, the relation of what precedes it to it being like the relation of human stages to the stage of intellect, or less than that relation, in which opens an eye by which he sees the unseen and what will be in the future, while matters of the intellect are cut off from it, just as the senses are cut off from the objects of the intellect. This is the stage of prophethood, the light of pure intellect's relation to which is not like the relation of the lamp's light to the sun. Therefore, the intellect's denial of what the Prophet (ﷺ) reports is nothing but ignorance, and it has no basis for its denial except that it has not reached it or attained it, so it supposes that it is not established in itself.

(Section)

Then reflect on how the bodies of the animals were clothed with this covering: hair, fur and wool; the birds were clothed with feathers; and some creatures were clothed with skin of the utmost hardness and strength, like the tortoise, while some were given feathers that are like spear-points. All of this according to their needs for protection from heat and cold and from the enemy who wishes to harm them. For since they have no way to make garments, to fashion clothing, or to make instruments of war, they were aided with garments and coverings that never leave them, and with weapons and arms by which they repel harm from themselves. They were also aided with hooves, cloven hoofs, and solid hooves, since they lack shoes and sandals; so each carries its own footwear and water-vessel. The horse, the mule and the donkey were specially given hooves, since they were created for galloping, running and speed; and this was also made a weapon for them when they defend themselves against their adversary, in place of horns, claws, fangs and talons.

So reflect on this subtle kindness and wisdom. For these are beasts without intellect, without hands or fingers prepared for benefit and defence, and without any share in the weaving and spinning that humans practise; and by the subtlety of His provision, their clothing was made part of their creation, remaining upon them for as long as they live, so that they have no need to change it, and they were given instruments and weapons by which to preserve themselves. All of this is so that the wisdom intended by and for them may be fulfilled.

As for the human being, he has intelligence and hands prepared for work; so he spins and weaves, makes clothing for himself, and changes it from one state to another. In this there is benefit for him from many aspects. Among them: he can rest when he removes his clothing whenever he wishes, and wear it whenever he wishes, unlike one compelled to carry a covering.

Among them: he makes for himself kinds of clothing for summer and kinds for winter, for summer clothing is not suitable for winter, and winter clothing is not suitable for summer; so he makes for himself in each season a suitable covering.

Among them: he makes it follow his desire and will.

Among them: he takes pleasure in various kinds of clothing just as he takes pleasure in various kinds of food. So his clothing was made varied and subject to his choice, just as his food was made so. He clothes himself with whatever kinds of garments he wishes, made from plants at times, such as cotton and linen; from animals at times, such as camel hair, wool and hair; from worms at times, such as silk and brocade; and from metals at times, such as gold and silver. Thus his clothing was made varied so that his pleasure, joy, delight and adornment with it may be complete. For this reason the clothing of the people of Paradise is separate from them, as it is in this world, and is not created from their bodies as an animal's is. This indicates that this is more perfect, more glorious and more complete in blessing.

Among them: the intention to distinguish him from the animals in his clothing, just as He distinguished him from them in his food, his dwelling, his speech, his intellect and his understanding. Among them: the variation of clothing and garments, and their diversity according to the diversity of his states, his crafts, his cold and warm seasons, his travelling and settling, his health and sickness, his sleeping and waking, and his comfort.

For each of these states there is a garment and covering particular to it, suitable only for it. He did not make his clothing one and the same in all these states, so that there is no way to change it. This is among His honouring him and preferring him over the rest of the animals.

(Section)

Among the evidence that the actions of servants are created is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah has made for you shade from what He has created, and has made for you refuges in the mountains, and has made for you garments that protect you from the heat, and garments that protect you from your violence.﴾ So He informed that He is the One who made the garments (sarabil), which are coats of mail and sewn clothing. Their raw material is not called sarabil except after human craftsmanship and labour have transformed it. So if they are made by Allah, then they are created by Him entirely: their form, their material, and their configuration.

A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a dwelling, and has made for you, from the hides of livestock, tents which you find light to carry on the day of your travel and the day of your residing.﴾

So He, glory be to Him, informed that the houses, whether fixed or portable, are made by Him, and they only became houses through human craftsmanship.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 16, verse 83:

Mujahid said: "The dwellings, the cattle, the garments (sarabil) and the iron: the disbelievers of Quraysh recognise it, and then they deny it by saying, 'This belonged to our forefathers, and we inherited it from them.'"

Awn ibn Abd Allah said: "They say, 'Were it not for so-and-so, such-and-such would not have happened.'"

al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba said: "They know that the blessings are from God, but they say, 'These come through the intercession of our gods.'"

Another group said: "The blessing here is Muhammad (ﷺ), and denying it is their rejection of his prophethood." This is reported from Mujahid and al-Suddi, and it is closer to the true sense of denial, for it is a denial of what is the greatest of blessings, that it should be a blessing.

As for the first, second and third views, when they attributed the blessing to other than God, they denied God's blessing by ascribing it to someone else. The one who says, "This belonged to our forefathers, and we inherited it from them," is one who, through inheritance from one great man to another, rejects God's blessing upon him and does not acknowledge it. He is like the leper and the bald man whom the angel reminded of God's blessings upon them; they denied it and said, "We inherited this from great men of old," and the angel said, "If you are lying, may God return you to what you were." Its being inherited from the forefathers is more eloquent of God's favour upon them, for He bestowed it upon their forefathers and then passed it down to them, so they and their forefathers enjoyed a blessing.

As for the words of the others, "Were it not for so-and-so, this would not have happened," they imply cutting off the attribution of the blessing from the one without whom it would not exist, and attributing it to one who owns neither harm nor benefit for himself or for others. At most he is a part of the components of the cause, through which God, exalted is He, caused His blessing to flow. A cause does not independently bring things into existence, and making him a cause is itself one of God's blessings upon him. He is the one who bestows that blessing and the one who bestows what made him a cause of it. So the cause and the caused are both part of His favour. He, glorified is He, may bless through that cause, or may bless without it so that it has no effect, or may strip it of its causal power, or may set up something opposing it to counter it, or may bring about the opposite of what the cause would normally produce. He alone is the true Bestower.

As for the saying of the one who speaks of "the intercession of our gods," it includes shirk along with attributing the blessing to other than its rightful owner. The gods that are worshipped besides God are too lowly and humiliated to intercede with God; they are brought forth in disgrace and punishment together with their worshippers. The nearest of creation to God and the most beloved to Him does not intercede with Him except after His permission, for whomever He is pleased with. Intercession by His permission is itself a blessing: He is the one who bestows the intercession, the one who bestows its acceptance, and the one who bestows the qualification of the one interceded for, since not everyone is fit to be interceded for. Who, then, is the true Bestower besides Him? God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from God﴾. So the servant has no escape from His blessing, bounty, grace and kindness for the blink of an eye, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. For this reason God, glorified is He, blamed the one to whom He gave some of His blessings and who said: ﴿I was only given it on account of knowledge I possess﴾.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 16, verse 84:

And His saying: ﴿Then they will not be permitted [to make amends], nor will they be asked to appease [their Lord]﴾. That is, they will not be asked to appease Us. Appeasing Him, exalted is He, means removing His displeasure (ʿatb) through repentance and righteous deeds. So on the Day of Resurrection they will not be asked to appease their Lord, that they might remove His displeasure by obeying Him and following His messengers.

Likewise His saying: ﴿So on that Day, their excuses will not benefit those who did wrong, nor will they be asked to appease [their Lord]﴾.

And the Prophet's ﷺ saying in the supplication at Ta'if: "To You is the ʿutbā" (al-ʿutbā).

It is a noun derived from al-iʿtāb, not from al-ʿatb. That is, You are the one whose displeasure is to be appeased. And for You is my obligation to appease You and to satisfy You through Your obedience, so do what You are pleased with from me, and what removes Your displeasure with me.

So ʿatb (displeasure) is from Him toward His servant, while al-ʿutbā and al-iʿtāb are from the servant toward Him.

Here there are four matters:

The first: ʿatb (displeasure) comes from Allah, exalted is He, for the servant does not become displeased with his Lord, since He is the Benevolent, the Just. It is inconceivable that His servant would be displeased with Him unless the servant is a wrongdoer. Whoever among the exegetes thinks otherwise has committed a most grievous error.

The second: iʿtāb (appeasing) is from Allah and from the servant, in two respects. Allah's appeasing of His servant is the removal of His own displeasure from His servant. The servant's appeasing of his Lord is the removal of Allah's displeasure with him. The servant has no power to do this except by taking up the means by which Allah's displeasure is removed.

The third: istiʿtāb (asking to be appeased) is also from Allah and from the servant, in both respects. Allah, exalted is He, asks His servants to appease Him, that is, He asks them to make Him content and remove His displeasure with them.

From this is the saying of Ibn Masʿūd when an earthquake struck Kufa: "Indeed your Lord asks you to appease Him, so appease Him."

And the servant asks his Lord to appease him, that is, he asks Him to remove His displeasure.

The fourth: al-ʿutbā is the noun of iʿtāb. So grasp firmly this distinction, which will protect you from the confusion of many who have corrupted these passages.

From this is the Prophet's ﷺ saying:

"None of you should wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him. If he is a doer of good, perhaps he will increase in it; and if he is a doer of evil, perhaps he will be asked to appease [his Lord]."

That is, he asks his Lord to appease Him by granting him the success of repentance and accepting it from him, so that His displeasure with him is removed.

Istiʿtāb is the counterpart of istirḍāʾ, which is seeking contentment (riḍā).

And in a narration: "Indeed the servant seeks the contentment of his Lord, and He is content with him."

And indeed Allah seeks contentment, and is content. But istirḍāʾ is higher than istiʿtāb, for it is the seeking of Allah's good pleasure, whereas istiʿtāb is the seeking of the removal of His anger and displeasure, and the two are mutually connected.

(Section)

The sixteenth rank: the leaders and imams of disbelief, and its callers, who disbelieved and barred the servants of God from faith and from entering His religion, whether through desire or fear. For these, the punishment is doubled, and they have two punishments: a punishment for their disbelief, and a punishment for barring people from entering faith. God the Exalted said: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God – We will add to them punishment upon punishment﴾ [al-Nahl: 88]. So one of the two punishments is for their disbelief, and the other punishment is for their barring [others] from the way of God.

It has been established by God's wisdom and justice that the caller to misguidance bears the like of the sins of those who follow him and respond to him. There is no doubt that the punishment of such a person is multiplied and increased according to the number of those who follow him and go astray through him.

This category among the wretched corresponds to the callers to guidance among the blessed. Those callers have their reward multiplied and their ranks elevated according to the number of those who follow them and are guided through them, and these are the opposite of them. For this reason, Pharaoh and his people were in the most severe punishment. God said concerning them: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening, and on the day the Hour arises: "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the severest punishment"﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. This is a reminder that Pharaoh himself is in a worse state than that, because they only entered the severest punishment following him, for it was he who made them light-minded so they obeyed him, and deceived them so they followed him. For this reason, on the Day of Resurrection he will be their leader and their forerunner to this watering-place, as God said: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them down into the Fire﴾ [Hud: 98].

The point is: they deserved the most severe punishment because of the grossness of their disbelief, their barring from the way of God, and their punishing those who believed in God.

Thus the punishment of the leaders in the Fire is not like the punishment of their followers. For this reason, in the Prophet's ﷺ letter to Heraclius was: "If you turn away, then upon you is the sin of the Aryisiyyin (peasants)."

According to the more sound reading of the wording, they are the followers. For this reason, the enemy of God, Iblis, is the most severely punished of the people of the Fire, and he is the first to be clothed in a garment of Fire, because he is the imam of every disbelief, polytheism and evil.

God was disobeyed only at his hands and because of him, then the most suitable and most suitable among his deputies on earth and his callers. There is no doubt that disbelief varies: one disbelief is grosser than another, just as faith varies: one faith is better than another.

Just as the believers are not of one rank but are degrees before God, likewise the disbelievers are not in one level and one drop; rather the Fire has degrees below (darakat), just as Paradise has degrees (darajat). God does not wrong any of His creatures. He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.

(Section)

The grossness of disbelief that necessitates grossness of punishment arises in three aspects. The first: in terms of the disbelieving creed itself, such as one who denies the Lord of the worlds altogether and nullifies the world of the Creator and Governor of it, not believing in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, or the Last Day. For this reason, the adherents of this disbelief are not accepted to pay the jizya according to many scholars, their slaughtered animals are not eaten, and their women are not married, by consensus, because of the grossness of their disbelief. These are the Mu'attilah (deniers of divine attributes), the Dahriyyah (materialists), many of the philosophers, and the people of Wahdah (unity of existence) who claim that there is no existence for the Lord, glorified and exalted, other than the existence of this world.

The second aspect: its grossness through obstinacy and deliberate misguidance with insight, such as the disbelief of one whose heart witnesses that the Messenger is true because of what he saw of the signs of his truthfulness, yet disbelieves out of obstinacy and rebellion, like the people of Thamud, the people of Pharaoh, and the Jews who recognized the Messenger as they recognized their own sons, and the disbelief of Abu Jahl, Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, and such like them.

The third aspect: striving to extinguish the light of God and barring His servants from His religion by whatever their power reaches. These are the most severely punished of the disbelievers, in proportion to the grossness of their disbelief. Some of them combine all three aspects, and some have two of them or only one; the punishment of these is not like the punishment of one who is below them in disbelief, one who is confused due to his ignorance. The believers are safe from his harm; no harm reaches them from him. His disbelief has not become as gross as theirs, rather he affirms God and His oneness, His angels, the kinds of books and messengers, and the Last Day.

And if he shares with them in their disbelief in the Messenger, they have added to it kinds of disbelief. Would the punishment of Abu Talib, Abu Lahab, Abu Jahl, Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and their like be equal in the Fire?

The point is that this rank, the rank of the leaders, the callers who bar from the religion of God, is not like the rank of those below them. It has been established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The least of the people of the Fire in punishment is Abu Talib." And it is known that the disbelief of Abu Talib was not like the disbelief of Abu Jahl and his like.

(Fa'ida)

Ibn 'Aqil said: "Ruthlessness (al-jirya) in permitting action within the legal authority by means of siyasa (governance by policy) is firmness (al-hazm), and no imam is free of it."

Al-Shafi'i said: "There is no siyasa except what agrees with the Shari'a."

Ibn 'Aqil said: "Siyasa is any action by which people come closer to righteousness and further from corruption, even if the Messenger did not establish it and no revelation descended concerning it. If you mean by your saying 'except what agrees with the Shari'a' that it does not contradict what the Shari'a has stated, then it is correct. But if you mean what the Shari'a has explicitly stated, then it is an error and a harshness toward the Companions. The Rightly-Guided Caliphs carried out killing and mutilation of a kind that no scholar of the Sunan would deny. Even if there were nothing but the burning of the mushafs, it was an opinion they relied on for the sake of public interest, and [there was] the burning of 'Ali in the trenches.

And he said:

'When I see a reprehensible matter, I kindle my fire and call Qanbar.'

And [there was] 'Umar's banishment of Nasr ibn Hajjaj."

I say: This is a place of slipping feet, a narrow station and a difficult battlefield. A group neglected it: they suspended the hudud (prescribed penalties), wasted rights, emboldened the wicked to corruption, considered the Shari'a deficient so that the interests of the servants could not be upheld by it, and closed on themselves many avenues of knowing truth from falsehood. Indeed, they suspended them while knowing with certainty, and others knowing, that these are valid proofs, out of their supposition that they contradict the principles of the Shari'a. What caused this for them was a kind of shortcoming in knowledge of the Shari'a. When the rulers saw that, and that people's affairs would not be set right except by something beyond what these men had understood of the Shari'a, they devised political laws by which the affairs of the world would be organized. From the shortcoming of those men regarding the Shari'a, and from the innovation of what these rulers devised as their policies, arose a long evil and a wide corruption, and the matter grew severe and its rectification became impossible. Another group went to excess and permitted from it what contradicts the judgment of Allah and His Messenger. Both groups came from their shortcoming in knowing what Allah sent His Messenger with. Allah sent His messengers and revealed His books so that people might establish justice (al-qist), which is the equity by which the heavens and the earth stand. So when the signs of justice appear and its direction becomes clear by whatever way, there is the Shari'a of Allah and His religion. Allah the Exalted did not confine the ways, proofs and signs of justice to one thing, nor negate other ways that are like them or stronger than them. Rather, He made clear that what He legislated, its purpose is the establishment of justice and people standing by equity. Whatever way justice and equity are extracted by, it is from the religion; it cannot be said that it contradicts it. So you do not say that just siyasa contradicts what the Shari'a has stated; rather it agrees with what it brought, and indeed it is a part of it. We call it siyasa only following your terminology, but in truth it is a right Shari'a. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ imprisoned someone on suspicion of tale-bearing and punished on accusation when signs of doubt appeared against the accused. Whoever releases every accused person and lets him go, while knowing his notoriety for corruption on earth, breaking into houses and frequent thefts, [is wrong].

And [the Prophet] said: 'I will not take him except with two just witnesses.'

So his saying is contrary to the legal siyasa.

Likewise, the Prophet ﷺ denied the ghal (one who embezzles from booty) his share of the spoils; the Rightly-Guided Caliphs burned his goods; likewise he took half the property of one who withholds zakat; likewise he imposed doubled fines on a thief of what does not reach the amputation threshold, as a punishment by flogging; likewise he imposed doubled fines on one who conceals a lost item. Likewise 'Umar burned the tavern of the wine-seller and burned his jars of wine, and burned the palace of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas when he secluded himself in it from the subjects; likewise he shaved the head of Nasr ibn Hajjaj and banished him; likewise he beat Subay'; likewise his removal of his governors; likewise his obligation on the Companions to reduce narrating hadith from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so that people would occupy themselves with the Qur'an and not neglect it; and other policies by which he governed the community, which became a sunna until the Day of Resurrection, whoever opposed them.

From this is Abu Bakr's (may Allah be pleased with him) burning of the apostates (al-wat'iyy); from this is 'Uthman's (may Allah be pleased with him) burning of the codices that differed from the dialect of Quraysh; from this is 'Umar's (may Allah be pleased with him) choice that people perform hajj as ifrad (solitary hajj) so that they perform 'umra in other months, so that the Sacred House remains continuously visited..

and up to many multiples of that from his siyasa, by which they governed the community, and which is by interpreting the Qur'an and his Sunna.

The division of people's rulings into shar'iyya (legal) and siyasiyya (political) is like the division of one who divides the path (tariqa) into shari'a and haqiqa, and that is a false division. Haqiqa is of two kinds: a haqiqa that is true and correct, which is the core of the shar'iyya and not its counterpart; and a false haqiqa, which opposes the Shari'a as error opposes guidance. Likewise siyasa is of two kinds: just siyasa, which is part of the Shari'a and one of its divisions, not its counterpart; and false siyasa, which opposes the Shari'a as injustice opposes justice.

Similar to this is the division by some people of discourse on religion into shar' (revelation) and 'aql (reason). This is a false division. Rather, the rational (ma'qul) is of two kinds: a kind that agrees with what the Messenger brought, which is rational; and [a kind that] contradicts it, which are false imaginings and doubts, because its holder supposes they are rational matters, when they are only imaginings and doubts. Likewise qiyas (analogy) and Shari'a: sound qiyas is the rational sense of the texts (ma'qul al-nusus), and false qiyas that contradicts the texts opposes the Shari'a.

This distinction is the difference between what the prophets inherited and what others have. Its root rests on one principle: the universality of his message by the Sunna to everything that the servants need in their knowledge, their sciences and their actions by which their welfare in this life and the next is achieved; and that there is no need for anyone other than him at all, and our only need is for one who conveys to us what he brought. Whoever does not firmly establish this in his heart has not firmly planted his foot in faith in the Messenger. Rather, it is obligatory to believe in the universality of his message in this respect, just as it is obligatory to believe in the universality of his message with respect to all those obligated. Just as no one among mankind is outside his message at all, likewise no right of knowledge or practice is outside what he brought. What he brought is the sufficient thing for which the community has no need of anything else. The need for other things arises only from the portion of knowledge and understanding of it that one has; according to the scarcity of his portion, his need is. Otherwise, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died, and there is no bird that flaps its wings in the sky except that he made known to the community knowledge of it. He taught them everything, even the etiquette of relieving oneself, the etiquette of intercourse, sleep, sitting, eating, drinking, riding and dismounting; he described to them the Throne, the Chair, the angels, Paradise, Hell, the Day of Resurrection and what is in it, until it was as if he had seen it with his own eyes; he made them know their Lord and Worshipped One with the most complete knowledge, until it was as if they saw Him through what he described of His perfect attributes and majestic qualities; he made them know the prophets and their peoples and what happened between them, until it was as if they had been among them; he made them know the paths of good and evil, both subtle and great, what no prophet had made known to his community before him; he made them know the states of death and what happens after it in the barzakh, and the bliss and punishment there for the soul and the body, making it so clear that it was as if they witnessed it; likewise he made them know the proofs of tawhid, prophethood and the return, and the refutation of all sects of unbelief and misguidance, such that whoever knows it has no need for anyone's words at all; likewise he made them know the stratagems of war, meeting the enemy and the ways of victory over it, which, if they had known and practiced them, no enemy would ever have stood against them; likewise he made them know Iblis's methods by which he approaches them and the means of guarding against his cunning and deceit and of repelling his evil, beyond which there is nothing more; and with that he guided them in their life to what, if they had done it, their worldly affairs would have been set right in the greatest uprightness. In sum, the Messenger of Allah brought them the good of this world and the next in its entirety, and Allah did not make them in need of anyone but him. For this reason Allah closed the register of prophethood with him and did not send any messenger after him, because the community is self-sufficient in him from anyone else. How then can it be supposed that his perfect, completing Shari'a needs a siyasa outside it, or a haqiqa outside it, or a qiyas outside it, or a rational matter outside it? Whoever supposes that is like one who supposes that people need another messenger after him. The cause of all this is that what he brought is hidden from the one who supposes this. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book being recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and reminder for a people who believe﴾ [29:51]. And He the Exalted said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an exposition of all things, and guidance and mercy and good tidings for the Muslims﴾ [16:89]. And He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [17:9]. And He the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you an instruction from your Lord and a cure for what is in the breasts and guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [10:57].

How can a book that does not fulfill a tenth of a tenth of what people need, by their false claim, cure what is in the breasts?

Wonder of wonders! How were the Companions and the Followers before these laws were devised and these opinions, analogies and sayings were extracted? Were they guided by the texts, or were they otherwise, until later scholars came who were more knowledgeable and better guided than them? Whoever has a remnant of intellect or shame does not suppose this. We seek refuge in Allah from abandonment. But whoever is granted understanding of the Book and the Messenger's hadith is sufficed by them over anything else, according to the understanding he is granted; and that is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills, and Allah is possessed of great bounty. This section, if expounded as it should be, would fill several volumes, but these are brief words pointing to what lies beyond them.

**[Section: Sins Expel the Servant from the Circle of Ihsan]**

Among its punishments is that it expels the servant from the circle of *ihsan* (excellence in worship and conduct) and deprives him of the reward of the *muhsinun* (those who do good). When *ihsan* penetrates the heart, it restrains a person from sins, for whoever worships Allah as if he sees Him, does so only because the remembrance of Him, His love, His fear, and His hope have taken hold of his heart, to the extent that he becomes as though he is witnessing Him. This will inevitably prevent him from intending disobedience, let alone committing it. When he leaves the circle of *ihsan*, he loses the companionship of his special intimate friends, their pleasant life, and their complete bliss. If Allah intends good for him, He keeps him within the circle of the general believers. But if he disobeys Him with sins that expel him from the circle of faith, then, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "A fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer, a wine-drinker does not drink wine while he is a believer, a thief does not steal while he is a believer, and a plunderer does not plunder a plunder of value at which people raise their eyes while he is a believer." So beware, beware! Repentance is still offered.

**[Section: Fahshaa' and Munkar]**

As for *fahshaa'* (grave indecency) and *munkar* (what is reprehensible), *fahshaa'* is an attribute of a noun that has been omitted, its use being abstracted to emphasize the attribute. It is "the indecent deed" or "the indecent trait," meaning that whose ugliness is evident to everyone and which every sound-minded person finds abominable. For this reason it has been explained as fornication and sodomy, and Allah called them *fahisha* (an indecency) because their ugliness is extreme. Likewise, ugly speech is called *fuhsh*, meaning that whose ugliness is exceedingly evident, such as vile abuse, slander, and the like.

As for *munkar*, it is also an attribute of an omitted noun, i.e., the *munkar* deed, which is what the intellects and natural dispositions (*fitar*) reject. Its relation to them is like the relation of a foul smell to the sense of smell, an ugly sight to the eye, a repugnant taste to the palate, and a disagreeable sound to the ear. Therefore, whatever the intellects and natural dispositions reject intensely is *fahisha*, just as the senses' rejection of these perceived things is intense.

So the *munkar* for them is that which they do not recognize and are not accustomed to, while the ugly and repugnant thing from which they recoil intensely is the *fahisha*. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "The *fahisha* is fornication, and the *munkar* is what has not been recognized in any law (*shari'a*) or practice (*sunnah*)."

Reflect, then, on his distinction between what is not known to be good and not familiar, and what has settled as ugly in the natural dispositions and intellects.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 16, verse 97 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, exalted is He, only made the good life for those who believe in Him and do righteous deeds, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ [al-Nahl: 97].

Thus He guaranteed for the people of faith and righteous deeds the recompense in this world through a good life, and the best reward (al-husna) on the Day of Resurrection. So they have the better of the two lives, and they are living in both abodes.

(Section)

The good life has been explained as contentment (qana'ah) and satisfaction (ridа), good provision, and other things besides. The correct view is that it is the life of the heart, its bliss, its joy and its happiness through faith, the knowledge of Allah, love for Him, turning to Him in repentance, and relying upon Him. For there is no life better than the life of its possessor, and no bliss above his bliss except the bliss of Paradise. As one of the knowers of Allah used to say: "There are times that pass over me in which I say: If the people of Paradise are in a state like this, then they are indeed in a good life." Another said: "There are times that pass over the heart in which it dances with delight."

When the life of the heart is a good life, the life of the limbs follows it, for it governs them. For this reason Allah made the straitened life (al-ma'ishah al-dank) for whoever turns away from His remembrance, and it is the opposite of the good life.

This good life exists in the three abodes, namely the abode of this world, the abode of the barzakh, and the abode of permanence. The straitened life also exists in the three abodes. So the righteous are in bliss here and there, and the wicked are in Hellfire here and there. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾ [al-Nahl: 30], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance; He will let you enjoy a good provision until a specified term, and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾ [Hud: 3].

So the remembrance of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, love for Him, obedience to Him, and turning to Him guarantee the best life in this world and the Hereafter, while turning away from Him, heedlessness, and disobedience to Him entail a troubled life and a straitened livelihood in this world and the Hereafter.

(Section: on the life which the author pointed to, which is the life of knowledge from the death of ignorance)

Ignorance is indeed a death for its people, as it has been said:

Within ignorance, before death, is a death for its people,
And their bodies, before the graves, are graves.

And their spirits are in loneliness away from their bodies,
So for them there is no resurrection until the Resurrection.

Indeed the ignorant person is dead in heart and spirit, even if he is alive in body; his body is a grave walking upon the face of the earth. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one whose example is in darkness, from which he cannot emerge?﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an, to warn whoever is alive and that the word may be justified against the disbelievers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 69-70]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾ [al-Naml: 80]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills, and you cannot make hear those who are in the graves﴾ [Fatir: 22].

He likened them, in the death of their hearts, to the people of the graves, for their spirits have died and their bodies have become graves for them. Just as the inhabitants of graves do not hear, so these do not hear. And since life is perception and movement and what necessitates them, these hearts, because they do not perceive knowledge and faith and do not move toward it, are truly dead. This is not a comparison of their death to the death of the body; rather, it is the death of the heart and spirit.

Imam Ahmad mentioned in the Kitab al-Zuhd from the sayings of Luqman that he said to his son: "O my son, sit with the scholars and crowd them with your knees, for Allah gives life to hearts with the light of wisdom, just as He gives life to the earth with heavy rain." Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: "Learn knowledge, for learning it for Allah is fear (of Allah), seeking it is worship, studying it is glorification (tasbih), researching it is jihad, teaching it to one who does not know it is charity, and giving it to its people is a means of nearness. For it is the markers of the lawful and the unlawful, the beacon of the paths of the people of Paradise. It is the companion in loneliness, the friend in estrangement, the confidant in solitude, the guide to happiness and hardship, the weapon against enemies, and the adornment among close friends. Allah raises by it peoples, making them leaders in good and imams whose traces are followed, whose deeds are emulated, and whose opinion is final. The angels desire their friendship and wipe them with their wings. Every moist and dry thing seeks forgiveness for them, and the fish of the sea and its creatures, and the beasts of the land and its cattle. For knowledge is the life of hearts from ignorance and the lamps of sight from darkness. By knowledge the servant reaches the stations of the righteous and the high ranks in this world and the Hereafter. Reflecting upon it is equal to fasting, and studying it is equal to standing in prayer at night. By it ties of kinship are maintained, and by it the lawful is known from the unlawful. It is the leader of action, and action follows it; the happy are inspired with it, and the wretched are deprived of it." Narrated by al-Tabarani, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others, and it has been transmitted as a marfu' hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, but the mawquf (stopping at the Companion) version is more sound.

What is intended here is his statement: "For knowledge is the life of hearts from ignorance." So the heart is dead, and its life is through knowledge and faith.

(Benefit)

Abandoning desires for the sake of Allah, though it saves one from the punishment of Allah and makes the attainment of His mercy obligatory, is the treasure of Allah and the store of righteousness. The sweetness of intimacy, longing for Him, joy and delight in Him do not occur in a heart in which there is other than Him, even if its owner is one of the people of worship, asceticism and knowledge. For He, glorified is He, refuses to place His treasures in a heart in which there is something else, while its aspiration is attached to other than Him. Rather, He deposits His treasures in a heart that sees poverty as richness with Allah, richness as poverty apart from Allah, might as humiliation apart from Him, humiliation as might with Him, bliss as torment apart from Him, and torment as bliss with Him.

In sum, such a person sees no life except with Him; and death, pain, worry, grief and sorrow are with him when He is not with him. For such a person there are two gardens: a garden in this world, hastened, and a garden on the Day of Resurrection.

(Section)

The people of happiness and success have in this world the best life, and for them in the barzakh and in the Hereafter is the best reward.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾. This refers to this world. Then He said: ﴿And We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾. This refers to the barzakh and the Hereafter.

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place, and the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾.

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance; He will let you enjoy a good provision until a specified term, and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾. This refers to the Hereafter.

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world is good, and the earth of Allah is spacious. Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾.

So these are four places in which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He recompenses the doer of good for his good with two recompenses: a recompense in this world and a recompense in the Hereafter.

Good deeds have a hastened recompense without fail, and evil deeds have a hastened recompense without fail.

Even if there were nothing for which the doer of good is rewarded except the expansion of his chest, the widening of his heart, his joy, and his delight in dealing with his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, in obeying Him, remembering Him, and the bliss of his spirit through His love, it would suffice.

His remembrance of and joy in his Lord, glorified and exalted is He, is greater than the joy of one close to a generous sultan in his sultan's favor.

And what the evildoer is recompensed with is tightness of chest, hardness of heart, its scattering, its darkness, its burning, its distress, its worry, its grief and its fear. This is a matter about which one who has even a little perception and life hardly doubts. Rather, distresses, worries, griefs and constriction are hastened punishments, a worldly fire, and Hell is present. Turning to Allah, exalted is He, repenting to Him, being content with Him and with what comes from Him, the heart being filled with His love, the tongue constantly on His remembrance, and joy and happiness in knowing Him are a hastened reward, a garden, and a life incomparable to the life of kings.

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his spirit, say: "Indeed in this world there is a garden; whoever does not enter it does not enter the garden of the Hereafter." He also said to me once: "What can my enemies do to me? My garden and my orchard are in my breast. If I travel, it goes with me and never leaves me. If I am imprisoned, it is seclusion; if I am killed, it is martyrdom; and if I am expelled from my land, it is a journey."

He used to say in his prison in the Citadel: "Even if I were to give the whole hall full of gold, it would not equal in my estimation the thanks for this blessing." Or he said: "I could not repay those who caused me this good, and similar words."

He used to say in his prostration while imprisoned: "O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You, and to worship You well, as much as You will."

He also said to me once: "The imprisoned one is he whose heart is imprisoned from his Lord, and the captive is he whom his desire has captured."

When he entered the Citadel and was within its wall, he looked at it and said: ﴿So a wall with a gate will be struck between them; its inner side will have mercy, and its outer side will have torment from before it﴾.

By Allah, I have never seen anyone with a better life than him, despite the narrowness of his living and his lack of ease and comfort, rather their opposite; and despite his imprisonment, threats and hardship. Yet he was, with all that, among the best of people in life, the most expansive in chest, the strongest in heart, and the most joyful in soul; the radiance of bliss shone upon his face.

Whenever fear grew intense upon us, suspicions became harsh, and the earth seemed narrow to us, we would come to him. No sooner did we see him and hear his words than all of that vanished and turned into expansion, strength, certainty and tranquility.

Glory be to Him who made His servants witness His garden before meeting Him, and opened its doors for them in the abode of action, so He gave them of its spirit, fragrance and goodness what drained their strength in seeking it and in racing toward it.

One of the knowers used to say: "If the kings and the sons of kings knew what we are in, they would fight us over it with swords."

Another said: "The poor people of this world, they left it without tasting the best of what is in it?"

It was said: "And what is the best of what is in it?"

He said: "The love of Allah, the knowledge of Him, and His remembrance."

Or similar to this.

Another said: "There are times that pass over the heart in which it dances with delight."

Another said: "There are times that pass over me in which I say: If the people of Paradise are in a state like this, then they are indeed in a good life."

So the love of Allah, the knowledge of Him, the lasting of His remembrance, tranquility in Him, calm in Him, singling Him out with love, fear, hope, reliance and dealing, such that He alone dominates the worries, resolves and will of the servant, is the garden of this world and the bliss to which no bliss is comparable. It is the coolness of the eyes of lovers and the life of the knowers.

People's eyes are cooled by it in proportion to the coolness of their eyes in Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Whoever has his eye cooled in Allah, every eye is cooled by him; and whoever does not have his eye cooled in Allah, his soul is consumed by sighs over the world.

This is only true of one who has life in his heart. As for the dead-hearted, he will bring you desolation of what is his; so take comfort in his absence as much as you can, for only his presence with you will bring you desolation. When you are tried with him, give him your outward self, but travel away from him in your heart, separate from him in your secret, and do not occupy yourself with him from what is more fitting for you.

Know that the greatest regret is occupying yourself with one whose occupation with you only causes you to miss your portion and share from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and your cutting off from Him, the loss of your time, the weakening of your resolve, and the scattering of your aspiration.

So when you are afflicted with this—and there is no escape from it for you—deal with Allah in it, seek reward from Him for it as much as you can, draw near to Allah through seeking His pleasure in it, and make your meeting with him a trade for you, not a loss. Be with him like a man traveling on his way who is confronted by a man who stops him from his journey. Strive to take him along with you and travel with him, so that you carry him and he does not carry you. If he refuses, and there is no hope in his traveling along, then do not stop with him without a caravan of the road; leave him and do not turn to him, for he is a highway robber, whoever he may be. Save your heart, guard your day and night, lest the sun set on you before you reach the station and you are seized, or the dawn rise before you find your provision.

(Section)

The words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾

The intended meaning is not the life shared by believers and disbelievers, the righteous and the wicked, and the good food, clothing, drink and marriage; for the enemies of Allah may even exceed His friends in that by manifold multiples. Rather, Allah, glorified is He, guaranteed for everyone who does righteous deeds that He will give him a good life. He is the true of promise who does not break His promise. And what life is better than the life of one whose concerns have all gathered and become one single concern in seeking the pleasure of Allah? His heart is not scattered; rather, he turns to Allah, and his will and thoughts, which were divided into every valley, become one, directed to Allah. Thus his remembrance of his Most High Beloved, his love, his longing for meeting Him, and his intimacy with His nearness become what dominates him, and upon it revolve his concerns, his will and his intentions, with every thought of his heart. If he is silent, he is silent for Allah; if he speaks, he speaks for Allah; if he hears, he hears by Him; if he sees, he sees by Him; by Him he grasps, by Him he walks, by Him he dwells, by Him he lives, by Him he dies, and by Him he is raised. As in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from him ﷺ, relating from his Lord, blessed and exalted is He, that He said: "My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. And My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary deeds until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. By Me he hears, by Me he sees, by Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him; and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely protect him. I do not hesitate in anything I am doing as I hesitate in taking the soul of My believing servant who dislikes death, and I dislike hurting him, but he has no escape from it."

This noble divine hadith—whose meaning and intent it is forbidden for one of coarse nature and hard heart to grasp—contains the restriction of the causes of His love to two matters: performing His obligations, and drawing near to Him through voluntary acts.

He, glory be to Him, informed that performing His obligatory duties (fara'id) is the dearest means by which those who draw near to Him seek nearness, and that after them come the voluntary acts (nawafil). The lover continues to increase in voluntary acts until he becomes beloved to Allah. When he becomes beloved to Allah, Allah's love for him brings about a second love from Him, above the first. This love occupies his heart so that he has no thought or concern for anything other than his Beloved. It takes possession of his soul, and no room remains in him for anyone other than his Beloved at all. Remembrance of his Beloved, love for Him, and His exalted example become his, and He holds the reins of his heart and takes control of his soul, as the Beloved takes control of the love of the sincere lover in his love, a love in which all the powers of his love have gathered for Him.

There is no doubt that if this lover hears, he hears by his Beloved; if he sees, he sees by Him; if he grasps, he grasps by Him; if he walks, he walks by Him. He is in his heart, with him, his companion and his friend. Here the bi' (ب) (the particle "bi," meaning "with") indicates accompaniment, an accompaniment without equal, which is not attained merely by being informed of it or knowing about it. The matter is therefore one of state (ḥāl), not purely of knowledge ('ilm).

If the created being finds this in the love of a created being, for which he was not made and upon which he was not naturally formed, as one of the lovers said:

"Your image is in my eye, your remembrance is on my tongue,
and your dwelling is in my heart, so where could you be absent?"

Another said:

"And it is a wonder that I yearn for them,
so I ask about them of whoever I meet, while they are with me.
My eye seeks them while they are in its blackness,
and my heart longs for them while they are between my ribs."

And this is more subtle than the words of another:

"If I say, 'You are absent,' my heart does not believe me,
since you are in it like the secret place, you were never absent.
Or if I say, 'You were not absent,' the glance says, 'That is a lie,'
so I am bewildered between truth and falsehood."

Nothing is closer to the lover than his beloved. Love may take such firm hold of him that the beloved becomes closer to him than his own self, so that he forgets himself and is not forgotten by the Beloved, as one said:

"I want to forget her remembrance, but it is as if
Layla is presented to me on every path."

Another said:

"The heart is asked to forget you,
but natures refuse the one who conveys the request."

In the hadith, He specified the hearing, the sight, the hand and the foot for mention, because these are the instruments of perception and the instruments of action. The hearing and the sight bring will and aversion to the heart, and they bring love and hatred to it, and then the hand and the foot act. So when the servant's hearing is by Allah and his sight is by Allah, he is protected in the instruments of his perception, and he is protected in his love and hatred, and so he is protected in his grasping and his walking.

Reflect on how He sufficed with mentioning the hearing, the sight, the hand and the foot, rather than the tongue. The perception of hearing sometimes happens by choice and sometimes without choice, and likewise sight may occur suddenly without choice. Likewise the movement of the hand and the foot, which the servant cannot do without, so how much more so the movement of the tongue, which occurs only with intention and choice? The servant may dispense with it, except where he is commanded to use it.

Moreover, the tongue's response to the heart is more complete than the response of the other limbs, for it is the heart's interpreter and its messenger.

Reflect on how He, exalted is He, affirmed that the servant's hearing, sight, grasping and walking are by Him through His saying, in the hadith: "I was his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks," affirming that He is with His servant, and that His servant is in his perceptions, by his hearing, his sight, and the movements of his hands and feet.

Reflect on how He said, "by Me he hears, and by Me he sees," and did not say, "for Me he hears, and for Me he sees." Some may think that the particle lām (لِ, "for") is more appropriate in this place, since it indicates purpose, and that these acts occur for Allah, which is more specific than occurring by Him. This is an error and a mistake, because the bā' (بِ) here is not merely for seeking help. The movements and perceptions of both the righteous and the wicked come about only through Allah's aid to them. The bā' here indicates accompaniment: that is, he hears, sees, grasps and walks while I am his companion with him. This is like His saying in another hadith: "I am with My servant as long as he remembers Me and his lips move with My remembrance." This is the special companionship mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us﴾ (At-Tawbah 9:40).

Also the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What do you think of two whose third is Allah?" and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed Allah is with the doers of good﴾ (Al-'Ankabut 29:69). And His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾ (An-Nahl 16:128). And His saying: ﴿And be patient; indeed Allah is with the patient﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:46). And His saying: ﴿Never! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara' 26:62). And His saying, exalted is He, to Musa and Harun: ﴿Indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:46).

So this bā' conveys the meaning of this companionship, not the lām. Sincerity, patience and reliance on Allah cannot be realized by the servant, nor can he reach the stations of servanthood, except through this bā' and this companionship.

Whenever the servant is by Allah, difficult burdens become light for him, and fears are turned in his favor. By Allah every hardship becomes easy, every difficulty becomes simple, and every distant thing becomes near. By Allah, worries, griefs and sorrows vanish. There is no anxiety with Allah, and no grief or sorrow, except where the servant loses the meaning of this bā'. Then his heart becomes like a fish when it leaves the water: it leaps and writhes until it returns to it.

When this agreement from the servant with his Lord in what He loves is realized, the Lord's agreement with His servant in his needs and requests is realized as well. So He said: "If he asks Me, I will certainly give it to him, and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will certainly grant him refuge." That is: just as he agreed with My will by complying with My commands and drawing near by what I love, so I agree with him in his desire and his fear regarding what he asks Me to do for him, and what he seeks refuge from so that it does not befall him. This agreement grows strong on both sides, to the point that it requires the Lord, glory be to Him, to hesitate about causing His servant to die, because the servant dislikes death, and the Lord, exalted is He, dislikes what His servant dislikes and dislikes his distress. For this reason, the consideration would be that He not cause him to die, but His wisdom and the servant's benefit lie in his death. He caused him to die only so that He might give him life, and He caused him to fall ill only so that He might restore his health, and He made him poor only so that He might enrich him, and He withheld only so that He might give. He did not remove Adam from the Garden while he was in his father's loins except that He would return him to it in the best of conditions, and He did not say to his father, "Go down from it," except that He intended to return him to it. This is the true Beloved, not any other. Indeed, even if every hair-root of the servant contained complete love for Allah, it would still be only a small part of what He deserves from His servant.

"Shift your heart wherever you wish among desires;
love is only for the first Beloved."

"How many dwellings on earth has the youth grown fond of,
yet his longing is always for the first dwelling."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 16, verse 98 (part 1 of 2):

Section

God Most High says: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord. His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him.﴾ [al-Nahl: 98-100].

The meaning of "istaʿidh bi-Llah" (seek refuge in God) is: take shelter in Him, hold fast to Him, and seek refuge with Him. Its verbal noun is al-ʿawdh, al-ʿiyadh, and al-maʿadh. It is most often used with the one sought refuge in, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "You have indeed sought refuge (ʿudhti) with one who grants refuge (Muʿadh)."

The root of the word is from clinging to a thing and drawing near to it. From the speech of the Arabs: "The finest meat is that which clings (ʿawdhuhu) to the bone," meaning the part that has adhered to the bone and is attached to it. A she-camel that is ʿaʾidh is one whose young cling to her, and its plural is ʿawdh, like ḥumr. And from the hadith of al-Ḥudaybiyah: "With them are the ʿawdh and the maṭāfīl."

The maṭāfīl is the plural of miṭfal, which is the she-camel that has her young with her.

A group, including the author of Jāmiʿ al-Uṣūl, said: he used this as a metaphor for the women, meaning that with them were their women and children. But there is no need for that; rather the wording is in its literal sense, namely that they came out to you with their beasts and mounts, even bringing with them the she-camels that had their young. So God, glory be to Him, commanded seeking refuge in Him from Satan when reciting the Qur'an.

In this there are several aspects:

First: The Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts. It removes what Satan casts into them of whisperings, desires, and corrupt intentions. It is a remedy for what Satan has made bitter within them. So He commanded that the source of the disease be expelled and the heart be emptied of it, so that the remedy meets an empty place and takes hold and has effect, as it has been said:

"Her love came to me before I knew love, and it found an empty heart and settled in it."

Thus this healing remedy comes to a heart that has been emptied of anything contending with or opposing it, so it takes effect in it.

Second: The Qur'an is the source of guidance, knowledge, and goodness in the heart, just as water is the source of plants, while Satan is a fire that burns plants little by little. Whenever he senses the sprouting of goodness in the heart, he strives to corrupt and burn it. So He commanded that one seek refuge in God, Mighty and Majestic, from him, lest he spoil what is gained through the Qur'an.

The difference between this aspect and the one before it is that seeking refuge in the first aspect is for the sake of attaining the benefit of the Qur'an, while in the second it is for its continuance, preservation, and firmness.

It seems that whoever said that seeking refuge is after the recitation had noticed this meaning, and by the life of God it is a fine observation. However, the Sunnah and the reports of the Companions only came with seeking refuge before beginning the recitation, and this is the view of the majority of the Community among the early and later scholars, and it achieves both matters.

Third: The angels draw near to the reciter of the Qur'an and listen to his recitation, as in the hadith of Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr when he was reciting and saw something like a canopy in which were something like lamps, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Those were the angels."

Satan is the opposite and enemy of the angel. So He commanded the reciter to ask God, Most High, to keep His enemy far from him, so that the angels and His chosen ones may attend him. This is a feast at which angels and devils do not gather.

Fourth: Satan comes against the reciter with his horses and his foot soldiers, to occupy him from the purpose of the Qur'an, which is reflecting upon it, understanding it, and knowing what the Speaker, glory be to Him, intended by it. He strives with all his effort to come between his heart and the aim of the Qur'an, so that the reciter does not fully benefit from it. So He commanded that at the beginning one seek refuge in God, Mighty and Majestic, from him.
