Fifth: The reciter is in private conversation with God, Most High, through His speech, and God, Most High, listens more attentively to the reciter with a beautiful voice reciting the Qur'an than the master of a singing slave-girl listens to his slave-girl. Satan's recitation is poetry and singing. So He commanded the reciter to drive him away by seeking refuge when conversing with the Most High and when the Lord listens to his recitation.

Sixth: God, glory be to Him, informed that He did not send any messenger or prophet except that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish. All the early scholars agreed that the meaning is: when he recited, Satan cast into his recitation, as the poet said about ʿUthmān:

"He wished for the Book of God at the start of his night, and at its end he met the fate of the decrees."

If this was his action with the messengers, peace be upon them, then how about others? For this reason the reciter sometimes makes errors, and the recitation becomes confused for him, and it disturbs him: his tongue gets tangled, or his mind and heart become distracted. When he comes to recite, the reciter does not lack one or the other of these, and perhaps both together. So among the most important matters is seeking refuge in God, Most High, from him when reciting.

Seventh: Satan is most intent upon a person when he is about to begin something good or enters upon it. He then presses hard upon him to cut him off from it. In the authentic collection, on the authority of the Prophet ﷺ: "A devil escaped from me last night, intending to cut off my prayer," and the hadith continues.

The more beneficial an act is for the servant and the more beloved to God, Most High, the more Satan's opposition to him increases. In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, on the authority of Sabrah ibn Abi al-Fākih, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Satan sat in wait for the son of Adam on his paths. He sat for him on the path of Islam and said: 'Will you embrace Islam and abandon your religion and the religion of your fathers and forefathers?' He disobeyed him and embraced Islam. Then he sat for him on the path of emigration and said: 'Will you emigrate and leave your land and your sky? The likeness of the emigrant is like a horse in its tether.' He disobeyed him and emigrated. Then he sat for him on the path of jihad, which is the jihad of the self and wealth, and said: 'You will fight and be killed, and then the woman will be married and the wealth will be divided?' He said: He disobeyed him and strove."

So Satan lies in ambush for the human being on the road of every good.

Mujāhid, may God have mercy on him, said: "No caravan sets out for Mecca except that Iblis equips with them a host like their number." Narrated by Ibn Abi Ḥātim in his Tafsir. So he lies in ambush, especially when reciting the Qur'an. Thus God, glory be to Him, commanded the servant to fight his enemy who cuts off the road, and to seek refuge in God, Most High, from him first, and then to set out on his journey, just as a traveler, when a highwayman confronts him, occupies himself with repelling him, and then pushes on in his journey.

Eighth: Seeking refuge before the recitation is a heading and an announcement that what follows is the Qur'an. For this reason seeking refuge is not prescribed before the speech of another. Rather, seeking refuge is a preface and an alert to the listener that what follows is recitation. So when the listener hears the seeking of refuge, he prepares himself to listen to the speech of God, Most High. Then it was prescribed for the reciter as well, even if he is alone, for the reasons we have mentioned and others.

These are some of the benefits of seeking refuge.

Aḥmad said in the narration of Ḥanbal: "He should not recite in prayer or outside prayer without seeking refuge, because of the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98]."

He said in the narration of Ibn Mushish: "Whenever he recites, he seeks refuge."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Aḥmad said: "I heard my father: whenever he recited, he sought refuge, saying: 'I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan; indeed God is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.'"

In the Musnad and at-Tirmidhi, on the authority of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: "When the Prophet ﷺ stood for prayer, he began, then said: 'I seek refuge in God, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan: from his pressing (hamz), his blowing (nafkh), and his spitting (nafth).'"

(Section)

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan﴾, then according to what we have mentioned, the expression of the intention of an act by the act itself is the well-known view. There is a subtler aspect than this, which is that the Arabs sometimes express by the verb the beginning of undertaking it, and sometimes express its completion. They say "I did" at the start and "I did" at the finish. This is a true usage. On this basis, the meaning of "recite" in the verse is the beginning of the act: that is, when you commence and begin the recitation, then seek refuge. The seeking of refuge is thus ordered upon the commencement, which is the initial stage, preface, and forerunner of the act.

From this is His saying: "He prayed the dawn prayer until dawn broke."

Narrated by Muslim, at-Tirmidhi, and an-Nasa'i. That is, he began the prayer at its appearance.

As for his saying: "Then he prayed it the next day after it had become bright," the correct view is that what is meant is the beginning. A group said what is meant is the end, including as-Suhaylī. They erred in that, and the hadith is explicit that he performed it on the first day early and delayed it on the second day to show the beginning and the end of its time.

﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾ (99)

Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, and the exegetes said: "He has no proof."

The correct view is that it should be said: he has no way by which he can dominate them, neither through proof nor through power. Power is included in the meaning of authority (sulṭān), and proof is only called authority because its holder dominates by it just as the holder of power dominates by his hand. God, glory be to Him, has informed that His enemy has no authority over His sincere, reliant servants. He said in Surat al-Ḥijr:

﴿He said: "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will certainly make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all, except among them Your chosen servants." He said: "This is a path [that leads] to Me, straight. Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators."﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 39-42].

And He said in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord. His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 99-100].

This contains two matters: first, the negation and nullification of his authority over the people of tawḥīd and sincerity. Second, the affirmation of his authority over the people of shirk and over whoever takes him as an ally.

When the enemy of God knew that God would not give him power over the people of tawḥīd and sincerity, he said: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your chosen servants among them﴾ [Ṣād: 82-83].

So the enemy of God knew that whoever holds fast to God, Mighty and Majestic, and sincerely devotes himself to Him and relies upon Him, cannot be overpowered by him to be led astray or misguided. Rather, his authority is over those who take him as an ally and associate others with God; these are his subjects, and he is their guardian, their ruler, and their leader.

If it is said: You have affirmed for him authority over His allies here, so how did He negate it in His saying, quoting him and confirming him: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: "Indeed, God promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. And I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me."﴾

And He, Most High, said: ﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except for a party of believers. And he had no authority over them, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it.﴾

It is answered: The authority that He affirmed for him over them is other than the authority that He negated, in two respects.

The first: The authority affirmed is the power to control them, to toy with them, and to drive them wherever he wills, by their enabling him through their obedience and allegiance to him. The authority negated is the authority of proof. Iblis had no proof through which he could dominate them; he merely invited them and they responded without proof or evidence.

The second: God did not make for him any authority over them at the outset at all; rather they gave him authority over themselves by their obedience to him and their entering into the body of his army and his party. He did not dominate them by his strength, for his plotting is weak. He only dominated them by their own will and choice.

The point is: whoever is targeted by the greatest of His allies, friends, and advisors, and he seizes him and seizes his children and household and hands them over to His enemy, then among his punishment is that this very enemy is given power over him.

And in I'lām al-Lahfān he said:

If it is said: You have affirmed for him authority over His allies in this place, so how does He negate it in His saying: ﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except for a party of believers. And he had no authority over them, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾ [Saba': 20-21].

It is answered: If the pronoun in His saying "And he had no authority over them" [Saba': 21] refers to the believers, then the question falls away, and the exception is disjunctive: that is, "But We tested them with Iblis, so that We might know who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it." If it refers to what it referred to in His saying "And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him" [Saba': 20], which is the apparent reading, then the disjunctive exception is valid because it occurs after a negation, and the meaning becomes: "We did not give him power over them except so that We might know who believes in the Hereafter."

Ibn Qutaybah said: "When Iblis asked God for respite, he said: 'I will surely mislead them, I will surely lead them astray, I will surely command them to such and such, and I will surely take from Your servants an appointed portion.' At the time of this statement he was not certain that what He had decreed for him would be fulfilled; he spoke only as one who assumes. When they followed him and obeyed him, what he assumed about them was confirmed. So God, Most High, said: 'Our giving him power over them was only so that We might know the believers from the doubters,' meaning: We know them as existing and manifest, so the word is realized and the recompense takes place."

On this basis, the authority here is over those who did not believe in the Hereafter and doubted it, and they are those who took him as an ally and associated others with Him. So the authority is affirmed, not negated, and this verse agrees with all the other verses.

If it is said: Then what do you make of the one in Surat Ibrahim, where he says to the people of the Fire: ﴿And I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me﴾ [Ibrahim: 22].

It is answered: The authority negated in this place is proof and evidence: that is, I had no proof or evidence against you by which I could argue against you, as Ibn ʿAbbas said: "I had no proof by which to argue against you." That is: I did not show you any proof, except that I invited you and you responded to me, and you believed my words and followed me without evidence or proof.

As for the authority affirmed in His saying: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾ [al-Nahl: 100],

it is his domination over them through misguidance and leading astray, and his empowerment over them, to the extent that he drives them toward disbelief and association and provokes them to it, and does not leave them to abandon him, as God, Most High, said: ﴿Have you not seen that We sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ [Maryam: 83].

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He urges them, urging them strongly." In another narration: "He incites them to incitement." In another wording: "He urges them to urging." In another: "He drives them to sins, driving them." In another: "He sets them aflame," that is, he moves them as water is moved by kindling beneath it. Al-Akhfash said: "He ignites them."

The reality of this is that "al-azz" is moving and stirring up, and from it is said of the boiling of a pot: al-aziz, because the water moves when boiling. From the hadith: "In his chest there is a sound like the boiling of a cauldron from weeping."

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "Al-aziz is the blazing and the movement, like the flaring of fire in firewood. It is said: 'Stir up your pot,' that is, kindle the fire beneath it. And the pot 'boiled' (ayyatha) when its boiling became intense." So al-azz has two meanings: the first is moving, and the second is kindling and inflaming. They are close, for it is a specific movement with driving and inflaming.

This is the authority he has over his allies and the people of shirk, but he does not have over that a proof or evidence of authority. They responded to him merely by his invitation to them, because it agreed with their desires and aims. They are the ones who aided against themselves and enabled their enemy to have authority over them by agreeing with him and following him. When they gave themselves over and submitted to him, he was given power over them as a punishment. By this the meaning of His saying, Glory be to Him, becomes clear: ﴿And God will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 141].

The verse is upon its generality and apparent meaning. The believers only commit from disobedience and opposition, which contradict faith, what makes the disbelievers have a way over them according to that disobedience. They are the ones who caused a way to be opened over them, just as they caused it at the Battle of Uhud through disobeying the Messenger and opposing him. God, glory be to Him, did not make for Satan any authority over the servant until the servant made for him a way to himself through obedience to him and association with Him. Then God made for him, at that point, a domination and subjugation over him. So whoever finds good, let him praise God, Most High, and whoever finds otherwise, let him blame none but himself.

Therefore tawhid (monotheism), tawakkul (trust in God) and ikhlas (sincerity) repel his authority, while shirk (association of partners with God) and its branches bring about his authority. All of it happens by the decree of the One in whose hand are the reins of affairs and to whom they all return, and to Him belongs the conclusive proof. Had He willed, He would have made mankind one community, but His wisdom, His praiseworthiness and His dominion refused anything other than this. ﴿So to God belongs all praise, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the worlds. And to Him belongs grandeur in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 36-37].

(Benefit)

People have raised a difficulty concerning the hadith about the killing of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, in which the Companions sought the Prophet's permission to say [something] about the Prophet (ﷺ), and that would contradict faith, yet he permitted them to do so.

Answers have been given to this, in several ways:

The first: The compulsion to utter a word of disbelief removes it from being disbelief while the heart remains at peace with faith. Ka'b had gone to great lengths in harming the Muslims and had exceeded the bounds in this, inciting [others] to fight them, and in killing him was the deliverance of the Muslims from that. So the people were compelled to speak what they spoke, and this compelled them to defend themselves with their tongues while their hearts remained at peace with faith. However, this answer is not strong.

The second answer: That killing and that speech were not explicit in containing disbelief, but rather allusive and equivocal, containing sound aims that gave the appearance of agreeing with his purpose. This may be permissible in war, which is "deception" (khud'ah).

The third answer: This speech and the disparagement were done with his permission, and the right belonged to him. When the holder of a right grants permission concerning his right for a general, lawful benefit, it is not forbidden.

For one who has been afflicted by a trial (fitnah), there is no remedy like patience. If he is patient, the trial becomes a means of purifying him and freeing him from sins, just as the furnace (kir) removes the impurities from gold and silver.

Consider carefully how He combined "tasting" (dhawq) and "clothing" (libas), so as to indicate the direct contact with what is tasted, its encompassing and its comprehensiveness. The report of its tasting conveys that it is a direct, actual occurrence that is not awaited, for fear may be anticipated without being directly experienced. The report of its clothing conveys that it is all-encompassing and comprehensive, like clothing for the body.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 16, verse 120–121 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, glory be to Him, praised His friend Ibrahim with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a community (ummah), devoutly obedient to Allah, upright (hanif), and he was not of the polytheists. [He was] grateful for His favours; He chose him and guided him to a straight path.﴾

So these are four kinds of praise, which He opened with his being an ummah, and the ummah is the exemplar who is followed.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "The ummah is the one who teaches good."

It is on the pattern of fi'lah from al-i'timam (following), like qudwah (exemplar), and it is the one who is followed.

The difference between ummah and imam is in two respects:

The first: the imam is whatever is followed, whether that is by intention and awareness or not. For this reason the road is called an imam, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, the companions of the Thicket were wrongdoers. So We took retribution from them, and indeed, both [cities] are on a clear imam.﴾ [15:78–79]

That is, on a clear road that is not hidden from the traveller. The road is not called an ummah.

The second: the ummah carries an added meaning, namely the one who combines the qualities of perfection, both knowledge and action, to the extent that he remains a unique individual on his own. He is the one who gathers traits that are scattered among others, so it is as if he is distinguished from others by their being gathered in him, and their scattering or absence in others.

The word ummah conveys this meaning because of the doubled mim in it, which indicates gathering by its articulation and repetition. Likewise, the initial damma (u), for the vowel "u" comes from the waw, and its point of articulation is pursed when it is pronounced. And it is joined with the ta' which indicates unity, as in ghurfah (a single scoop) and luqmah (a single morsel).

From this is the hadith: "Indeed, Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as an ummah alone."

So gathering and collectiveness are inherent in the meaning of ummah, and from it is named the ummah that is the individual among nations, because they are people gathered upon one religion or in one era.

The second: His saying ﴿devoutly obedient to Allah (qanitan li-Allah)﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: "The qanit is the obedient one."

Qunut is explained in several ways, all of which return to constancy in obedience.

The third: His saying ﴿hanif﴾. The hanif is the one who turns toward Allah, and this meaning necessarily entails his turning away from everything else. Turning away is therefore an inherent meaning of hanif, not what it is linguistically coined for.

The fourth: His saying ﴿grateful for His favours (shakiran li-an'umih)﴾. Gratitude for blessings rests on three pillars: acknowledging the blessing, attributing it to the one who bestowed it, and spending it in what pleases Him and acting upon it in the way that is due. The servant is not truly grateful except by these three things.

The point is that He praised His friend with four qualities, all of which return to knowledge and acting upon it, teaching and spreading it. Thus all perfection returns to knowledge, acting upon it, and calling others to it.

[Section: The Station of Gratitude]

Among the stations of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the station of gratitude (shukr).

It is among the highest of stations, and it is above the station of contentment (ridha) and more. Contentment is included within gratitude, since gratitude is impossible to exist without it.

It is half of faith, as has preceded, and faith is two halves: half gratitude and half patience.

Allah has commanded it, forbidden its opposite, praised its people, described His elite creation with it, made it the goal of His creation and command, promised its people the best of rewards, made it a cause for more of His bounty, a guardian and protector of His blessing, informed that its people are those who benefit from His signs, and derived for them a name from His names. Indeed He, glory be to Him, is the Grateful (ash-Shakur), and He brings the grateful to what he is grateful for, rather He returns the grateful as one who is thanked. He is the Lord's ultimate aim from His servant, and its people are the few among His servants. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And be grateful for the blessing of Allah, if it is Him that you worship﴾ [16:114]; and He said: ﴿And be grateful to Me and do not be ungrateful﴾ [2:152]; and He said about His friend Ibrahim ﷺ: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a community, devoutly obedient to Allah, upright, and he was not of the polytheists — grateful for His favours﴾ [16:120–121]; and He said about Nuh (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾ [17:3].

And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing, and made for you hearing, sight and hearts that you might give thanks﴾ [16:78]; and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And worship Him and be grateful to Him; to Him you will be returned﴾ [29:17]; and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾ [3:144]; and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed: If you are grateful, I will surely increase you; but if you deny, indeed My punishment is severe﴾ [14:7]; and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every patient, grateful person﴾ [14:5].

He named Himself "the Grateful" (shakir) and "the Very Grateful" (shakur), and He named the grateful with these two names. So He gave them a share of His attribute and named them with His name. Sufficient for you with this is His love for the grateful and His bounty.

His returning the grateful as one who is thanked is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, this has been a reward for you, and your effort has been appreciated (mashkura)﴾ [76:22].

And the Lord's contentment with His servant for it is like His saying: ﴿And if you are grateful, He is pleased with you﴾ [39:7]; and the fewness of its people among the worlds indicates that they are His elite, like His saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [34:13].

In the two Sahihs, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he stood in prayer until his feet swelled. It was said to him: "You do this, while Allah has forgiven you what came before of your sin and what came after?" He said: "Shall I not be a grateful servant?"

And he said to Mu'adh: "By Allah, O Mu'adh, I love you. So do not neglect to say at the end of every prayer: O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You, and to worship You well."

In the Musnad and at-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to supplicate with these words: "O Allah, help me and do not help against me. Support me and do not support against me. Plan for me and do not plan against me. Guide me and make guidance easy for me. Support me against whoever transgresses against me. My Lord, make me thankful to You, remembering You, fearful of You, obedient to You, humble before You, returning to You, penitent. My Lord, accept my repentance, wash away my sin, answer my supplication, make my proof firm, guide my heart, make my tongue upright, and remove the rancour of my chest."

[Section: The Root Meaning of Shukr in Language]

The root meaning of shukr in the usage of the language is the clear manifestation of the effect of nourishment on the bodies of animals, clearly apparent. It is said: "The beast shakarat (thrived) yashkaru shukaran," on the pattern of "samina yasmanu simanan" (grew fat), when the effect of fodder appears upon it. And a beast that is shakur is one upon which fatness appears beyond what it eats and is given of fodder.

In Sahih Muslim: "So much so that the beasts thrive on their flesh," meaning they grow fat from the abundance of what they eat of it.

Likewise, its reality in servitude is the manifestation of the effect of Allah's blessing upon the tongue of His servant as praise and acknowledgment; upon his heart as witnessing and love; and upon his limbs as submission and obedience.

Shukr is built upon five foundations: the grateful one's submission to the one thanked; his love for Him; his acknowledgment of His blessing; his praise of Him for it; and that he does not use it in what He dislikes.

These five are the foundation of gratitude and its structure built upon them. Whenever one of them is lacking, one foundation of gratitude is defective.

Everyone who speaks of gratitude alone, his speech returns to these and revolves around them.

It has been said: its definition is acknowledging the blessing of the Benefactor in a manner of submission.

It has been said: it is praise of the Benefactor by mentioning His kindness.

It has been said: it is the heart's devotion to loving the blessings, the limbs' devotion to His obedience, the tongue's flowing with His remembrance and praise of Him.

It has been said: it is witnessing the favour and guarding its sanctity.

How subtle is what Hamdun al-Qassar said: "The gratitude for a blessing is that you see yourself in it as a freeloader (tufayli)."

Abu 'Uthman said: "Gratitude is recognising one's inability to be grateful."

It has been said: "Gratitude is attributing blessings to their giver with the description of humble submission to Him."

al-Junayd said: "Gratitude is that you do not see yourself as worthy of the blessing."

This is the meaning of Hamdun's words, that one sees oneself in it as a freeloader.

Ruwaym said: "Gratitude is exhausting one's capacity."

ash-Shibli said: "Gratitude is seeing the Benefactor, not seeing the blessing."

I say: his words may bear two meanings.

One: that one passes away through seeing the Benefactor from seeing His blessings.

The second: that the seeing and witnessing of the blessings does not veil one from seeing the Benefactor who bestowed them. This is more perfect. The first is stronger according to them.

Perfection is that you witness both the blessing and the Benefactor, because gratitude is in proportion to witnessing the blessing. The more complete it is, the more perfect the gratitude. Allah loves from His servant that he witnesses His blessings, acknowledges them to Him, praises Him for them, and loves Him because of them, not that he passes away from them and becomes absent from witnessing them.

It has been said: gratitude is the tether of existing blessings and the snare of missing blessings.

The gratitude of the common folk is for food, drink, clothing, and the sustenance of bodies.

The gratitude of the elite is for monotheism (tawhid), faith, and the sustenance of hearts.

Dawud (peace be upon him) said: "My Lord, how can I thank You, when my thanking You is itself a blessing from You that requires thanks?" He said: "Now you have thanked Me, O Dawud."

In another Israelite narration: Musa (peace be upon him) said: "My Lord, You created Adam with Your hand, breathed into him of Your spirit, made Your angels prostrate to him, taught him the names of all things, and You did and did. So how did he thank You?" Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "He knew that it was from Me, and his knowing that was his thanks to Me."

It has been said: gratitude is delighting in His praise, for blessings you did not deserve from His giving.

al-Junayd, when Sari asked him about gratitude while he was a boy, said: "Gratitude is that none of Allah's blessings be used in aid of His disobedience." He said: "From where do you have this?" He said: "From sitting with you."

It has been said: whoever's hands fall short of repaying kindnesses, let his tongue lengthen in gratitude.

Gratitude always brings increase, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [14:7]. So whenever you do not see your state in increase, return to gratitude.

In a divine narration: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "The people of My remembrance are the people of My company, the people of My gratitude are the people of My increase, the people of My obedience are the people of My honour, and the people of My disobedience — I do not despair them of My mercy. If they repent, I am their beloved; if they do not repent, I am their physician. I afflict them with calamities to purify them from their faults."

It has been said: whoever conceals a blessing has denied it, and whoever displays and spreads it has thanked for it.

This is taken from his saying ﷺ: "Indeed, when Allah bestows a blessing upon a servant, He loves to see the effect of His blessing upon His servant."

On this has been said:
"Among the misfortunes is that my gratitude is silent about what you have done, while your goodness speaks;
And I see your favour to me, then I conceal it; indeed then I would be a thief of the generosity of the noble."

[Section: Degrees of Gratitude]

[The First Degree: Gratitude for what is loved]

He said: it is in three degrees. The first degree: gratitude for what is loved. This is a gratitude in which Muslims, Jews, Christians and Magians share. And from the vastness of the mercy of the Creator, glory be to Him, is that He counted it as gratitude, promised increase for it, and made reward obligatory upon it.

When you know the reality of gratitude, and that part of its reality is seeking help from the blessings of the Benefactor in His obedience and pleasure, you know that the people of Islam are specifically concerned with this degree, and that the true reality of gratitude for what is loved is not for others.

Yes, others share some of its pillars and parts, such as acknowledging the blessing and praising the Benefactor for it. For all creation is in Allah's blessings, and everyone who affirms Allah as Lord, and as sole Creator and Benefactor, attributes his blessing to Him. But the matter lies in the completion of the reality of gratitude, which is seeking help through them in His pleasure. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, wrote to Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him: "The least that is owed to the Benefactor by one upon whom he has bestowed favour is that he not make what He has bestowed a path to disobeying Him."

The meaning of the Shaykh is known. That is, this gratitude is shared. It is the acknowledgment of His blessings, praise of Him for them, and kindness to His creation from them. Without doubt this necessitates their preservation for them and an increase of them. So this part of gratitude is shared, and its fruit may be in this world as hastened reward, and in the Hereafter as lightening of punishment, for the Fire has levels of punishment that differ.

[Section: The Second Degree: Gratitude in Adversities]

He said: this is for one to whom all states are equal, by displaying contentment; and for one who distinguishes between states: for restraining anger, concealing complaint, observing good manners, and following the path of knowledge. This grateful one is the first to be called to Paradise.

He means that gratitude for adversities is more severe and difficult than gratitude for what is loved, and for this reason it is above it in rank. It arises only from one of two men:

Either a man who does not distinguish between states, but for whom the disliked and the loved are equal. His gratitude is a display on his part of contentment with what has befallen him, and this is the station of contentment.

The second man: one who distinguishes between states. He does not love what is disliked, nor is he content with its descending upon him. So when something disliked befalls him, he thanks God for it, and his thanks becomes a suppression of the anger that struck him, a concealment of complaint, an observance of good manners (adab), and a following of the path of knowledge ('ilm). For knowledge and good manners both command thanking God in times of ease and times of hardship. Thus he takes this thanks as the path of knowledge, because he is thankful to God in the manner of one who is content with His decree, like the state of the one before him. The one before him is higher than him.

This thankful one was the first to be called to Paradise, because he receives adversities, which most people meet with impatience and anger, and the middling among them meet with patience, and the elite among them meet with contentment, while he meets them with something higher than all of that, which is thanks. So he was the foremost of them in entering Paradise, and the first of them to be called to it.

He divided the people of this rank into two categories: foremost (sabiqun) and those brought near (muqarrabun), according to their division into those for whom states are equal, whether disliked or loved, so that neither one is preferred over the other. Rather, by preferring what their Lord is pleased with for them over what they themselves would like for themselves, they have passed away (fana) in this preference. And [the second category is] those who prefer what is loved, but when what is disliked descends upon them, they meet it with thanks.

[Section: The Third Rank: that the servant witnesses none but the Bestower]

He said: The third rank is that the servant witnesses none but the Bestower. When he witnesses the Bestower as Master (ʿubudiyyah), he regards the blessing as great from Him. When he witnesses Him as Beloved (hubb), he finds hardship sweet from Him. And when he witnesses Him in singularity (tafrid), he witnesses from Him neither blessing nor hardship.

The one who holds this rank is absorbed, through witnessing the Bestower, away from the blessing. So his witnessing has no room for the Bestower and for other than Him.

He divided its people into three categories: the people of witnessing the servitude (shuhud al-ʿubudiyyah), the people of witnessing the love (shuhud al-hubb), and the people of witnessing the singularity (shuhud al-tafrid). And he assigned to each of them a ruling that is most fitting for it.

As for witnessing Him in servitude: it is the servant's observation of the Master with the reality of servitude and possession belonging to Him. When servants stand before their master, they forget the rank and nearness that they have been singled out with over others, through their total absorption in the courtesy of servitude and its due, and their attentiveness to their master, out of fear that he might signal to them with a command and find them heedless of his attention. This is a matter known to whoever has observed the conditions of kings and their close attendants.

This is the servant's witnessing of the Bestower through the attribute of his servitude to Him, and his being absorbed away from the favour, by what he has obtained from Him of nearness through which he is distinguished from others.

So the possessor of this witnessing: when his master bestows a favour upon him in this state, while he is standing in the station of servitude, it necessarily follows that he belittles himself in the presence of his master to the utmost degree of belittlement, together with his heart being filled with love for Him. Whatever bounty he receives from Him in this state, he regards it as great. Reality bears witness to this in the state of the perfectly loving lover, absorbed in witnessing his beloved, when he is handed something small: he sees it in that station as extremely great, and no one else sees it as such.

The second category: he witnesses the Truth with a witnessing of love that is overpowering and dominating over him, and he is absorbed in witnessing Him in this way. For in this state he finds hardship sweet from Him, because the lover finds the beloved's action toward him sweet.

At the least, in this witnessing: the burden of hardships becomes light for him, even if his soul does not permit him to find them sweet. Among the well-known accounts that people relate on this, there is enough that makes mentioning them unnecessary, such as the state of the man who was being struck with whips and did not move, until the last whip was struck. Then he cried out with a great cry. He was asked about that, and he said: "The eye that was looking at me at the time of the striking was preventing me from feeling the pain. When I lost it, I found the pain of the striking."

This state is incidental and not necessary, for nature refuses to find hostile things sweet as it finds agreeable things sweet.

Indeed, the authority of love may grow strong until the lover finds sweet what others find burdensome, finds light what others find heavy, finds comfort in what the unattached find frightening, and feels frightened by what he finds comforting, and finds gentle what others find rugged. The strength of this and its weakness depend on the degree to which the authority of love overpowers and dominates the heart of the lover.

The third category: that he witnesses Him in singularity. For he witnesses with Him neither blessing nor hardship.

He says: the witnessing of singularity annihilates the trace (rasm). This is the state of the all-absorbing annihilation (fana') in which one witnesses neither blessing nor calamity. For he is absorbed, by the One witnessed, away from his witnessing of himself, and passes away from himself in Him. So how could he witness with Him a blessing or a calamity?

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 16, verse 120–121 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, glory be to Him, praised His friend Ibrahim with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a community (ummah), devoutly obedient to Allah, upright (hanif), and he was not of the polytheists. [He was] grateful for His favours; He chose him and guided him to a straight path.﴾

So these are four kinds of praise, which He opened with his being an ummah, and the ummah is the exemplar who is followed.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "The ummah is the one who teaches good."

It is on the pattern of fi'lah from al-i'timam (following), like qudwah (exemplar), and it is the one who is followed.

The difference between ummah and imam is in two respects:

The first: the imam is whatever is followed, whether that is by intention and awareness or not. For this reason the road is called an imam, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, the companions of the Thicket were wrongdoers. So We took retribution from them, and indeed, both [cities] are on a clear imam.﴾ [15:78–79]

That is, on a clear road that is not hidden from the traveller. The road is not called an ummah.

The second: the ummah carries an added meaning, namely the one who combines the qualities of perfection, both knowledge and action, to the extent that he remains a unique individual on his own. He is the one who gathers traits that are scattered among others, so it is as if he is distinguished from others by their being gathered in him, and their scattering or absence in others.

The word ummah conveys this meaning because of the doubled mim in it, which indicates gathering by its articulation and repetition. Likewise, the initial damma (u), for the vowel "u" comes from the waw, and its point of articulation is pursed when it is pronounced. And it is joined with the ta' which indicates unity, as in ghurfah (a single scoop) and luqmah (a single morsel).

From this is the hadith: "Indeed, Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as an ummah alone."

So gathering and collectiveness are inherent in the meaning of ummah, and from it is named the ummah that is the individual among nations, because they are people gathered upon one religion or in one era.

The second: His saying ﴿devoutly obedient to Allah (qanitan li-Allah)﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: "The qanit is the obedient one."

Qunut is explained in several ways, all of which return to constancy in obedience.

The third: His saying ﴿hanif﴾. The hanif is the one who turns toward Allah, and this meaning necessarily entails his turning away from everything else. Turning away is therefore an inherent meaning of hanif, not what it is linguistically coined for.

The fourth: His saying ﴿grateful for His favours (shakiran li-an'umih)﴾. Gratitude for blessings rests on three pillars: acknowledging the blessing, attributing it to the one who bestowed it, and spending it in what pleases Him and acting upon it in the way that is due. The servant is not truly grateful except by these three things.

The point is that He praised His friend with four qualities, all of which return to knowledge and acting upon it, teaching and spreading it. Thus all perfection returns to knowledge, acting upon it, and calling others to it.

[Section: The Station of Gratitude]

Among the stations of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the station of gratitude (shukr).

It is among the highest of stations, and it is above the station of contentment (ridha) and more. Contentment is included within gratitude, since gratitude is impossible to exist without it.

It is half of faith, as has preceded, and faith is two halves: half gratitude and half patience.

Allah has commanded it, forbidden its opposite, praised its people, described His elite creation with it, made it the goal of His creation and command, promised its people the best of rewards, made it a cause for more of His bounty, a guardian and protector of His blessing, informed that its people are those who benefit from His signs, and derived for them a name from His names. Indeed He, glory be to Him, is the Grateful (ash-Shakur), and He brings the grateful to what he is grateful for, rather He returns the grateful as one who is thanked. He is the Lord's ultimate aim from His servant, and its people are the few among His servants. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And be grateful for the blessing of Allah, if it is Him that you worship﴾ [16:114]; and He said: ﴿And be grateful to Me and do not be ungrateful﴾ [2:152]; and He said about His friend Ibrahim ﷺ: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a community, devoutly obedient to Allah, upright, and he was not of the polytheists — grateful for His favours﴾ [16:120–121]; and He said about Nuh (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾ [17:3].

And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing, and made for you hearing, sight and hearts that you might give thanks﴾ [16:78]; and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And worship Him and be grateful to Him; to Him you will be returned﴾ [29:17]; and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾ [3:144]; and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed: If you are grateful, I will surely increase you; but if you deny, indeed My punishment is severe﴾ [14:7]; and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every patient, grateful person﴾ [14:5].

He named Himself "the Grateful" (shakir) and "the Very Grateful" (shakur), and He named the grateful with these two names. So He gave them a share of His attribute and named them with His name. Sufficient for you with this is His love for the grateful and His bounty.

His returning the grateful as one who is thanked is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, this has been a reward for you, and your effort has been appreciated (mashkura)﴾ [76:22].

And the Lord's contentment with His servant for it is like His saying: ﴿And if you are grateful, He is pleased with you﴾ [39:7]; and the fewness of its people among the worlds indicates that they are His elite, like His saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [34:13].

In the two Sahihs, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he stood in prayer until his feet swelled. It was said to him: "You do this, while Allah has forgiven you what came before of your sin and what came after?" He said: "Shall I not be a grateful servant?"

And he said to Mu'adh: "By Allah, O Mu'adh, I love you. So do not neglect to say at the end of every prayer: O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You, and to worship You well."

In the Musnad and at-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to supplicate with these words: "O Allah, help me and do not help against me. Support me and do not support against me. Plan for me and do not plan against me. Guide me and make guidance easy for me. Support me against whoever transgresses against me. My Lord, make me thankful to You, remembering You, fearful of You, obedient to You, humble before You, returning to You, penitent. My Lord, accept my repentance, wash away my sin, answer my supplication, make my proof firm, guide my heart, make my tongue upright, and remove the rancour of my chest."

[Section: The Root Meaning of Shukr in Language]

The root meaning of shukr in the usage of the language is the clear manifestation of the effect of nourishment on the bodies of animals, clearly apparent. It is said: "The beast shakarat (thrived) yashkaru shukaran," on the pattern of "samina yasmanu simanan" (grew fat), when the effect of fodder appears upon it. And a beast that is shakur is one upon which fatness appears beyond what it eats and is given of fodder.

In Sahih Muslim: "So much so that the beasts thrive on their flesh," meaning they grow fat from the abundance of what they eat of it.

Likewise, its reality in servitude is the manifestation of the effect of Allah's blessing upon the tongue of His servant as praise and acknowledgment; upon his heart as witnessing and love; and upon his limbs as submission and obedience.

Shukr is built upon five foundations: the grateful one's submission to the one thanked; his love for Him; his acknowledgment of His blessing; his praise of Him for it; and that he does not use it in what He dislikes.

These five are the foundation of gratitude and its structure built upon them. Whenever one of them is lacking, one foundation of gratitude is defective.

Everyone who speaks of gratitude alone, his speech returns to these and revolves around them.

It has been said: its definition is acknowledging the blessing of the Benefactor in a manner of submission.

It has been said: it is praise of the Benefactor by mentioning His kindness.

It has been said: it is the heart's devotion to loving the blessings, the limbs' devotion to His obedience, the tongue's flowing with His remembrance and praise of Him.

It has been said: it is witnessing the favour and guarding its sanctity.

How subtle is what Hamdun al-Qassar said: "The gratitude for a blessing is that you see yourself in it as a freeloader (tufayli)."

Abu 'Uthman said: "Gratitude is recognising one's inability to be grateful."

It has been said: "Gratitude is attributing blessings to their giver with the description of humble submission to Him."

al-Junayd said: "Gratitude is that you do not see yourself as worthy of the blessing."

This is the meaning of Hamdun's words, that one sees oneself in it as a freeloader.

Ruwaym said: "Gratitude is exhausting one's capacity."

ash-Shibli said: "Gratitude is seeing the Benefactor, not seeing the blessing."

I say: his words may bear two meanings.

One: that one passes away through seeing the Benefactor from seeing His blessings.

The second: that the seeing and witnessing of the blessings does not veil one from seeing the Benefactor who bestowed them. This is more perfect. The first is stronger according to them.

Perfection is that you witness both the blessing and the Benefactor, because gratitude is in proportion to witnessing the blessing. The more complete it is, the more perfect the gratitude. Allah loves from His servant that he witnesses His blessings, acknowledges them to Him, praises Him for them, and loves Him because of them, not that he passes away from them and becomes absent from witnessing them.

It has been said: gratitude is the tether of existing blessings and the snare of missing blessings.

The gratitude of the common folk is for food, drink, clothing, and the sustenance of bodies.

The gratitude of the elite is for monotheism (tawhid), faith, and the sustenance of hearts.

Dawud (peace be upon him) said: "My Lord, how can I thank You, when my thanking You is itself a blessing from You that requires thanks?" He said: "Now you have thanked Me, O Dawud."

In another Israelite narration: Musa (peace be upon him) said: "My Lord, You created Adam with Your hand, breathed into him of Your spirit, made Your angels prostrate to him, taught him the names of all things, and You did and did. So how did he thank You?" Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "He knew that it was from Me, and his knowing that was his thanks to Me."

It has been said: gratitude is delighting in His praise, for blessings you did not deserve from His giving.

al-Junayd, when Sari asked him about gratitude while he was a boy, said: "Gratitude is that none of Allah's blessings be used in aid of His disobedience." He said: "From where do you have this?" He said: "From sitting with you."

It has been said: whoever's hands fall short of repaying kindnesses, let his tongue lengthen in gratitude.

Gratitude always brings increase, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [14:7]. So whenever you do not see your state in increase, return to gratitude.

In a divine narration: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "The people of My remembrance are the people of My company, the people of My gratitude are the people of My increase, the people of My obedience are the people of My honour, and the people of My disobedience — I do not despair them of My mercy. If they repent, I am their beloved; if they do not repent, I am their physician. I afflict them with calamities to purify them from their faults."

It has been said: whoever conceals a blessing has denied it, and whoever displays and spreads it has thanked for it.

This is taken from his saying ﷺ: "Indeed, when Allah bestows a blessing upon a servant, He loves to see the effect of His blessing upon His servant."

On this has been said:
"Among the misfortunes is that my gratitude is silent about what you have done, while your goodness speaks;
And I see your favour to me, then I conceal it; indeed then I would be a thief of the generosity of the noble."

[Section: Degrees of Gratitude]

[The First Degree: Gratitude for what is loved]

He said: it is in three degrees. The first degree: gratitude for what is loved. This is a gratitude in which Muslims, Jews, Christians and Magians share. And from the vastness of the mercy of the Creator, glory be to Him, is that He counted it as gratitude, promised increase for it, and made reward obligatory upon it.

When you know the reality of gratitude, and that part of its reality is seeking help from the blessings of the Benefactor in His obedience and pleasure, you know that the people of Islam are specifically concerned with this degree, and that the true reality of gratitude for what is loved is not for others.

Yes, others share some of its pillars and parts, such as acknowledging the blessing and praising the Benefactor for it. For all creation is in Allah's blessings, and everyone who affirms Allah as Lord, and as sole Creator and Benefactor, attributes his blessing to Him. But the matter lies in the completion of the reality of gratitude, which is seeking help through them in His pleasure. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, wrote to Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him: "The least that is owed to the Benefactor by one upon whom he has bestowed favour is that he not make what He has bestowed a path to disobeying Him."

The meaning of the Shaykh is known. That is, this gratitude is shared. It is the acknowledgment of His blessings, praise of Him for them, and kindness to His creation from them. Without doubt this necessitates their preservation for them and an increase of them. So this part of gratitude is shared, and its fruit may be in this world as hastened reward, and in the Hereafter as lightening of punishment, for the Fire has levels of punishment that differ.

[Section: The Second Degree: Gratitude in Adversities]

He said: this is for one to whom all states are equal, by displaying contentment; and for one who distinguishes between states: for restraining anger, concealing complaint, observing good manners, and following the path of knowledge. This grateful one is the first to be called to Paradise.

He means that gratitude for adversities is more severe and difficult than gratitude for what is loved, and for this reason it is above it in rank. It arises only from one of two men:

Either a man who does not distinguish between states, but for whom the disliked and the loved are equal. His gratitude is a display on his part of contentment with what has befallen him, and this is the station of contentment.

The second man: one who distinguishes between states. He does not love what is disliked, nor is he content with its descending upon him. So when something disliked befalls him, he thanks God for it, and his thanks becomes a suppression of the anger that struck him, a concealment of complaint, an observance of good manners (adab), and a following of the path of knowledge ('ilm). For knowledge and good manners both command thanking God in times of ease and times of hardship. Thus he takes this thanks as the path of knowledge, because he is thankful to God in the manner of one who is content with His decree, like the state of the one before him. The one before him is higher than him.

This thankful one was the first to be called to Paradise, because he receives adversities, which most people meet with impatience and anger, and the middling among them meet with patience, and the elite among them meet with contentment, while he meets them with something higher than all of that, which is thanks. So he was the foremost of them in entering Paradise, and the first of them to be called to it.

He divided the people of this rank into two categories: foremost (sabiqun) and those brought near (muqarrabun), according to their division into those for whom states are equal, whether disliked or loved, so that neither one is preferred over the other. Rather, by preferring what their Lord is pleased with for them over what they themselves would like for themselves, they have passed away (fana) in this preference. And [the second category is] those who prefer what is loved, but when what is disliked descends upon them, they meet it with thanks.

[Section: The Third Rank: that the servant witnesses none but the Bestower]

He said: The third rank is that the servant witnesses none but the Bestower. When he witnesses the Bestower as Master (ʿubudiyyah), he regards the blessing as great from Him. When he witnesses Him as Beloved (hubb), he finds hardship sweet from Him. And when he witnesses Him in singularity (tafrid), he witnesses from Him neither blessing nor hardship.

The one who holds this rank is absorbed, through witnessing the Bestower, away from the blessing. So his witnessing has no room for the Bestower and for other than Him.

He divided its people into three categories: the people of witnessing the servitude (shuhud al-ʿubudiyyah), the people of witnessing the love (shuhud al-hubb), and the people of witnessing the singularity (shuhud al-tafrid). And he assigned to each of them a ruling that is most fitting for it.

As for witnessing Him in servitude: it is the servant's observation of the Master with the reality of servitude and possession belonging to Him. When servants stand before their master, they forget the rank and nearness that they have been singled out with over others, through their total absorption in the courtesy of servitude and its due, and their attentiveness to their master, out of fear that he might signal to them with a command and find them heedless of his attention. This is a matter known to whoever has observed the conditions of kings and their close attendants.

This is the servant's witnessing of the Bestower through the attribute of his servitude to Him, and his being absorbed away from the favour, by what he has obtained from Him of nearness through which he is distinguished from others.

So the possessor of this witnessing: when his master bestows a favour upon him in this state, while he is standing in the station of servitude, it necessarily follows that he belittles himself in the presence of his master to the utmost degree of belittlement, together with his heart being filled with love for Him. Whatever bounty he receives from Him in this state, he regards it as great. Reality bears witness to this in the state of the perfectly loving lover, absorbed in witnessing his beloved, when he is handed something small: he sees it in that station as extremely great, and no one else sees it as such.

The second category: he witnesses the Truth with a witnessing of love that is overpowering and dominating over him, and he is absorbed in witnessing Him in this way. For in this state he finds hardship sweet from Him, because the lover finds the beloved's action toward him sweet.

At the least, in this witnessing: the burden of hardships becomes light for him, even if his soul does not permit him to find them sweet. Among the well-known accounts that people relate on this, there is enough that makes mentioning them unnecessary, such as the state of the man who was being struck with whips and did not move, until the last whip was struck. Then he cried out with a great cry. He was asked about that, and he said: "The eye that was looking at me at the time of the striking was preventing me from feeling the pain. When I lost it, I found the pain of the striking."

This state is incidental and not necessary, for nature refuses to find hostile things sweet as it finds agreeable things sweet.

Indeed, the authority of love may grow strong until the lover finds sweet what others find burdensome, finds light what others find heavy, finds comfort in what the unattached find frightening, and feels frightened by what he finds comforting, and finds gentle what others find rugged. The strength of this and its weakness depend on the degree to which the authority of love overpowers and dominates the heart of the lover.

The third category: that he witnesses Him in singularity. For he witnesses with Him neither blessing nor hardship.

He says: the witnessing of singularity annihilates the trace (rasm). This is the state of the all-absorbing annihilation (fana') in which one witnesses neither blessing nor calamity. For he is absorbed, by the One witnessed, away from his witnessing of himself, and passes away from himself in Him. So how could he witness with Him a blessing or a calamity?

[Section: The Reward of the Sincere One]

And His saying: "So what do you think of the reward with God in His swift provision and the treasuries of His mercy?"

He intends by this to magnify the reward of the sincere one, and that it is a swift provision, whether for the heart, for the body, or for both. His mercy is stored in His treasuries. God, glorified is He, rewards the servant for the good he has done in this world without fail, and then in the Hereafter He pays him his full reward, as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And you will only be paid your wages in full on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 185]. What is obtained in this world as recompense for righteous deeds is not a full payment (tawfiyah), even though it is another kind of reward, as He said, Exalted is He, concerning Abraham: ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 27]. This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him good in this world, and indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ [al-Nahl: 122]. So He informed, glorified is He, that He gave His Friend (khalil) his reward in this world in the form of the blessings He bestowed upon him in his self, his heart, his children, his wealth, and his good life. But that is not a full payment. The Qur'an has indicated in more than one place that whoever does good receives two rewards: his deed is recompensed in this world, and his reward is completed for him in the Hereafter. As in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better, and excellent is the abode of the righteous﴾ [al-Nahl: 30]. And in another verse: ﴿And those who emigrated for God after they had been wronged, We will surely settle them in this world in a good place, and the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew﴾ [al-Nahl: 41]. He also said in this surah: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them with their best deeds﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]. And He said in it concerning His Friend: ﴿And We gave him good in this world, and indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ [al-Nahl: 122]. This meaning has been repeated in this surah alone, and not elsewhere, in four places, for a wondrous secret. This is the surah of blessings, in which God, glorified is He, enumerated the roots and branches of blessings. So He made His servants aware that for them with Him in the Hereafter are blessings many times these, whose difference cannot be grasped, and that these are some of His swift blessings upon them. And that if they obey Him, He will add to these blessings other blessings, and then in the Hereafter He will pay them the wages of their deeds in full. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And that you should seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance; He will let you enjoy a good provision until an appointed term and give every person of virtue his virtue﴾ [Hud: 3]. Therefore the Commander of the Believers said: "So what do you think of the reward with God in His swift provision and the treasuries of His mercy? And peace."

This is some of what relates to the book of the Commander of the Believers, may God be pleased with him, of the wisdoms and benefits. And praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.

The commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 16, verse 125:

God, glory be to Him, made the levels of da'wah (calling to God) correspond to the levels of people.

The one who responds, who is receptive, intelligent, does not oppose the truth or reject it, is called with wisdom (al-hikmah).

The one who is receptive but has some heedlessness and delay is called with good admonition (al-maw'izah al-hasanah). This is the command and prohibition coupled with encouragement (targhib) and warning (tarhib).

The stubborn denier is argued with in the best manner (bi-llati hiya ahsan).

This is the correct meaning of this verse,

not what is claimed by the captive of Greek logic: that wisdom is the syllogism of demonstrative proof (qiyas al-burhan, i.e., demonstration). This, they say, is the calling of the elite, and good admonition is the syllogism of rhetoric (qiyas al-khitabah), which is the calling of the common people.

And argumentation in the best manner is the dialectical syllogism (al-qiyas al-jadali), which is repelling the troublemaker's sophistry with a dialectical syllogism whose premises are accepted.

This is false. It is built upon the principles of philosophy, it contradicts the principles of the Muslims and the foundations of the religion in many respects, and this is not the place to mention them.

(Section)

God, glory be to Him, mentioned the levels of da'wah and divided them into three categories according to the state of the one being called. He is either a seeker of the truth, desiring it, loving it, and preferring it over others once he knows it. Such a person is called with wisdom and needs neither admonition nor argument.

Or he is averse and occupied with the opposite of the truth, but if he knew it, he would know it, prefer it, and follow it. Such a person needs, along with wisdom, admonition through encouragement and warning.

Or he is stubborn and opposing. Such a person is argued with in the best manner. If he returns to the truth, well and good; otherwise, the argument passes from debate to force, if that is possible.

So the refutation of the falsifier has two benefits:

The first: that he turns back from his falsehood and returns to the truth.

The second: that his evil and enmity are restrained and people see clearly that what he holds is falsehood.

All these aims cannot be achieved by anything better than the proofs of the Qur'an and its discourse with the sects, for it is sufficient for this in the most complete way for one who reflects upon it, ponders it, and is granted understanding of it. Its proofs, although they are among the highest kinds of proof, follow a method other than the method of the theologians (mutakallimun) and the masters of dialectic and rational argument. They are the nearest thing to grasp, the clearest in indication, the strongest in demonstration, and the furthest from any doubt or suspicion.

As for the method of the theologians and the masters of dialectic, it is as the one who knows it said:

"Proofs that collapse like glass; you think them
truth, but every breaker is broken."

Its most distinctive feature is that it gives you the contradiction of the opponents and the disorder of their statements, but as for giving you knowledge and guidance:

"If you send a guide to the salt marshes seeking the gardens, you have wronged the guide."

If this is its condition, and it is inferior to the method of the philosophers and farther from the truth, how then is revelation opposed by these methods, and how are these preferred over it?

(Section)

The author of Manazil al-Sa'irin (Sahib al-Manazil) said: The foundations of remembrance (abniyat al-tadhakkur) are three: benefiting from admonition (al-intifa' bi-l-'izah), discerning insight through lessons (al-istibsar bi-l-'ibrah), and attaining the fruit of reflection (al-zafar bi-thamarat al-fikrah).

Benefiting from admonition is that the spark of fear and hope strikes the heart so that it moves to action, seeking deliverance from fear and desiring the attainment of what is hoped for.

Admonition is the command and prohibition coupled with encouragement and warning.

Admonition is of two kinds: admonition through what is heard, and admonition through what is witnessed. Admonition through what is heard is benefiting from the guidance and right direction he hears, from the counsels that came by the tongues of the messengers and what was revealed to them. Likewise is benefiting from admonition from every adviser and guide in matters of religion and worldly welfare.

Admonition through what is witnessed is benefiting from what he sees and observes in the world of places of lessons, the decrees of destiny (ahkam al-qadar), its courses, and the signs of God that he witnesses which indicate the truthfulness of His messengers.

As for discerning insight through lessons, it is the increase of insight beyond what one had in the station of reflection, through the power of recollection, because remembrance holds fast the meanings that were acquired through reflection upon the signs and lessons. He attains them through reflection, and they become polished and clear to him through remembrance. Thus resolve grows strong for the journey according to the strength of this discernment, for it necessitates focusing attention on what moves the desire, since seeking is a branch of awareness. Whenever awareness of the beloved grows strong, the heart's journey toward it intensifies, and whenever thought occupies itself with it, awareness of it, insight into it, and remembrance of it increase.

As for attaining the fruit of reflection, this is a subtle station.

Reflection has two fruits: the attainment of the sought object completely, as far as possible, and acting according to its requirement, observing its right. For the heart, during reflection, had become weary from its labors in obtaining the sought object. When the meanings were acquired and fermented in the heart, and the intellect rested, it returned to remember what it had acquired and surveyed, and it rejoiced and was delighted by it. In this station it corrects what it had missed in the station of reflection, because it has already approached it in the station of remembrance, which is higher than it. Then it begins on the intended fruit, which is acting according to its requirement, observing its right, for righteous action is the fruit of beneficial knowledge, which is the fruit of reflection.

If you wish to understand this through a sensible example: the seeker of wealth, as long as he is earnest in his seeking, is in weariness and exhaustion. When he attains it, he rests from the toil of seeking, returns from the journey of trade, surveys what he has gained and seen, and in this state corrects whatever he may have erred in while occupied with seeking. When it is sound for him and his gain is cool and pleasant to him, he begins to spend the wealth in the ways of benefit that are desired from it. And God knows best.

(Section) He said: One benefits from admonition only after three things are present: intense need for it, blindness to the faults of the admonisher, and the remembrance of promise and threat.

The servant's need for admonition, which is encouragement and warning, becomes intense only when his turning back to God and his remembrance grow weak. Otherwise, when his turning back and remembrance are strong, his need for reminder, encouragement, and warning does not become intense. Rather, his need becomes intense for knowledge of the command and the prohibition.

Admonition is intended in two senses: the command and prohibition coupled with desire and fear, and the desire and fear themselves. The one who turns back and remembers has an intense need for command and prohibition. The heedless one who is averse has an intense need for encouragement and warning. The arrogant opponent has an intense need for argument.

These three were thus given for these three in His saying: ﴿Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition, and argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. He stated wisdom without qualifying it with the description of goodness, since all of it is good, and the description of goodness belongs to it essentially. As for admonition, He qualified it with the description of goodness, since not every admonition is good.

Likewise, argument may be in the best manner or otherwise. This may refer to the state of the arguer, his harshness or gentleness, his sharpness or kindness, so that he is commanded to argue with them in the best state. It may also be a description of what one argues with, the proofs, demonstrations, and words that are the best and clearest, the most indicative of the intended meaning, and the most conducive to the goal. The verification is that the verse covers both types.

As for what some of the later scholars mentioned, that this is an indication of the kinds of syllogisms, so that wisdom is the method of demonstration (burhan), good admonition is the method of rhetoric (khitabah), and argument in the best manner is the method of dialectic (jadal), the first being by stating demonstrative premises for one who will accept nothing but demonstration and submits to nothing but it, namely the elite; the second by stating rhetorical premises that stir desire and fear for one who is satisfied with rhetoric, namely the common people; and the third by stating dialectical premises for the opponent who is moved by dialectic, namely the adversaries. This makes the revelation of the Qur'an subject to the laws and terminology of the people of Greek logic. This is definitely false in many respects, which is not the place to mention. It was mentioned here only as a digression from the subject of admonition, and that the one who turns back and remembers does not have as intense a need for it as the heedless and averse one. The heedless one has an extremely intense need for admonition so that he may remember what he has forgotten and thus benefit from remembrance.

As for blindness to the faults of the admonisher, when one is occupied with them, he is deprived of benefit from the admonition, because souls are naturally disposed against benefiting from the words of one who does not act by his own counsel and does not benefit from it. This is like one whom a physician prescribes a medicine for an illness which the physician himself has, while the physician neglects it and does not heed it. Indeed, the physician in their eyes is in a better state than this admonisher who contradicts what he preaches, for another medicine may serve in his place, or he may think he has the strength to forgo treatment, or he may be content with the healing power of nature and other things. But what this admonisher preaches is a specific path to salvation, which nothing else can replace, and it is indispensable. Because of this aversion, Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) said to his people: ﴿And I do not wish to oppose you in that which I forbid you﴾ [Hud: 88].

Some of the early generations (salaf) said: If you want the command and prohibition to be accepted from you, then when you command something, be the first to do it and to comply with it, and when you forbid something, be the first to refrain from it. And it has been said:

"O you man who teaches others,
why is not this teaching for yourself?

You prescribe the remedy for the one with wasting disease,
while from that wasting disease you yourself are ill.

Do not forbid a character trait while you do its like;
it is a disgrace upon you when you do the blameworthy.

Begin with yourself and restrain it from its error;
when it desists from it, then you are wise.

There the words you say will be accepted and followed,
and from you the teaching will benefit."

So blindness to the faults of the admonisher is among the conditions for the complete benefit from his admonition.

As for the remembrance of promise and threat, this necessitates fear of Him and caution against Him. Admonition benefits only the one who believes in it, fears it, and hopes in it. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter﴾ [Hud: 103]. He said: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾ [al-A'la: 10]. He said: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45]. Even more explicit is His saying: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ [Qaf: 45]. Therefore, belief in promise and threat, and remembering them, is a condition for benefiting from admonitions, signs, and lessons, and its attainment is impossible without it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 16, verses 126–127 (part 1 of 4):

If it is said: Which of the two kinds of patience is more beloved to Allah: the patience of one who is patient in carrying out His commands, or the patience of one who is patient in refraining from what He has forbidden?

It is said: This is a matter on which people have disagreed. One group said that patience in refraining from transgressions is superior, because it is more difficult and arduous. Acts of righteousness are performed by both the righteous and the wicked, but only the sincere believers (al-siddiqun) are patient in refraining from transgressions.

They said: Also, patience in refraining from what is forbidden is patience in opposing the desires of the soul (hawa al-nafs), and this is the most difficult thing and the most excellent.

They said: Also, abandoning what the souls love is evidence that the one for whose sake it is abandoned is more beloved to him than his own soul and desire. This is unlike performing what the Beloved loves, for that does not necessarily entail this.

They said: Also, manliness (muruwwa) and chivalry (futuwwa) are entirely in this patience.

Imam Ahmad said: "Chivalry is abandoning what you desire for what you fear."

So a servant's manliness and chivalry are in proportion to this patience.

They said: The wonder is not at one who is patient in carrying out commands, for most of them are loved by sound souls because of what they contain of justice, goodness, sincerity and righteousness, and these are beloved to pure and virtuous souls. Rather, the wonder is at one who is patient in refraining from prohibitions, most of which are desired by the souls. Such a person abandons the immediate beloved in this world for the deferred beloved in another abode, while the soul is inclined to love the immediate, so its patience in refraining from it is contrary to its nature.

They said: Also, prohibitions have four incitements that call to them: the human soul (nafs), his devil (shaytan), his desire (hawa), and his worldly life (dunya).

One does not abandon them until one struggles against these four, and that is the most difficult and arduous thing for souls.

They said: Prohibitions belong to the category of the soul's restraint from what it craves and enjoys, and restraint (hamiyya) while the impulse to indulge is present and strong is among the most difficult and arduous things.

They said: Because of this, the approach to what is forbidden is entirely closed, whereas the commandments are only carried out to the extent one is able, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If I command you with something, do of it what you are able; and what I forbid you, avoid it."

This shows that the gate of prohibited things is narrower than the gate of commanded things, and that no allowance is granted for committing any part of them, whereas allowance is granted for neglecting some commanded acts due to incapacity and excuse.

They said: Because of this, most punishments, such as the prescribed penalties (hudud) and others, are for committing prohibited acts, unlike neglecting a command. Allah, glorified is He, did not prescribe a specific penalty for neglecting it. The most important of the commands is prayer, and the scholars have differed over whether there is a prescribed penalty for one who abandons it or not.

This is some of what the first group argued.

(Section)
