Another group said: Rather, patience in performing a command is superior and more exalted than patience in abstaining from what is prohibited, because performing the command is more beloved to Allah than abstaining from what is prohibited, and patience in the more beloved of the two matters is superior and higher. This is explained in several ways:

First: Performing the command is sought for its own sake. It is legislated as an end in itself (shar' al-maqasid). The knowledge of Allah, His Oneness, His worship alone, turning to Him in repentance, relying upon Him, sincerely doing deeds for Him, loving Him, being pleased with Him, and standing in His service, is the goal for which creation was created and for which the command was established. This is something sought for itself. The prohibitions were forbidden only because they obstruct this, or distract from it, or cause its perfection to be lost. Therefore their degrees of prohibition are in proportion to how much they obstruct the command, hinder it, and deprive it of its perfection. So the prohibited things are sought for something else, while the commanded thing is sought for itself. Had wine and gambling not barred one from the remembrance of Allah, from prayer, and from the mutual affection and love that Allah placed among His servants, He would not have prohibited them. Likewise, had they not come between the servant and his intellect, by which he knows Allah, worships Him, praises Him, glorifies Him, and prays and prostrates to Him, He would not have prohibited them. Likewise, all that He prohibited, He prohibited only because it obstructs what He loves and is pleased with, and stands between the servant and his perfection.

Second: The commanded acts are connected to the knowledge of Allah, His Oneness, His worship, His remembrance, His thanks, His love, reliance upon Him, and turning to Him in repentance. Their object is the Essence of the Lord, the Exalted, and His Names and Attributes. The object of the prohibitions is the essences of the things that are forbidden. The difference between them is among the greatest differences.

Third: The servant's need and necessity for performing the command is greater than his need to abstain from what is prohibited. He has no need more pressing or more acute than his need to know his Lord, to affirm His Oneness, to devote his deeds sincerely to Him, to single Him out in worship, love and obedience. His need for this is greater than his need for himself, and his self and his life are greater than his need for his nourishment, which sustains his body. Indeed, this is for his heart and spirit like life and nourishment are for his body. He is only a human being by his spirit and heart, not by his body and frame, as it has been said:

"O servant of the body, how much you suffer in serving it,
For you are a human by the heart, not by the body."

Abstaining from what is forbidden is only prescribed as a means to attain this matter, which is necessary for him, and how much he needs it and how poor he is without it.

Fourth: Abstaining from what is forbidden belongs to the category of restraint (hamiyya), whereas performing the command belongs to the category of preserving strength and nourishment, without which the structure cannot stand and life cannot be attained. A person may live while maintaining restraint even if his body is extremely ill, but he cannot live without strength and the nourishment that preserves it. This is the likeness of commands and prohibitions.

Fifth: All sins return to these two roots: abandoning a command and committing a prohibited act. If the servant commits all the prohibited acts from beginning to end, but comes with the least, smallest weight of an atom's worth of the command of faith, he is saved thereby from eternal abiding in the Fire. But if he abstains from every prohibition and does not come with the command of faith, he will abide forever in the blazing Fire. So where is the one who has only the weight of atoms of it (faith) that comes out of the Fire, compared to the one who has the weight of mountains of it, multiplied many times over, which does not require eternal abiding in the Fire when the command or the least of it is present?

Sixth: All prohibitions, from beginning to end, fall away through the command of repentance (tawba), while the commands do not all fall away through the disobedience of opposing them, except by shirk or dying upon it. There is no disagreement among the Muslim community that every prohibited act falls away by repenting from it. They disagreed about whether obedience is nullified by disobedience, and there is dispute and detail in this matter that is not the place for this discussion.

Seventh: The sin of the father (Adam) was committing a prohibited act, and its outcome was that his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him. The sin of Iblis was by abandoning a command, and its outcome was what Allah, glorified is He, mentioned. He made this a lesson for the descendants until the Day of Resurrection.

Eighth: The commanded act is beloved to the Lord, and the prohibited act is hateful to Him. He, glorified is He, decreed and ordained it only because it is a means to attaining His beloved from His servant and from Himself, exalted is He.

As for what He attains from His servant: repentance, seeking forgiveness, humility, submission, and brokenness, and other such things.

As for what He attains from Himself: forgiveness, turning to the servant in mercy, pardoning him, overlooking, forbearance, and passing over his right, and other things that are more beloved to Him, exalted is He, than their loss would be through not decreeing what He dislikes. When it is known that He decreed what He dislikes only because it becomes a means to what He loves, it is known that His beloved is the ultimate goal. Thus the loss of His beloved is more hateful to Him and more disliked by Him than the occurrence of what is hateful to Him. Indeed, if what is hateful to Him results in something else He loves from another aspect, then the hateful thing is willed by Him with the will of means, just as its prohibition and His disliking of it were for that reason.

As for the beloved, His will for it is the will of ends, as previously mentioned. He, glorified is He, created creation only for the sake of His beloved and His command, which is His worship alone, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56].

He decreed what He dislikes and what He hates in order to complete this goal for which He created His creation. From it there result commands that would not have been realized without its decree, such as jihad, which is the most beloved of deeds to Him, and loyalty and enmity for His sake. Had He not loved these commands, He would not have decreed the disliked thing that becomes a cause for their attainment.

Ninth: Abstaining from what is forbidden is not an act of nearness (qurba) unless it is accompanied by performing the command. If the servant abstains from every prohibition but does not carry out the command, Allah will not reward him for it until it is accompanied by the command of faith. Likewise, the believer's abstaining from what is forbidden is not an act of nearness until it is accompanied by the command of intention, such that his abstention is for Allah. So abstaining from prohibitions, for it to be an act of nearness for which one is rewarded, depends on performing the command. But performing the command, for it to be an act of nearness and obedience, does not depend on abstaining from what is forbidden. Had it depended on that, Allah would never accept the obedience of one who disobeys Him. This is among the most utterly false notions.

Tenth: What is forbidden is sought to be eliminated, and what is commanded is sought to be brought into being. The aim is to bring this into being and eliminate that. So if both the command and the prohibition are assumed to be absent or present, their presence is better than their absence. When the command is absent, the absence of the prohibition does not benefit, whereas if the command is present, it may be used to repel the prohibited thing or its effect. Thus the presence of strength is better than the presence of sickness, and the absence of life and sickness is also better.

Eleventh: In the domain of commands, a good deed is rewarded tenfold up to seven hundredfold and up to many multiples. In the domain of prohibitions, a bad deed is recompensed with its like, and it is subject to removal through repentance, seeking forgiveness, good deeds that erase (sins), afflictions that expiate, the seeking of forgiveness by the angels for the believers, and the seeking of forgiveness by some of them for others, and other such things. This indicates that the presence of the command is more beloved to Allah than the absence of the prohibited thing.

Twelfth: In the domain of prohibitions, Allah, glorified is He, erases it and nullifies its effect through many things, from the servant's own deeds and from others. He nullifies it by sincere repentance, by seeking forgiveness, by good deeds that erase sins, by afflictions that expiate, by the seeking of forgiveness by the angels, and by the supplication of the believers. These are six during his life. Then there is the severity of death, its anguish, and its agony upon him; this is at the moment of his departure from this world. Then there is the terror of the final sight, the fright of the two angels in the grave, its squeezing and compression upon him, the severity and hardship of the standing (on the Day of Judgment), and the intercession of those who intercede for him, and the mercy of the Most Merciful of the merciful toward him. If these things fail to remove it, then he must enter the Fire, and his remaining in it will be in proportion to the remaining of his impurity and filth. For Allah has forbidden Paradise to every pure person. So as long as his filth, dirt and impurity remain in him, he is in the furnace of purification until he is cleansed of that filth and impurity. As for the domain of commands, nothing nullifies it except shirk.

Thirteenth: The reward for commands is recompense, which belongs to the category of beneficence, grace and mercy. The punishment for prohibitions is retribution, which belongs to the category of wrath and justice. His mercy overcomes His wrath. What is connected to mercy and grace is more beloved to Him than what is connected to wrath and justice, and the nullification of what is connected to mercy is more hateful to Him than the performance of what is connected to wrath.

Fourteenth: In the domain of prohibitions, one single (prohibited act) may cancel out thousands upon thousands of commands. In the domain of commands, one single (command) does not cancel out thousands upon thousands of prohibitions.

Fifteenth: What the commands are connected to is action, and action is an attribute of perfection; indeed the perfection of a created being lies in his actions, for action is existence, so it becomes perfect. What the prohibition is connected to is abstention, and abstention is nonexistence. Insofar as it is so, it is not a perfection, for pure nonexistence is not a perfection. It becomes a perfection only through what it contains or entails of existential action, which is the cause of perfection.

As for whether pure abstention, which is pure nonexistence, is a perfection or a cause of perfection: it is not.

An example of this: if one abstains from prostrating to an idol, this abstention alone is not his perfection unless he prostrates to Allah. For if he abstains from prostrating to Allah and to the idol, that is not a perfection. Likewise, if one abstains from denying the Messenger and from opposing him, he is not thereby a believer unless he does the opposite of that, namely affirmation, love, allegiance to him, and obedience to him. It is therefore known that the perfection is entirely in the command, and that the prohibition, unless it is connected to the performance of the command, benefits nothing and is not a perfection. If a man said to the Messenger: "I will not deny you, nor affirm you, nor give you my allegiance, nor oppose you, nor fight you, nor fight those who fight you," he would be a disbeliever, and he would not be a believer by abstaining from opposing, denying and fighting him, unless he performs the existential action he was commanded to perform.

Sixteenth: When the servant performs what he is commanded to do in its proper manner, he necessarily abstains from what is forbidden. The aim is the performance of the command, and with its performance done correctly, the committing of the prohibited act becomes impossible. The forbidden thing is in reality the exposure of the command to being neglected. For when the servant does what he is commanded, such as justice and chastity, and refrains from committing injustice and immoralities, the very act of justice includes abstention from injustice, and the very act of chastity includes abstention from immoralities. Thus abstention from what is forbidden enters into what is commanded, implicitly and as a consequence. This is not the case in reverse, for abstaining from what is forbidden does not include performing what is commanded, since one may abstain from both together, as previously mentioned. It is therefore known that the aim is establishing the command in its proper form, and with that, committing the prohibited act is absolutely impossible. Whereas abstaining from what is forbidden entails establishing the command.

Seventeenth: When the Lord, the Exalted, commands His servant to do one thing and forbids him from another, and he does both, then he has attained both what is beloved to the Lord and what is hateful to Him. What he has done of what is beloved to Him will repel the evil of what is hateful and its opposition. This is especially so if performing that beloved thing is more beloved to Him than abstaining from that hateful thing. So He will grant him forgiveness for his offense through what he did of obedience, and He will overlook what he did of the other.

A parallel to this among people is a man who kills an enemy of the king whom the king was eager to kill, and who drinks an intoxicant the king forbade him to drink. The king will overlook this slip for him, and even similar ones, in light of what he accomplished of what the king loved. But if he abandons what the king loves and what the king hates, then abstaining from what the king hates never counts as a benefit that outweighs performing what the king loves. For example, if the king commands his servant to kill his enemy and forbids him from drinking an intoxicant, and he disobeys in killing his enemy though he is able to do so, but abstains from drinking the intoxicant, the king will not forgive his offense for abandoning his command in return for abstaining from what he forbade. Allah has created His servants with this disposition. Thus it is with masters and their servants, fathers and their children, kings and their soldiers, and wives and their husbands. The one who abandons what his commander loves and hates is not in the same position as the one who performs what his commander loves and hates.

It is clarified by the Eighteenth Aspect: The one who performs what the Lord loves cannot possibly perform all that He hates. Rather, he abstains from what He hates to the extent of what he has done of what He loves. It is impossible to commit all that He hates while doing what He loves and hates. The best that can be said is that the two matters are combined, so the Lord loves him from one aspect and hates him from another. But if he abandons the commanded thing entirely, then nothing that the Lord loves is established in him. For the mere abstention from what is forbidden is not obedience unless it is accompanied by the command, as previously mentioned. So He does not love him for mere abstention, while He, glorified is He, hates him and dislikes him for opposing the command. Thus he becomes hateful to the Lord, exalted is He, in every respect, since there is nothing in him that the Lord loves. So reflect on this.

It is clarified by the Nineteenth Aspect: Allah, glorified is He, did not attach His love except to an existential command that He commanded, whether obligatory or recommended, and He did not attach it to abstention as abstention, nor in a single place. For He loves those who repent (al-tawwabin), He loves the good-doers (al-muhsinin), He loves the grateful (al-shakirin), He loves the patient (al-sabirin), He loves those who purify themselves (al-mutatahhirin), He loves those who fight in His cause in ranks as if they were a solid structure (bunyan marsus), He loves the God-fearing (al-muttaqin), He loves those who remember Him (al-dhakirin), and He loves those who give charity (al-mutasaddiqin). So He, glorified is He, attached His love only to His commands, since these are the aim of creation and the command, as He said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾. So He did not create creation except for the establishment of His commands, and He did not forbid them except from what prevents them from establishing His commands and hinders them from it.

It is clarified by the Twentieth Aspect: If the prohibited things did not obstruct the commanded things and prevent their occurrence in the manner Allah commanded, there would be no meaning to forbidding them. He forbade them only because they oppose His commands, hinder them, and obstruct them. So the prohibition of them belongs to the category of completing and perfecting the command. It is like clearing the channels of water so that it flows in its courses unobstructed. The command is like the water sent down into a river for the life of the lands and the people, and the prohibition is like cleaning its channels and its course and purifying them of whatever obstructs the water. The command is like strength and life, and the prohibition is like the restraint that preserves strength and the remedy that serves it.

They said: When it has become clear that performing the command is superior, then patience in it is the best kind of patience, and by it, patience in refraining from what is forbidden and patience in the decreed (al-maqdur) becomes easy. For patience in the greater includes patience in the lesser, but not vice versa. It has become clear to you from this that the three kinds (of patience) are interconnected, and each kind helps the other two. Some people have strong patience regarding the decreed, but when command and prohibition come, their patience there is weak. Others are the reverse. Some have stronger patience on the side of commands, and others are the reverse. And Allah knows best.

[Section: The Types of Patience]
[Patience by Allah, for Allah, and with Allah]

It is of three kinds: patience by Allah (sabr billah), patience for Allah (sabr lillah), and patience with Allah (sabr ma'a Allah).

The first is the patience of seeking help from Him, and seeing that He is the one who grants patience, and that the servant's patience is by his Lord, not by himself, as the Exalted said: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except by Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 127]. That is, if He does not grant you patience, you would not be patient.

The second kind is patience for Allah. It means that what motivates a person to be patient is love of Allah, seeking His face, and drawing near to Him, not showing off his strength of soul, seeking praise from people, or any other such worldly aim.

The third kind is patience with Allah. It means the servant revolves with Allah's religious purpose for him and with His religious rulings. He makes himself patient with them, travels with their journey, stays where they stay, turns wherever their riding beasts turn, and halts wherever their tents are pitched.

This is the meaning of being patient with Allah: he has devoted himself to His commands and to what He loves. This is the most severe and difficult kind of patience. It is the patience of the truthful (al-siddiqun).

Al-Junayd said: "Travelling from this world to the Hereafter is easy and light for the believer. But leaving people behind for the sake of Allah is hard, and travelling from the self to Allah is very hard. Patience with Allah is harder still."

He was asked about patience and said: "It is swallowing bitterness without frowning."

Dhu al-Nun al-Misri said: "Patience is keeping far from what opposes Allah, remaining calm when swallowing the bitter gulps of affliction, and showing wealth while poverty has settled into the courtyards of one's livelihood."

It was said: "Patience is standing firm with affliction with good manners."

It was said: "It is annihilation in trial, without display and without complaint."

It was said: "It is training the self to rush toward what is hateful."

It was said: "It is remaining with affliction with good companionship, just as one remains with well-being."

ʿAmr ibn ʿUthman said: "It is steadfastness with Allah, and receiving His trial with openness and ease."

Al-Khawwas said: "It is steadfastness upon the rulings of the Book and the Sunnah."

Yahya ibn Muʿadh said: "The patience of those who love is harder than the patience of the ascetics. How strange! How do they bear it?" And he recited:

*Patience is becoming in every situation,*
*except before you, for it is not becoming there.*

It was said: "Patience is seeking help from Allah."

It was said: "It is leaving off complaint."

It was said:

*Patience is like its name: its taste is bitter,*
*but its consequences are sweeter than honey.*

It was said: "Patience is that you accept the loss of your soul for the pleasure of the one you love," as it was said:

*I shall be patient so that you may be pleased, and I will suffer sorrow,*
*and it is enough for me that you are pleased, even if my patience destroys me.*

It was said: "The ranks of the patient are five: the patient (sabir), the one who seeks patience (mustabtir), the one who forces himself to be patient (mutasabbir), the very patient (sabur), and the greatly patient (sabbar). The sabir is the most general. The mustabtir is one who acquires patience and is filled with it. The mutasabbir is one who exerts himself and bears himself to it. The sabur is one whose patience is great, greater than the patience of others. The sabbar is one of abundant patience. The first is about quality and manner, and the rest are about amount and degree."

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Patience is a mount that never stumbles."

A man came to al-Shibli and asked: "Which patience is hardest on the patient?" He said: "Patience in Allah." The man said: "No." He said: "Patience for Allah." He said: "No." He said: "Patience with Allah." He said: "No." Al-Shibli said: "What is it, then?" He said: "Patience away from Allah." Al-Shibli let out a cry that nearly took his soul.

Al-Jurayri said: "Patience is that one does not differentiate between the state of blessing and the state of love, while the heart remains calm in both. Being patient (tasabbur) is calmness amid affliction while feeling the weight of the trial."

Abu ʿAli al-Daqqaq said: "The patient have won the honour of both abodes, because they have attained Allah's companionship, for Allah is with the patient."

It was said regarding the verse ﴿O you who believe, be patient, outdo others in patience, and stand ready (rabitu)﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 200] that it is a movement from the lower to the higher. Patience (sabr) is below mutual endurance (musabara), and mutual endurance is below standing ready (muraabata). Muraabata is a form of the verb from rabt, which means binding and tying. The one who stands ready is called murabit because such people tie up their horses, waiting for the moment of alarm. Then every person who waits, having bound himself to an obedience he is waiting for, is called murabit. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I not tell you what Allah erases sins by and raises ranks by? It is completing wudu' in hardship, walking much to the mosques, and waiting for prayer after prayer. That is ribat, that is ribat."

And he (ﷺ) said: "A day of ribat in the way of Allah is better than the world and everything in it."

It was said: "Be patient with your souls in obedience to Allah. Be patient with your hearts in trials for Allah. Stand ready with your inner secrets in longing for Allah."

It was said: "Be patient for Allah. Be patient through Allah. Stand ready with Allah."

It was said: "Be patient in times of blessing, be patient in hardship and adversity, stand ready in the house of the enemies, and fear the God of the earth and heaven, that you may prosper in the abode of permanence."

So patience is with your self, mutual endurance is between you and your enemy, and standing ready is steadfastness and preparing one's equipment. Just as ribat is staying at the frontier so the enemy cannot storm through it, likewise ribat is staying at the frontier of the heart so that Satan does not storm upon it, take possession of it, ruin it, or scatter it.

It was said: "Swallow patience. If it kills you, it kills you as a martyr; if it keeps you alive, it keeps you alive honoured."

It was said: "Patience for Allah is sufficiency. Through Allah is permanence. In Allah is trial. With Allah is loyalty. From Allah is estrangement. Patience in pursuit is the sign of success, and patience in tribulations is the sign of relief."

It was said: "The servant's state with Allah is his standing ready, and whatever is other than Allah is his enemy."

In the Kitab al-Adab of al-Bukhari, it is recorded that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about faith, and he said: 'Patience and generosity.'" He mentioned this from Musa ibn Isma'il, who said: "Suwayd related to us, saying: ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr related to us, from his father, from his grandfather, and he mentioned it."

This is among the most comprehensive and greatest of statements in proof, and the most inclusive of the stations of faith from beginning to end.

The self is required to do two things: to give what it has been commanded to give, and to abstain from what it has been forbidden. What drives it to give is generosity (al-samaha). What drives it to abstain and keep away from what is forbidden is patience.

Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, has commanded in His Book beautiful patience (sabr jamil), beautiful forgiveness (safh jamil), and beautiful avoidance (hajr jamil). I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya (may Allah sanctify his spirit) say: "Beautiful patience is that in which there is no complaint, and none accompanies it. Beautiful forgiveness is that in which there is no reproach. Beautiful avoidance is that in which there is no harm."

In an Israelite report, Allah revealed to one of His prophets: "I sent down My trial upon My servant, and he called upon Me. I delayed answering him, so he complained about Me. I said: 'My servant, how can I have mercy on you from something with which I have mercy on you?'"

Ibn ʿUyayna commented on the verse ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient﴾ [al-Sajda: 24]: "They took hold of the essence of the matter, so He made them leaders."

It was said: "The best form of the patience of worshippers is that it be preserved, and the best form of the patience of lovers is that it be rejected (i.e., they neglect it, being overwhelmed)." As it was said:

*On the day of separation it became clear that their resolve to be patient*
*was one of the false suspicions.*

Complaint to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not contradict patience. Ya'qub (peace be upon him) pledged to have beautiful patience, and a prophet does not break his pledge. Then he said: ﴿I only complain of my distress and grief to Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 86]. Likewise Ayyub: Allah reported that He found him patient, even though he said: ﴿Harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾ [al-Anbiya': 83].

What contradicts patience is complaining about Allah, not complaining to Allah. As one of them saw a man complaining to another about poverty and dire need, he said: "O you, do you complain to one who has mercy on you about one who has no mercy on you?" Then he recited:

*When affliction befalls you, be patient with it,*
*the patience of the noble, for He knows best what is in you.*

*When you complain to a son of Adam, you are only complaining*
*of the Merciful to one who does not show mercy.*

[Section: On the division of patience into praiseworthy and blameworthy]

The blameworthy is patience away from Allah, from His will, from His love, and from the heart's journey toward Him. This patience entails abandoning the servant's perfection entirely and missing out on what he was created for. Just as this is the most reprehensible patience, it is also the greatest and most extreme, for there is no patience more extreme than that of someone who is patient away from his beloved, without whom he has no life at all. Just as there is no asceticism more extreme than the asceticism of someone who renounces what Allah has prepared for His friends of His honour, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. So renunciation in this matter is the greatest kind of renunciation, as a man said to one of the ascetics, marvelling at his asceticism: "I have never seen anyone more ascetic than you!" He replied: "You are more ascetic than I am. I renounced this world, which has no permanence and no fulfilment. You renounced the Hereafter, so who is more ascetic than us?"

Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi said: "The patience of lovers is more wondrous than the patience of ascetics. How strange, how do they endure!"

On this, it was said:

*Patience is praised in all situations,*
*except before you, for there it is not praised.*

A man stood before al-Shibli and said: "Which patience is hardest on the patient?"
He said: "Patience in Allah."
He said: "No."
He said: "Patience for Allah."
He said: "No."
He said: "Patience with Allah."
He said: "No."
He said: "What is it, then?"
He said: "Patience away from Allah." Al-Shibli cried out such a cry that his soul nearly departed.

It was said: "Patience with Allah is loyalty, and patience away from Allah is harshness. People have agreed that patience away from the beloved is not praiseworthy. How much more so when the servant's perfection and success lie in loving Him? Lovers have always been reproached for being patient away from their beloveds, as it was said:

*Patience away from you has bitter consequences,*
*while patience in all other things is praiseworthy.*

Another said regarding patience away from his beloved:

*When men play with everything,*
*you see love playing with men.*
*How can one be patient with one who has taken a place in me*
*like the right hand beside the left?*

Another complained to his beloved about what he suffered from love, and she said: "If you were truthful, you would not have been patient away from me." And he said:

*When I complained of love, she said: "You are lying to me."*
*Do you see how the lover is patient away from his beloved?*

[Section] As for praiseworthy patience, it is of two kinds: patience for Allah and patience through Allah. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but through Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 127], and He said: ﴿So be patient with the decree of your Lord, for indeed you are under Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48]. People have disputed which of the two kinds of patience is more perfect. One group said patience for Him is more perfect, for what is for Allah is more complete than what is through Allah. What is for Him is the goal, and what is through Him is the means, and goals are nobler than means. For this reason, fulfilling a vow is obligatory when it is made as an act of devotion or as a means of drawing near to Allah, since it is a vow made to Him. But fulfilling it is not obligatory if it takes the form of an oath, since it is an oath sworn by Him. What is for His Exalted self relates to His divinity (uluhiyya), and what is through Him relates to His lordship (rububiyya). What relates to His divinity is nobler than what relates to His lordship. For this reason, the tawhid of divinity is what saves from shirk, not the tawhid of lordship on its own. The idol-worshippers acknowledged that Allah alone is the creator of all things, their lord and sovereign, but since they did not bring the tawhid of divinity, which is worshipping Him alone with no partner, the tawhid of His lordship did not benefit them.

Another group said: patience through Allah is more perfect. Indeed, patience for Him cannot be realised except through patience with Him, as Allah said: ﴿And be patient﴾, commanding patience, and the one commanded is the one for whose sake the act is done. Then He said: ﴿And your patience is not but through Allah﴾. This is a declarative sentence, distinct from the imperative sentence preceding it, informing that it is impossible for him to be patient except through Allah. This implies two matters: seeking help from Him, and the special companionship indicated by the preposition "bi" of accompaniment, as in His saying: "by Me he hears, by Me he sees, by Me he grasps, by Me he walks." This "bi" does not mean help, for that is common to both the obedient and the disobedient, since what does not happen through Allah does not happen at all. Rather, it is the "bi" of accompaniment and companionship, whose meaning is stated in His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is with the patient﴾. This is the companionship granted to His servant who draws near to Him through supererogatory acts until he becomes beloved to Him: by Him he hears, by Him he sees, and likewise by Him he is patient. He does not move, rest, or perceive except that Allah is with him. Whoever is like this is able to be patient for Him and to bear burdens for His sake, as in the divine report: "And what the bearers bear for My sake." So His saying ﴿And your patience is not but through Allah﴾ shows that whoever does not have Allah with him cannot be patient, and how can one who does not have Allah with him be patient with the command, in obeying, executing, and conveying it, or with the decree, in bearing it and undertaking it? Whoever does not have Allah with him should not hope for the level of praiseworthy patience whose consequences are good, just as whoever does not have his hearing, sight, grasping, and walking through Allah should not hope for the beloved nearness.

This is the meaning of his saying: "I was his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees, his hand by which he grasps, and his foot by which he walks." It does not mean that I was the very essence of these limbs and faculties, as the enemies of Allah, the proponents of unity of existence (Ahl al-Wahda), suppose, that the essence of the servant is the essence of the Lord, may Allah be exalted far above the statement of the brotherhood of Christians. If it were as they suppose, there would be no difference between this servant and any other, nor between his two states of drawing near to his Lord through supererogatory acts and of being hated by Him through sins. There would be no one who draws near and no one drawn to, no servant and no one worshipped, no lover and no beloved. The whole hadith refutes their false claim in about thirty ways that are evident to one who reflects.

The meaning of "I was his hearing, sight, hand, and foot" is explained by his saying: "By Me he hears, by Me he sees, by Me he grasps, by Me he walks." This companionship, which results from drawing near to Him through what He loves, is expressed in the most delicate and beautiful phrase, indicating the strength and permanence of the companionship, until He becomes for him like his hearing, sight, hand, and foot.

A parallel to this is his saying: "The Black Stone is the right hand of Allah on earth. Whoever shakes hands with it and kisses it, it is as if he shook hands with Allah and kissed His right hand."

Such usage is acceptable in speech: that something is described as taking the place of what accompanies and is joined to it, just as a lover says to his beloved: "You are my soul, my hearing, and my sight." This has two meanings. One is that he has become to him like his soul, heart, hearing, and sight. The second is that his love and remembrance of him, having taken possession of his heart and soul, have made him present with him and as his companion, as in the hadith: "Allah, the Exalted, says: 'I am the companion of whoever remembers Me.'"

In another hadith: "I am with My servant as long as he remembers Me and his lips move with My remembrance."

And in another hadith: "When I love My servant, I become his hearing, his sight, his hand, and his support."

Ibn al-Qayyim, *al-Tafsir al-Qayyim*, on surah 16, verses 126–127 (part 3 of 4)

No expression conveys this meaning more complete, more excellent, or more subtle than this phrase, and explaining this phrase only makes it more distant and obscure.

The purpose here is to mention patience (*sabr*) through God, and that the servant's patience depends on his share of God's companionship (*ma'iyya*) with him. When God is with him, he is able to produce a kind of patience that no one else can produce. Abu 'Ali said: "The patient have won the honour of both abodes, because they attained God's companionship." God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾.

Here is a wondrous secret: whoever clings to one of the attributes of the Lord, exalted is He, that attribute brings him in and delivers him to Him. The Lord, exalted is He, is *al-Sabur* (the Most Patient). Indeed, no one is more patient in bearing harm he hears from others. It has been said that God, glorified is He, revealed to Dawud (David): "Take on the characteristics of my character, for among My characters is that I am *al-Sabur*." The Lord, exalted is He, loves His names and attributes, and loves what their requirements are and the appearance of their effects in the servant. He is beautiful and loves beauty. He is *'Afuw* (Pardoning) and loves those who pardon. He is *Karim* (Generous) and loves the generous. He is *'Alim* (All-Knowing) and loves the learned. He is *Witr* (One) and loves those who are odd-numbered. He is *Qawi* (Strong), and the strong believer is more beloved to Him than the weak believer. He is *Sabur* and loves the patient. He is *Shakur* (Appreciative) and loves the grateful. When He, glorified is He, loves those who are characterized by the effects of His attributes, He is with them according to their share of this characterization. This specific companionship is expressed in His words: "I was his hearing, his sight, his hand, and his supporter."

[Section]

Some of them added a third type of patience, namely patience with God, and they made it the highest type of patience. They said it is fidelity (*wafa'*). If someone were asked about the reality of patience with God, he could not define it except by the three types already mentioned: patience upon His decrees, patience upon His commands, and patience refraining from His prohibitions. If he claims that patience with God is to remain steadfast with Him upon His rulings, turning wherever they turn, so that he is always with God and not with himself, then he is with God through love and conformity. This meaning is true, but it revolves around the types of patience mentioned above. And if he claims that patience with God is what encompasses all types of patience, this is true, but making it a fourth type of patience is not correct.

Know that the reality of patience with God is the heart's firmness through steadfastness with Him, that it does not swerve from Him like the swerving of foxes, here and there. The reality of this is steadfastness toward Him and the heart's devotion to Him. Some of them added another type, which they called "patience in Him," and this too is not outside the types of patience mentioned, and there is no understanding of patience in Him other than patience for Him. This is like saying: "I did this *in* God and *for* God," as Khubayb said:

*That is in the Essence of God, and if He wills, He will bless the scattered limbs of a torn body.*

God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾. And He said: ﴿And strive for Allah﴾.

In the hadith of Jabir: "When God brought his father back to life, He said to him, 'Ask for what you wish.' He said: 'O Lord, that You return me to the world so that I may be killed for You a second time.'"

And he said: "I was harmed for God, and no one is harmed [as I was]."

From this, two meanings can be understood. One is that it is in seeking His pleasure, His obedience, and His path, and this applies to what a person does by choice. As in the hadith: "I learned knowledge *for You*."

The second is that it happened because of Him and on account of Him, and this applies to what befalls a person without his choice. Most of the time, the phrase "that is in God" carries this meaning.

So reflect on his saying "I was harmed *for* God," and Khubayb's saying "that is *in* the Essence of God," and 'Abdullah ibn Haram's saying "until I am killed *in* You." Likewise His words: ﴿And those who strive for Us﴾, for harm follows from it in relation to Him, glorified is He.

Here "*fi*" (in) is neither for location nor merely for causation, although causation is its original sense. Consider his saying: "In the soul of a believer are a hundred camels," and his saying: "A woman entered the Fire *because of* a cat." How do you find in it a meaning beyond causation? "*Fi*" is not used in the sense of a container in all its meanings. So your saying "I did this *in* Your pleasure" carries a meaning beyond your saying "I did this *for* Your pleasure." And when you say "I was harmed *in* God," this expression cannot be replaced by saying "I was harmed *for* God," or "because of God."

When the meaning is understood, the rule of the expression is set aside. The point is that patience *in* God, if it is meant in this sense, is true. If it is meant as something outside patience upon His decrees, upon His commands, and in refraining from His prohibitions, and not for Him and by Him, then it has not been achieved. The one who is patient *in* God is like the one who strives *in* God, and striving *in* Him does not depart from the meaning of striving *by* Him and *for* Him. And God is the Granter of success.

As for the saying of some of them: "Patience *for* God is sufficiency (*ghina'*), patience *by* God is endurance (*baqa'*), patience *in* God is trial (*bala'*), patience *with* God is fidelity (*wafa'*), and patience *away from* God is harshness (*jafa'*)." This is a statement whose speaker need not be accepted, because he only mentioned what occurred to him and conceived it. Acceptance is due only to a transmitted report from an infallible speaker. We will explain these words.

As for his saying "patience *for* God is sufficiency": patience for God means leaving the self's portions and desires for the sake of God's desire. This is the hardest and most difficult thing for the self, because crossing the wasteland between the self and God, so as to travel from it to God, is extremely difficult for the self. This is unlike the journey to the Hereafter, which is easy, as al-Junayd said: "The journey from this world to the Hereafter is easy, meaning for the believer. Abandoning people for the sake of the Truth is hard. The journey from the self to God is very hard. Patience *with* God is harder."

As for his saying "patience *by* God is endurance": when the servant is *by* God, everything becomes light for him. He bears heavy burdens and does not feel their weight. When he is *by* God and not by people or by himself, his heart and spirit have a different existence and a different state from when he is by himself and by people. In this state he does not feel the toil or bitterness of patience. The burdens of obligation turn into bliss and comfort for him. As one of the ascetics said: "I treated night prayer as a remedy for a year, and I enjoyed it for twenty years." Whoever has the comfort of his eye in prayer does not find hardship or burden in it.

As for his saying "patience *in* God is trial": trial is above toil, and patience in Him is above patience for Him and more specific than it, as has been explained. Patience in Him is like striving in Him, and it is harder than striving for Him. So every one who strives *in* God and is patient *in* God also strives *for* Him and is patient *for* Him, but not vice versa. A man may strive and be patient for God once, so that the name of one who did this *for* God applies to him, but the name of one who did this *in* God does not apply to him. That name applies only to one who has fully immersed himself in striving and patience and entered Paradise.

As for his saying "patience *with* God is fidelity": patience with Him is steadfastness with Him upon His rulings, the heart not turning away from repentance to Him, nor the limbs from obedience. Thus the companionship receives its due fulfilment, as God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And Abraham, who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾, meaning he fulfilled what he was commanded by his patience with God in His commands.

[Section: On the names of patience in relation to its object]

Since praiseworthy patience is the soul's inner, chosen restraint from answering the call of blameworthy desire, its levels and names depend on its object. If it is patience from forbidden sexual desire, it is called chastity (*'iffa*), and its opposite is debauchery (*fujur*), fornication (*zina*), and lewdness (*'ahr*). If it is restraint from the appetite of the belly, not hastening to food, or taking only what is fitting, it is called nobility of soul and contentment of soul, and its opposite is greed, baseness, and lowliness of soul. If it is restraint from uttering what should not be uttered, it is called keeping a secret, and its opposite is disclosure, spreading, accusation, immorality, abuse, lying, or slander. If it is restraint from the excesses of life, it is called asceticism (*zuhd*), and its opposite is greed (*hirs*). If it is contentment with what suffices from this world, it is called contentment (*qana'a*), and its opposite is also greed. If it is restraint from answering the call of anger, it is called forbearance (*hilm*), and its opposite is hastiness. If it is restraint from answering the call of haste, it is called dignity and steadiness, and its opposite is recklessness and lightness. If it is restraint from answering the call of flight, it is called courage, and its opposite is cowardice and weakness. If it is restraint from answering the call of vengeance, it is called pardon and forgiveness, and its opposite is retaliation and punishment. If it is restraint from answering the call of holding back and stinginess, it is called generosity, and its opposite is miserliness. If it is restraint from answering the call of food and drink at a specific time, it is called fasting (*sawm*). If it is restraint from answering the call of incapacity and laziness, it is called shrewdness (*kays*). If it is restraint from answering the call of casting burdens on people and not carrying them all, it is called manliness (*muruwwa*). So for every act and abstention there is a name specific to its object, and the name that encompasses all of this is patience (*sabr*). This shows you the connection of all the stations of religion to patience, from its beginning to its end. Likewise it is called justice when it concerns equalizing between equals, and its opposite is injustice. It is called magnanimity when it concerns giving what is obligatory and recommended willingly and by choice. On this basis are all the stations of religion.

[Section: On the means that help one to patience]

Since patience is commanded, God, glorified is He, has made for it means that help one to it and lead to it. Likewise, whatever God commands, He has helped toward it and set up means to sustain it and assist it. Just as He has not decreed a disease except that He has decreed a remedy for it, or guaranteed healing through its use, patience, though difficult and unpleasant for souls, is attainable. It is composed of two elements: knowledge and action. From these two are composed all the remedies with which hearts and bodies are treated. So there must be a cognitive part and a practical part. From these the remedy that is most beneficial of remedies is compounded. As for the cognitive part, it is the perception of the good, benefit, pleasure, and perfection in what is commanded, and the perception of the evil, harm, and deficiency in what is forbidden. When one perceives these two kinds of knowledge as they should be perceived, he adds to them firm resolve, lofty aspiration, pride, and human manliness, and combines this part with that part. Whenever he does this, patience is achieved for him, its hardships become easy for him, its bitterness becomes sweet for him, and its pain turns into pleasure.

It has already been mentioned that patience is a wrestling between the motive of reason and religion and the motive of desire and the self. When two opposing forces each seek to overcome the other, the way to do so is to strengthen the one who wants victory and weaken the other, just as with the case of strength and sickness. So when the motive of forbidden sexual intercourse grows strong, to the point that one cannot control his private parts, or can control them but not his gaze, or can control his gaze but not his heart, and it continues to inspire him with what is there, promising him and wishing for him, diverting him from the realities of remembrance and reflection on what benefits him in this world and the Hereafter, then when he resolves to treat this disease and resist it, he should first weaken it by several means.

The first: he should look at the source of the desire's strength and restrict it by limiting foods that stimulate desire, either by their type or by their quantity, so as to cut off this source by reducing it. If it is not cut off, he should hasten to fasting, for it weakens the channels of desire and breaks its intensity, especially when his eating at the time of breaking the fast is moderate.

The second: he should restrain the motive of longing, which is looking. So let him restrain the reins of his gaze as much as he can, for the call of will and desire is stirred only by looking, and looking stirs the heart with desire. In the *Musnad* (a hadith collection arranged by Companion) it is reported from him: "The gaze is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis." Iblis sends this arrow toward the heart, and it finds no shield before it, and nothing protects it except lowering the gaze, or turning aside and deviating from the direction of the shot. For this arrow is shot only from the bow of forms. If you do not stand on its path, the arrow misses. But if you set your heart as a target, it is about to be killed by one of those poisoned arrows.

The third: consoling the self with what is permissible, in place of what is forbidden. For whatever the nature desires, God, glorified is He, has permitted in the lawful, which makes one independent of the unlawful. This is the beneficial remedy for most people, as the Prophet indicated. The first remedy resembles cutting fodder from a wild animal or a ferocious dog to weaken their strength. The second remedy resembles hiding meat from a dog and barley from a beast, so that their strength is not stirred at the sight of it. The third remedy resembles giving them food that their nature inclines to, according to need, so that their strength remains and they obey their master, and are not overpowered by giving them more than that.

The fourth: reflection on the worldly corruptions likely to result from fulfilling this desire. For even if there were no Paradise and no Fire, there would be in worldly corruptions enough to forbid answering this call. If we tried to count them, they would exceed enumeration. But the eye of desire is blind.

The fifth: reflection on the ugliness of the image toward which the self calls him, if it is known to be answered by him and by others. Let him honour himself from drinking at a pool that dogs and wolves frequent, as it has been said:

*I will leave their union out of honour and dignity, because of the baseness of all the partners in it.*

Another said:

*When flies swarm over food, I raised my hand, though my soul desired it.*

*The lions avoid a watering place, when dogs have lapped in it.*

Let him remember that mixing his saliva with the saliva of every wicked person is mixing with a disease, for the saliva of a sinner is a disease, as has been said:

*Console yourself, O heart, from a generous man who gives his life, lavished upon everyone who meets him, soiling him.*

*Like water to every hunter who comes to drink from it, and like a branch to every breeze that bends it.*

*Even if a saliva is sweet, remember its bitterness in a mouth with bad breath, which sucks and sips it.*

Whoever has even a little dignity and pride will be ashamed for himself to associate with one of this character. If his soul does not incline to turning away and he accepts sharing, then let him look beyond this beauty and outward splendour to the hidden ugliness. For whoever allows his soul to commit ugly acts, his soul is uglier than the souls of beasts. No animal at all consents to such a thing, except what is reported about the pig, that among beasts there is no male who commits sodomy except it. So whoever consents to this for himself has made himself like the pig. This ugliness covers all beauty and charm in face and body, except that love makes one blind and deaf. If the image is female, she has betrayed God and His Messenger, her people, her husband, and herself, and she has passed this on to those after her among her offspring. So she bears a share of their burden and their shame. The beauty of her image has no comparison with this ugliness at all. If you wish to know this, look at the ugliness that overtakes the face of one of them in old age, and how God, glorified is He, turns those beauties into ugliness, until desolation and ugliness cover her face, as it has been said in verse:

*If the lover reflected on the extremity of the beauty that captivates him, he would not be captivated.*

The details of these aspects would be very long, so it suffices to mention their principles.

[Section: As for strengthening the motive of religion, it occurs through several matters]

The first: honouring God, blessed and exalted is He, so that He is not disobeyed while He sees and hears. Whoever has in his heart the witnessing of His majesty, his heart will never submit to that.

The second: witnessing His love, glorified is He, so that one abandons disobedience to Him out of love for Him. For the lover is obedient to the one he loves. The best abstention is the abstention of lovers, just as the best obedience is the obedience of lovers. There is a vast difference between the abstention of one who loves and his obedience, and the abstention of one who fears punishment and his obedience.

The third: witnessing favour and kindness. For the noble does not repay kindness with harm. Only the base of people do that. So let the witnessing of God's kindness and favour keep him from disobedience, out of shame before Him that God's goodness and bounty are descending to him, while his disobediences, sins, and ugly deeds are ascending to his Lord. One angel descends with this, and another ascends with that. How ugly a comparison!

The fourth: witnessing wrath and retribution. For the Lord, exalted is He, when the servant persists in disobedience, becomes angry, and when He is angry nothing can stand against His anger, let alone this weak servant.

The fifth: witnessing loss, which is what one loses through disobedience of good in this world and the Hereafter, and what befalls him through it of every name that is blameworthy by reason, law, and custom, and what departs from him of praiseworthy names by law, reason, and custom. It suffices in this witnessing to witness the loss of faith, of which even the smallest atom is better than this world and all it contains many times over. How then can one sell it for a desire that passes in its pleasure and leaves its consequence? The desire passes, and the wretchedness remains. It is authentically reported from the Prophet that he said: "The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer." Some Companions said: "Faith is removed from him until it remains above his head like a canopy. If he repents, it returns to him." Some of the Successors said: "Faith is removed from him as a shirt is removed, and if he repents he puts it on again." This is why it is reported from the Prophet in the hadith narrated by al-Bukhari: "Adulterers are naked in the oven," because they have been stripped of the garment of faith, and the oven of desire that was in their hearts becomes an apparent oven heated upon them in the Fire.

The sixth: witnessing subjugation and victory. For subduing desire and triumphing over Satan brings sweetness, joy, and happiness to one who tastes it, greater than triumphing over his human enemy. Its effect is sweeter and its joy more complete. As for its outcome, it is the most praiseworthy outcome, like the outcome of drinking a beneficial medicine that removes a disease of the body and returns it to health and balance.

The seventh: witnessing the recompense, which is what God, glorified is He, has promised as compensation to one who abandons forbidden things for His sake and restrains his self from its desire. Let him weigh the recompense against what was given up, and whichever of the two is more worthy of preference, let him choose it and be content with it for himself.

The eighth: the contemplation of companionship (al-ma'iyya). It is of two kinds: general companionship and special companionship. General companionship is the Lord's observation of him and that He is with him in His knowledge, so that his condition is not hidden from Him; this has already been mentioned. What is intended here is special companionship, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who are patient﴾ and His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾ and His saying ﴿And indeed, Allah is with the doers of good﴾. This special companionship is better and more beneficial in his worldly life and his Hereafter than [the companionship of] one who fulfils his need and attains his desire completely from the beginning of his life to its end. So how could he prefer over it a troubled, sorrowful pleasure in a brief span of life, which is only like the dreams of a sleeper or the shadow that passes away?

The ninth: the contemplation of being seized suddenly and hastened upon. It is that he fears that his term will overtake him, so that Allah takes him unawares, and between him and what he desires of the pleasures of the Hereafter a barrier is placed. How great a regret! How bitter and how hard it is, but none knows it except one who has experienced it. In some of the earlier books it is said: "O you who does not feel safe for himself even for the blink of an eye, and whose joy is not complete on the day of caution, beware, beware."

The tenth: the contemplation of affliction and well-being. Indeed, affliction in reality is nothing but sins and their consequences, and absolute well-being is acts of obedience and their consequences. So the people of affliction are the people of disobedience, even if their bodies are healthy, and the people of well-being are the people of obedience, even if their bodies are sick.

Some scholars said concerning the narration that has been related: "When you see the people of affliction, ask Allah for well-being," that the people of affliction are those afflicted with the disobedience of Allah, turning away from Him and heedlessness of Him. And although this is the greatest affliction, the wording includes all kinds of those afflicted in their bodies and their religion. And Allah knows best.

The eleventh: that the motive and incentives of religion return by gradual struggle against the caller of desire and resistance to it, little by little, until he attains the pleasure of victory. Then his resolve is strengthened, for whoever tastes the pleasure of something, his resolve grows in obtaining it. Habituation to hard works increases the strengths from which those works proceed; for this reason you find the strength of porters and people of hard crafts increasing, unlike the cloth-seller and the tailor and the like. Whoever abandons struggle entirely, the motive of religion weakens in him and the motive of desire grows strong in him, and whenever he accustoms his soul to opposing desire, it overcomes him whenever he wishes.

The twelfth: cutting off the thoughts of the soul. When the passing thoughts come to him, he rejects them and does not shelter them or dwell with them, for they turn into wishes, and they are the capital of the bankrupt. Whenever he dwells with the thoughts, they become wishes, then they grow stronger and become concerns, then they grow stronger and become intentions, then they grow stronger and become a resolve accompanied by the desired act. Repelling the first thought is easier and simpler than repelling the effect of what has been decreed after its occurrence and then avoiding its recurrence.

The thirteenth: cutting off the ties and causes that invite him to comply with desire. The intention is not that he should have no desire, but rather that he direct his desire to what benefits him and employ it in carrying out the will of the Lord, the Exalted, for this repels from him the evil of using it in His disobedience. Indeed, everything of man that he uses for Allah, Allah protects him from the evil of its use for himself and for Satan; and what he does not use for Allah, he uses for his own self and his desire, without fail. Knowledge, if it is not for Allah, is for the self and desire; work, if it is not for Allah, is for showing off and hypocrisy; wealth, if it is not spent in obedience to Allah, is spent in obedience to Satan and desire; rank and status, if he does not use them for Allah, its owner uses them for his desire and his portions; and strength, if he does not use it in the command of Allah, it is used by him in disobeying Him. Whoever accustoms his soul to work for Allah, nothing is harder for him than working for other than Him; and whoever accustoms his soul to work for his desire and his portion, nothing is harder for him than sincerity and working for Allah. This applies to all the chapters of actions. Nothing is harder for one who spends for Allah than spending for other than Him, and likewise the reverse.

The fourteenth: directing thought to the wonders of the signs of Allah, which He has urged His servants to reflect upon, namely His recited signs and His manifest signs. When that takes hold of his heart, it repels from him the whispering of Satan, his conversation, and his waswasa. How great is the loss of one who is able never to cease conversing with the Merciful, His Book, His Messenger, and the Companions, yet turns away from that to conversing with the satans of mankind and jinn. There is no loss after this loss, and Allah is the One sought for help.

The fifteenth: reflection on the world and the swiftness of its passing and the nearness of its end. He does not accept for his soul that he should provision himself from it for the abode of his permanence and eternity with the lowest and least beneficial of it, except one of low resolve, base manliness, and dead heart. For his regret will intensify when he witnesses the reality of what he has provisioned and it becomes clear to him that it does not benefit him. How much more so if leaving off provisioning what benefits him, in favour of a provision by which he is tormented and by which he attains the utmost pain. Rather, if he provisions what benefits him but leaves what is more beneficial than it, that is a regret for him and a loss.

The sixteenth: his exposing himself to the One in whose hand are the hearts, between whose two fingers they are, and in whose hand are the reins of affairs, and to whom every matter returns continually. Perhaps he will encounter the moments of divine breaths (nafahat), as in the well-known narration: "Indeed, for Allah in the days of your time are breaths, so expose yourselves to His breaths, and ask Allah to conceal your faults and secure your frights." Perhaps, through his frequent exposure, he will encounter an hour in which he asks Allah for nothing except that He gives it to him. Whoever is granted the scroll of supplication is granted the answer, for if He did not intend to answer him, He would not have inspired him with supplication, as it has been said:

"Had you not intended to grant what I hope for and seek / from the generosity of your palm, you would not have accustomed me to asking."

Let him not be made to feel lonely by the apparent state, for Allah, glorified is He, deals with His servant in the manner of One for whom there is nothing like Him in His acts, just as there is nothing like Him in His attributes. He has not withheld except to give, nor made him ill except to heal him, nor made him poor except to enrich him, nor caused him to die except to revive him, and He did not expel his two parents from Paradise except to return them to it in the most perfect state, as it has been said: "O Adam, do not be distressed by my words to you and go out from it, for it is for you that I created it, and I will return you to it."

So the Lord, the Exalted, bestows favour upon His servant through his trial, gives to him through his deprivation, and keeps company with him in his sickness. The servant should not feel lonely about any state that distresses him at all, except if it angers Him with him and removes him from Him.

The seventeenth: that the servant knows that within him are two opposing pullers, and his trial lies between the two pullers: one pulling him to the Exalted Companion of the people of 'Illiyyin, and another pulling him down to the lowest of the low. Whenever he yields to the upper puller, he ascends a degree until he reaches the place fitting for him in the highest abode; and whenever he yields to the lower puller, he descends a degree until he reaches his place in Sijjin. Whenever he wishes to know whether he is with the Exalted Companion or the lowest, let him look at where his spirit is in this world, for when it departs the body it will be in the Exalted Companionship to which it was drawn in the world, and it is more deserving of it. A person is with whom he loves, by nature, by reason, and by part; everyone concerned with something is drawn to it and to its people by nature, and every person inclines to what suits him. Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Say: Each acts according to his manner﴾. So the lofty souls are drawn by their essence, their concern, and their deeds upward, and the base souls downward.

The eighteenth: that the servant knows that emptying the place is a condition for the descent of the rain of mercy, and cleansing it of weeds is a condition for the perfection of the crop. Whenever the place is not emptied, the rain of mercy does not encounter a receptive place in which to descend. And if he empties it so that the rain of mercy reaches it, but does not cleanse it of weeds, the crop will not be a complete crop; rather, the weeds may overcome the crop and be in charge. This is like one who prepares his land and readies it to receive the crop, sows its seeds in it, and awaits the descent of rain. When the servant purifies his heart, empties it of the will of evil and its passing thoughts, sows in it the seed of remembrance, reflection, love, and sincerity, and exposes it to the winds of mercy, awaiting the descent of the rain of mercy at its time, then he is worthy of the attainment of the harvest. And just as hope for the descent of rain at its time grows strong, so too hope grows strong for encountering the breaths of the Merciful, glorified is His majesty, in the virtuous times and noble states, especially when resolves are gathered and hearts assist one another and the gathering is great, such as the gathering at 'Arafah, the gathering for prayer for rain, and the gathering of the people of Friday prayer. For the gathering of resolves and breaths are causes that Allah has established, which necessitate the attainment of good and the descent of mercy, just as He established all other causes as necessitating their effects. Indeed, these causes for the attainment of mercy are stronger than sensory causes in attaining their effects. But the servant, through his ignorance, is overcome by the good analogy of the visible over the unseen, and through his injustice he prefers what this one judges and necessitates over what the other judges and necessitates. Had the servant emptied the place, prepared it, and set it right, he would have seen wonders, for the bounty of Allah is not turned back except by the obstacle within the servant; if that obstacle were removed, bounty would hasten to him from every direction. Consider the case of a great river that waters every land it passes over: between it and some thirsty, fertile land there stands a thick dam and barrier, so its owner complains of drought while the river runs right beside his land.

The nineteenth: that the servant knows that Allah, glorified is He, created him for a permanence with no end, for a might with no humiliation in it, for a security with no fear in it, for a sufficiency with no poverty with it, for a pleasure with no pain accompanying it, and for a perfection with no deficiency in it. He tested him in this abode with a permanence that is swiftly followed by extinction, a might that is accompanied by humiliation and followed by humiliation, a security that is accompanied by fear and followed by fear; and likewise sufficiency, pleasure, joy, happiness, and bliss here are mixed with their opposite, for their opposite follows them, and they are swift to vanish. Most people erred in this station, for they sought bliss, permanence, might, dominion, and rank in other than their proper place, and so they missed them in their proper place. Most of them did not attain what they sought from that, and what they did attain is only a little enjoyment, and its vanishing is near, for it swiftly leaves them. The messengers, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them, came only with the call to lasting bliss and great dominion. Whoever answers them attains the most delightful and purest of what is in this world, and his life in it becomes more pleasant than the life of kings and those below them. For asceticism in this world is a present dominion, and Satan envies the believer for it with the greatest envy, so he is most eager that he should not attain it. When the servant has mastery over his desire and his anger, and both submit to him in following the call of religion, then he is truly the king, for the possessor of this kingdom is free. But the king who is led by his desire and anger is a slave to his desire and anger; he is subjugated and owned, in the dress of an owner, led by the reins of desire and anger as a camel is led. The deceived and tricked one fixes his gaze on the apparent kingdom whose form is that of a king while its inside is bondage, and on the desire whose beginning is pleasure and whose end is regret. The insightful and successful one turns his gaze from beginnings to ends and from starting points to outcomes. That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.

The twentieth: that the servant should not be deceived into believing that mere knowledge of what we have mentioned is sufficient for attaining the goal. Rather, he must add to it the exertion of effort in putting it into practice, and the expenditure of all his capacity and strength in it. The key to this is departing from habits, for they are the enemies of perfection and success. No one succeeds who remains forever bound to his habits. He should seek help in departing from habits by fleeing from the places of trial and distancing himself from them as far as he can. The Prophet said: "Whoever hears of the Dajjal, let him keep far away from him." Nothing is a better aid to deliverance from evil than distancing oneself from its causes and places.

Here is a subtle trick of Satan from which none escapes except a skilful person: that he appears to him, in the places of evil, with some measure of good, and calls him to obtain it, and when he draws near to it, he casts him into the net. And Allah knows best.

[Section: The difference between patience and hardness of heart]

The difference between patience (sabr) and hardness (qaswa) is that patience is an acquired disposition which the servant cultivates in himself: it is restraining the soul from anxiety, panic, and complaint, so that it restrains the self from resentment, the tongue from complaint, and the limbs from what should not be done; it is the steadfastness of the heart upon the decrees of destiny and the Law.

As for hardness, it is a dryness in the heart that prevents it from being affected, and a coarseness that prevents it from being moved by calamities; it is not moved because of its coarseness and hardness, not because of its patience and forbearance.

((End of Part Nine))

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 16, verses 126–127 (part 1 of 4):

If it is said: Which of the two kinds of patience is more beloved to Allah: the patience of one who is patient in carrying out His commands, or the patience of one who is patient in refraining from what He has forbidden?

It is said: This is a matter on which people have disagreed. One group said that patience in refraining from transgressions is superior, because it is more difficult and arduous. Acts of righteousness are performed by both the righteous and the wicked, but only the sincere believers (al-siddiqun) are patient in refraining from transgressions.

They said: Also, patience in refraining from what is forbidden is patience in opposing the desires of the soul (hawa al-nafs), and this is the most difficult thing and the most excellent.

They said: Also, abandoning what the souls love is evidence that the one for whose sake it is abandoned is more beloved to him than his own soul and desire. This is unlike performing what the Beloved loves, for that does not necessarily entail this.

They said: Also, manliness (muruwwa) and chivalry (futuwwa) are entirely in this patience.

Imam Ahmad said: "Chivalry is abandoning what you desire for what you fear."

So a servant's manliness and chivalry are in proportion to this patience.

They said: The wonder is not at one who is patient in carrying out commands, for most of them are loved by sound souls because of what they contain of justice, goodness, sincerity and righteousness, and these are beloved to pure and virtuous souls. Rather, the wonder is at one who is patient in refraining from prohibitions, most of which are desired by the souls. Such a person abandons the immediate beloved in this world for the deferred beloved in another abode, while the soul is inclined to love the immediate, so its patience in refraining from it is contrary to its nature.

They said: Also, prohibitions have four incitements that call to them: the human soul (nafs), his devil (shaytan), his desire (hawa), and his worldly life (dunya).

One does not abandon them until one struggles against these four, and that is the most difficult and arduous thing for souls.

They said: Prohibitions belong to the category of the soul's restraint from what it craves and enjoys, and restraint (hamiyya) while the impulse to indulge is present and strong is among the most difficult and arduous things.

They said: Because of this, the approach to what is forbidden is entirely closed, whereas the commandments are only carried out to the extent one is able, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If I command you with something, do of it what you are able; and what I forbid you, avoid it."

This shows that the gate of prohibited things is narrower than the gate of commanded things, and that no allowance is granted for committing any part of them, whereas allowance is granted for neglecting some commanded acts due to incapacity and excuse.

They said: Because of this, most punishments, such as the prescribed penalties (hudud) and others, are for committing prohibited acts, unlike neglecting a command. Allah, glorified is He, did not prescribe a specific penalty for neglecting it. The most important of the commands is prayer, and the scholars have differed over whether there is a prescribed penalty for one who abandons it or not.

This is some of what the first group argued.

(Section)

Another group said: Rather, patience in performing a command is superior and more exalted than patience in abstaining from what is prohibited, because performing the command is more beloved to Allah than abstaining from what is prohibited, and patience in the more beloved of the two matters is superior and higher. This is explained in several ways:

First: Performing the command is sought for its own sake. It is legislated as an end in itself (shar' al-maqasid). The knowledge of Allah, His Oneness, His worship alone, turning to Him in repentance, relying upon Him, sincerely doing deeds for Him, loving Him, being pleased with Him, and standing in His service, is the goal for which creation was created and for which the command was established. This is something sought for itself. The prohibitions were forbidden only because they obstruct this, or distract from it, or cause its perfection to be lost. Therefore their degrees of prohibition are in proportion to how much they obstruct the command, hinder it, and deprive it of its perfection. So the prohibited things are sought for something else, while the commanded thing is sought for itself. Had wine and gambling not barred one from the remembrance of Allah, from prayer, and from the mutual affection and love that Allah placed among His servants, He would not have prohibited them. Likewise, had they not come between the servant and his intellect, by which he knows Allah, worships Him, praises Him, glorifies Him, and prays and prostrates to Him, He would not have prohibited them. Likewise, all that He prohibited, He prohibited only because it obstructs what He loves and is pleased with, and stands between the servant and his perfection.

Second: The commanded acts are connected to the knowledge of Allah, His Oneness, His worship, His remembrance, His thanks, His love, reliance upon Him, and turning to Him in repentance. Their object is the Essence of the Lord, the Exalted, and His Names and Attributes. The object of the prohibitions is the essences of the things that are forbidden. The difference between them is among the greatest differences.

Third: The servant's need and necessity for performing the command is greater than his need to abstain from what is prohibited. He has no need more pressing or more acute than his need to know his Lord, to affirm His Oneness, to devote his deeds sincerely to Him, to single Him out in worship, love and obedience.
